extended by the ``prime'' $-1$: the bilinear lattice gains the directions
$\pi^2=-(\log(-1))^2$ and $i\pi\log p$.

\begin{statusbox}{\statusnew{} --- the independence criterion of
Section~\ref{sec:logproduct}, extended to this larger lattice, covers the multivalued reading
as well, and it remains a consequence of Schanuel's conjecture.  The four exponentials
conjecture masters the multivalued reading wholesale, because the branch logarithms stay
$\Q$-independent: it gives $x\in\Q$, and then the modulus argument forces $x\in\Z$ with all
phases trivial.  The predicted answer is unchanged; only the wall widens.}
\end{statusbox}

\subsection{Complexifying the codomain: the Gaussian version is equivalent}

Since extending the domain is free, the proper place to look for new content is the codomain.

\begin{theorem}[Gaussian equivalence]
\label{va:thm-gaussian}
The statement ``$2^x,3^x\in\Z[i]\Rightarrow x\in\Z$'' is equivalent to
Conjecture~\ref{conj:AE}.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
One direction is trivial since $\Z\subset\Z[i]$.  Conversely assume the conjecture and let
$2^x,3^x\in\Z[i]$ with $x=s+it$.  Taking norms, $N(2^x)=2^{2s}$ and $N(3^x)=3^{2s}$ are
positive integers, which is the real hypothesis at exponent $2s$, so $2s\in\Z$.  Now $3$ is
inert in $\Z[i]$, so a Gaussian integer of norm $3^{2s}$ is a unit times $3^{k}$ with
$9^{k}=3^{2s}$, forcing $s=k\in\Z$: the inert prime upgrades the half-integer ambiguity to
integrality.  Then $2^{2s}=4^{s}$ shows that $2^x$ is divisible only by the ramified prime
$1+i$, so $2^x=u(1+i)^{2s}=2^{s}i^{s}u$.  In both bases the values are $2^{s}$ and $3^{s}$
times fourth roots of unity, the only Gaussian integers of modulus one, so the argument
conditions read $t\log2,\ t\log3\in(\pi/2)\Z$, and irrationality of $\thetaq$ kills $t$ as in
Theorem~\ref{va:thm-complex-real}.
\end{proof}

\begin{statusbox}{\statusnew{} --- a self-contained equivalence whose only inputs are Gaussian
factorization, irrationality of $\thetaq$, and the real conjecture as a hypothesis.  It is a
low-cost Lean target on top of \lean{ComplexSolutions}.}
\end{statusbox}

Two boundary markers make the picture sharp.  Replacing $\Z[i]$ by $\Q(i)$ breaks the argument
at exactly one point: unit-modulus elements of $\Q(i)$ need not be roots of unity, as
$(3+4i)/5$ shows, so the imaginary slice reopens as a genuine unit-circle four-exponentials
instance.  It is integrality up to units, not rationality, that closes the argument direction.
Replacing $\Z[i]$ by the integers of an imaginary quadratic field in which $2$ or $3$
\emph{splits} --- for instance $\Q(\sqrt{-2})$, where $3$ splits and $1+\sqrt{-2}$ has modulus
$\sqrt3$ --- destroys the root-of-unity conclusion, and eliminating $t$ produces relations
mixing $\thetaq\pi$ with logarithms of complex algebraic numbers: the product-of-logarithms
wall again, with more rooms.  These split-prime variants are recorded as open rather than
pursued; they meet the same wall with worse constants.

\subsection{Summary}

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{p{0.34\textwidth}p{0.58\textwidth}}
\toprule
Reading & Status \\
\midrule
Exponent in $\C$, principal branch, values in $\Z$ & reduces to the real integer formulation,
\statuslean \\
Exponent in $\C$, principal branch, values in $\Q$ & reduces to the real rational-output
formulation at paper level; equivalence to integer AE still needs the denominator-support
lemma of Proposition~\ref{va:prop-rational-cost} \\
Values in $\Qbar$, exponent real & two-base: four exponentials; conclusion $\Q$, sharp \\
Values in $\Qbar$, exponent in $\C$ & splits into real and unit-circle slices \\
Three bases, values in $\Qbar$, exponent in $\C$ & solution set exactly $\Q$, \statusknown \\
Multivalued branches & wall widened by $\log(-1)$, \statusnew \\
Values in $\Z[i]$ & unconditionally equivalent, \statusnew \\
Values in $\Q(i)$ or split-prime rings & open \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

In every reading the answer the conjecture predicts is the same.

\section{Hausdorff moments and M\"untz invisibility}
\label{sec:hausdorff-moments}

The minimal transcendence and fractional-normalization inputs are already part of the
accepted corpus.  The new direction is the additive
adjacency of the $\{2,3\}$-smooth numbers and the Hausdorff moment problem it creates.

\subsection{The explicit moment measure}
\label{mom:moments}

For $0<\alpha<1$ define
\[
 d_j=(j+2)^\alpha-(j+1)^\alpha\qquad(j\ge0).
\]
These are the moments of the finite positive measure
\begin{equation}
 d\mu_\alpha(q)=\frac{\alpha}{\Gamma(1-\alpha)}
 (1-q)(-\log q)^{-\alpha-1}\,dq,
 \qquad
 d_j=\int_0^1q^j\,d\mu_\alpha(q).
 \label{mom:eq-hausdorff}
\end{equation}
The same Mellin identity holds for every real exponent $z>-1$.  It follows from the gamma
integral for $t^{\alpha-1}$ and Tonelli after $q=e^{-s}$.  The density is positive on
$(0,1)$, integrable at both endpoints, and has full support.  Consequently
\begin{equation}
 (-1)^k\Delta^kd_j=\int_0^1q^j(1-q)^k\,d\mu_\alpha(q)>0,
 \label{mom:eq-complete-monotone}
\end{equation}
every finite Hankel matrix $(d_{i+j})$ is positive definite, and strict H\"older gives
\[
 d_j^{\,k-i}<d_i^{\,k-j}d_k^{\,j-i}\qquad(0\le i<j<k).
\]
These analytic identities are \statusnew{} paper proofs using classical integration.

The only adjacent positive $\{2,3\}$-smooth pairs are
\[
 (1,2),\quad(2,3),\quad(3,4),\quad(8,9),
\]
by coprimality and Catalan--Mih\u{a}ilescu.  Thus under a hypothetical fractional solution,
with $u=2^\alpha$ and $v=3^\alpha$, the adjacent endpoints force
\begin{equation}
 d_0=u-1,\qquad d_1=v-u,\qquad d_2=u^2-v,\qquad d_7=v^2-u^3
 \label{mom:eq-forced-moments}
\end{equation}
to be rational and positive.  This is a list of the four moments whose rationality is
\emph{forced by adjacent smooth endpoints}; it does not exclude accidental rationality of
other moments.

\subsection{Exact arithmetic defects and finite rational simulation}
\label{mom:defects}

Write $u=P/2^r$ and $v=Q/3^s$ in lowest terms.  The first Hankel defect and three
nonconsecutive log-convexity defects are
\[
 \mathcal H=d_0d_2-d_1^2,\quad
 \mathcal F_{017}=d_0^6d_7-d_1^7,\quad
 \mathcal F_{127}=d_1^5d_7-d_2^6,\quad
 \mathcal F_{027}=d_0^5d_7^2-d_2^7.
\]
They are strictly positive, and their exact reduced denominators are respectively
\begin{equation}
 2^{3r}3^{2s},\qquad 2^{9r}3^{7s},\qquad
 2^{12r}3^{7s},\qquad 2^{14r}3^{7s}.
 \label{mom:eq-defect-denominators}
\end{equation}
Parity and reduction modulo $3$ show that the displayed positive numerators are coprime to
these denominators.  The four common-denominator identities and their local-unit conclusions
are \statuslean{} in \lean{MomentArithmetic}; positivity comes from
\eqref{mom:eq-hausdorff} and remains the paper layer.

Finite positivity data cannot distinguish the special measure.  If rational
$m_0>m_1>m_2>0$ satisfy $m_0m_2>m_1^2$, then
\begin{equation}
 \left(m_0-\frac{m_1^2}{m_2}\right)\delta_0
 +\frac{m_1^2}{m_2}\delta_{m_2/m_1}
 \label{mom:eq-two-atom}
\end{equation}
is a positive rational two-atom measure reproducing $m_0,m_1,m_2$.  This identity is also
\statuslean{} in \lean{MomentArithmetic}.  More generally, a finite family of
rational polynomial observations lying in the interior of the closed moment cone admits a
positive rational finite quadrature: one first passes to the closed cone, uses
$\operatorname{int}C=\operatorname{int}\overline C$, and then perturbs a finite generating
set to rational nodes.  This is a \statusnew{} finite-dimensional paper theorem.

\subsection{All smooth linear observations remain invisible}
\label{mom:muntz}

Put
\[
 \Lambda=\{N-1:N=2^a3^b\ge2\},\qquad
 K_m(q)=\frac{1-q^m}{1-q}.
\]
Unique factorization gives the convergent reciprocal sum
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{m\in\Lambda}\frac1m\le4.
 \label{mom:eq-muntz-sum}
\end{equation}
The full $L^1$ M\"untz theorem on an interval away from zero, followed by Hahn--Banach, now
gives an exact infinite-dimensional no-go.  For every $0<a<b<1$ there is a nonzero bounded
real $g$, supported in $[a,b]$, such that
\begin{equation}
 \int_0^1K_m(q)g(q)\,d\mu_\alpha(q)=0\qquad(m\in\Lambda).
 \label{mom:eq-invisible}
\end{equation}
For sufficiently small $\varepsilon>0$, the distinct positive measures
$(1\pm\varepsilon g)\mu_\alpha$ therefore have every same $\{2,3\}$-smooth linear
observation, agree with $\mu_\alpha$ near both endpoints, and change the $j$th ordinary
moment by only $O(b^j)$.  This is a \statusnew{} theorem conditional only on the classical
M\"untz/Hahn--Banach inputs.  It is a no-go for reconstruction among positive measures; the
perturbations need not belong to the one-parameter family $\{\mu_\beta\}$ and therefore do
not produce another exponent.

\begin{statusbox}{The exact two-atom and denominator arithmetic is \statuslean{} in
\lean{MomentArithmetic}.  The Hausdorff integral,
finite moment-cone quadrature, and M\"untz invisible perturbations are paper/classical
arguments with the scopes stated above.  They prove that positivity and all smooth linear
observations are insufficient, not that the conjecture fails or holds.}
\end{statusbox}

\section{Depth-two rank geometry and rational symmetrization}
\label{sec:rank-geometry}

The restricted matrix-coefficient, formal prime-symbol, and external-rank reductions are
already carried by
\lean{RestrictedMatrixCoefficient}, \lean{FormalPrimeDeterminant}, and the accepted
external-rank modules.  The new layer is a quadratic-rank classification and a
rational symmetric normal form for the multiplicatively dependent branch.

\subsection{Baker excludes quadratic rank at most two}
\label{rankgeom:baker-rank}

Let $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_t$ be $\Q$-independent logarithms of positive algebraic
numbers.  A nonzero rational quadratic form $q$ of rank at most two cannot vanish at these
logarithms.  Over $\Qbar$, such a form factors as $q=L_1L_2$; vanishing would give a
nontrivial algebraic linear relation among the $\lambda_i$, contrary to Baker's homogeneous
linear-independence theorem.  This is a classical Baker consequence; its application to the
two-star tensor is new to this corpus.

In prime-exponent space put $a=\nu(M)$, $b=\nu(N)$ and
\[
 q_{a,b}=e_2b-e_3a\in\operatorname{Sym}^2(V).
\]
Its period specialization is
$\log2\log N-\log3\log M$.  A nonintegral solution makes this zero but does not make the
formal tensor zero, so Baker forces $\operatorname{rank}(q_{a,b})\ge3$.

\subsection{Hyperbolic pullback and the rank-three conic}
\label{rankgeom:hyperbolic}

For independent $e,f$ and arbitrary $a,b$, the universal tensor
$eb-fa$ is the pullback of the hyperbolic form $z_1z_2-z_3z_4$.  If
$r=\dim\operatorname{span}\{e,b,f,a\}$, its rank is four for $r=4$ and at most two for
$r\le2$.  At $r=3$, write the unique relation as
\[
 c_1e+c_2b+c_3f+c_4a=0.
\]
The restricted form has rank three exactly when
\begin{equation}
 c_1c_2-c_3c_4\ne0;
 \label{rankgeom:eq-tangency}
\end{equation}
otherwise its rank is two.  Combining this finite classification with Baker shows that a
hypothetical counterexample has equal multiplicative and quadratic rank, necessarily three
or four.  In rank three the two external prime-exponent vectors lie on one rational ray, and
the determinant relation becomes a nondegenerate split ternary conic.  This is a compression
of the dependent branch, not a nonvanishing theorem for its prime-log point.

The hyperbolic normal identity and exact conic determinant are \statuslean{} in
\lean{RankGeometry}.  Baker's theorem and the passage from the actual two-star tensor
to the rank classification are the paper/classical layer.  An earlier draft wrote the
rank-three and rank-four kernel strata as intersections equal to $\{0\}$; literally those
intersections must be empty, because the zero tensor is not in either stratum.  The unified
formulation uses the corrected nonvanishing statement.

The same conic has a useful scalar factorization.  In the rank-three branch write the
external prime support on a primitive ray as
\[
 M=2^{m_2}3^{m_3}C^r,
 \qquad
 A=2^{a_2}3^{a_3}C^s,
 \qquad C>1,\quad (C,6)=1,
\]
where the displayed exponents are nonnegative and $r+s>0$.  Put
$X=\log2$, $Y=\log3$, and $Z=\log C$.  The determinant relation becomes
\begin{equation}
 -a_2X^2+(m_2-a_3)XY+m_3Y^2+(rY-sX)Z=0.
 \label{rankgeom:eq-external-conic}
\end{equation}
If
\[
 D=a_2r^2-(m_2-a_3)rs-m_3s^2,
\]
then direct elimination in~\eqref{rankgeom:eq-external-conic} gives
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{DXY=(rY-sX)(a_2rX+m_3sY+rsZ).}
 \label{rankgeom:eq-external-ray-factorization}
\end{equation}
The existing conic determinant is $2D$, and Baker's rank-at-most-two exclusion gives
$D\ne0$.  When $r,s>0$, the second factor on the right is positive, so
\begin{equation}
 \operatorname{sgn}D=\operatorname{sgn}(rY-sX),
 \qquad
 |r\thetaq-s|\ge
 \frac{\thetaq}{x(r\thetaq+s)}.
 \label{rankgeom:eq-external-ray-bound}
\end{equation}
The edge cases $r=0$ or $s=0$ follow directly from the same factorization.  This is a
quantitative rational-approximation constraint internal to the dependent branch, not a
contradiction.  The conic determinant is kernel-checked in \lean{RankGeometry};
\eqref{rankgeom:eq-external-ray-factorization} is an elementary paper identity.

The same integer $D$ is also the determinant of the natural M\"obius parametrization; this
identifies two descriptions that otherwise look unrelated.  Put
\begin{equation}
 U=sm_2-ra_2,\qquad V=sm_3-ra_3.
 \label{rankgeom:eq-mobius-uv}
\end{equation}
Eliminating $Z$ from the two output logarithms gives
\begin{equation}
 x=\frac{U+V\thetaq}{s-r\thetaq},\qquad
 D=-rU-sV,\qquad
 \frac{d}{dt}\frac{U+Vt}{s-rt}\bigg|_{t=\thetaq}
 =-\frac{D}{(s-r\thetaq)^2}.
 \label{rankgeom:eq-mobius-determinant}
\end{equation}
Thus the M\"obius map is nonconstant exactly when the ternary conic has rank three.
Elementary height bounds give
\begin{equation}
 1\le|D|\le
 \frac{3\log2\log3}{(\log5)^2}\,x^3
 =0.8819474591\ldots\,x^3.
 \label{rankgeom:eq-mobius-height}
\end{equation}
Here one uses $r\le x\log_5 2$, $s\le x\log_5 3$ and the corresponding
structural-prime bounds.  This is a finite-height certificate, not a contradiction.

There is a particularly clean classification when the cross primes are absent:
\begin{equation}
 3\nmid M,\qquad 2\nmid A,\qquad\text{so}\qquad m_3=a_2=0.
 \label{rankgeom:eq-no-cross-primes}
\end{equation}
The primitive-depth alternative $m_2=0$ or $a_3=0$, together with $D\ne0$, forces
$r,s>0$ and exactly one of
\begin{align}
 &m_2=0,\quad a_3=d>0,\quad
 M=C^r,\quad A=3^dC^s,\quad r\thetaq>s,\quad
 x=\frac{rd\thetaq}{r\thetaq-s},
 \label{rankgeom:eq-no-cross-plus}\\
 &a_3=0,\quad m_2=d>0,\quad
 M=2^dC^r,\quad A=C^s,\quad s>r\thetaq,\quad
 x=\frac{sd}{s-r\thetaq}.
 \label{rankgeom:eq-no-cross-minus}
\end{align}
Both are equivalently summarized by the localized radical equation
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{C^{|r\thetaq-s|}=3^d},\qquad C>1,\quad(C,6)=1,\quad r,s,d\ge1.
 \label{rankgeom:eq-localized-radical}
\end{equation}
It produces a second sharp Four Exponentials square with bases $2,C$ and exponents
$\thetaq,\eta$, where
$\eta=\log_C 3=|r\thetaq-s|/d$: the four values
$2^{\thetaq},2^\eta,C^{\thetaq},C^\eta$ are algebraic, while both base logarithms and both
exponents are rationally independent.  This is another exact $2\times2$ frontier, not an
application of the available Six Exponentials theorem; compare
Section~\ref{sec:fourexp}.

More generally the entire rank-three branch reduces to one explicitly parameterized radical.
Define
\begin{equation}
 \rho_*=
 \frac{a_2+(a_3-m_2)\thetaq-m_3\thetaq^2}{r\thetaq-s},
 \qquad
 x_*=m_2+m_3\thetaq+r\rho_*.
 \label{rankgeom:eq-special-radical-parameters}
\end{equation}
For nonnegative integral data with $(r,s)\ne(0,0)$, $r\thetaq\ne s$, and
$\rho_*,x_*>0$, there is an integer $C>1$, coprime to $6$, satisfying
\[
 2^{x_*}=2^{m_2}3^{m_3}C^r,\qquad
 3^{x_*}=2^{a_2}3^{a_3}C^s
\]
if and only if the single number
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{C_*=2^{\rho_*}}
 \label{rankgeom:eq-one-special-radical}
\end{equation}
is such an integer.  In that case $C=C_*$ uniquely; when the data come from an existing
rank-three solution, its exponent is $x_*$.  This equivalence simply solves the logarithmic
conic for $\log_2C$ and isolates the remaining arithmetic obstruction without claiming to
remove it.

\begin{statusbox}{The conic determinant and its nonvanishing core are already
\statuslean{} in \lean{RankGeometry}.  The M\"obius identification, height estimate,
no-cross classification, localized radical equation, and one-special-radical equivalence are
\statusnew{} paper refinements.  They compress the rank-three branch and expose another
Four Exponentials threshold; they do not prove that the special radical is nonintegral.}
\end{statusbox}

\subsection{A rational symmetric normal form}
\label{rankgeom:symmetrization}

Let $L\in M_2(\R)$ be nonzero and singular, suppose its entries span a three-dimensional
rational vector space, and let its unique rational coefficient relation have matrix
\[
 C=\begin{pmatrix}\gamma&\alpha\\ \delta&\beta\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad \Delta=\gamma\beta-\delta\alpha\ne0.
\]
The explicit right multiplier
\begin{equation}
 Q=\begin{pmatrix}-\delta&\gamma\\-\beta&\alpha\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad \det Q=\Delta,
 \label{rankgeom:eq-symmetrizer}
\end{equation}
makes $LQ$ symmetric.  If $L=r(1,x)$ has rank one, symmetry forces
\[
 LQ=\kappa rr^T.
\]
For a rank-three counterexample, $r=(\log2,\log3)^T$; after changing the global sign,
$\kappa>0$, and the three entries
\[
 \kappa(\log2)^2,\qquad \kappa\log2\log3,\qquad \kappa(\log3)^2
\]
are independent logarithms of positive algebraic numbers in geometric progression.  Thus
there would be a positive algebraic $\eta>1$ for which
\begin{equation}
 \eta,\qquad \eta^{\thetaq},\qquad \eta^{\thetaq^2}
 \quad\text{are algebraic and multiplicatively independent}.
 \label{rankgeom:eq-algebraic-orbit}
\end{equation}
Current transcendence theorems do not exclude this two-step orbit.  The determinant,
right-multiplication symmetry, invertible-multiplier construction, and symmetric outer-product
normal form are \statuslean{} in \lean{RankGeometry}; algebraicity and the application
to the counterexample remain the \statusnew{} paper layer.

\begin{statusbox}{The low-rank exclusion is a classical Baker consequence, and the hyperbolic
pullback and rational symmetrization are new exact
reductions.  The finite matrix identities are kernel-checked in
\lean{RankGeometry}.  The remaining rank-three and rank-four depth-two period
nonvanishing statements are open; neither the conic nor the symmetric orbit proves the
conjecture.}
\end{statusbox}

\section{Unimodular gaps, transported secants, and finite-order barriers}
\label{sec:unimodular-gaps}

The elementary and Four/Six Exponentials reductions are already part of the accepted
material.  The new contribution here is a determinant-distance law for binomial gaps, an associated family of
rational secant brackets, and two precise no-go theorems for finite order data and bounded
entrywise jets.

\subsection{Determinant distance and adjacent gap coprimality}
\label{gapjet:gaps}

Let $A,B\ge2$ be coprime, let $p,q,r,s$ be positive integers, and put
$D=|ps-rq|>0$.  Then
\begin{equation}
 \gcd(B^q-A^p,B^s-A^r)\mid\gcd(A^D-1,B^D-1).
 \label{gapjet:eq-gap-gcd}
\end{equation}
Indeed a common divisor is prime to $AB$; eliminating first $B$ and then $A$ from the two
power congruences gives $A^D\equiv B^D\equiv1$.  When $D=1$ the converse congruence is also
automatic, so the exact identity is
\begin{equation}
 \gcd(B^q-A^p,B^s-A^r)=\gcd(A-1,B-1).
 \label{gapjet:eq-unimodular-gap}
\end{equation}
Without coprimality, the same statement holds primewise away from $AB$.  Consecutive
continued-fraction convergents to $\log_2 3$ have determinant distance one; hence their
signed gaps $3^{q_j}-2^{p_j}$ are pairwise coprime at adjacent indices.  For a hypothetical
output pair $(M,N)=(2^x,3^x)$, the corresponding adjacent output-gap gcd is
$\gcd(M-1,N-1)$ when $M,N$ are coprime, with the same away-from-$MN$ restriction otherwise.
These are \statusnew{} exact paper theorems.  The generic commutative-group collision and
both determinant orientations of the modular implication are \statuslean{} in
\lean{UnimodularGapCollision}; the integer gcd packaging remains the paper layer.

In the canonical odd-core branch the determinant-one ladder also forms an exact radix-shadow
square.  Write $M=2^aw^d$ and $x=a+d\log_2w$, take adjacent convergents $p_n/q_n$ to
$d\log_2w$, put $r_n=aq_n+p_n$, and restrict to the subsequence
$\epsilon_n=q_nd\log_2w-p_n>0$.  Discarding finitely many terms, assume also
$\epsilon_n<\log_3 2$.  Then
$0<\mathcal B_n<2^{p_n}$ and $0<\mathcal C_n<3^{r_n}$ for the synchronized gaps
\[
 \mathcal B_n=w^{dq_n}-2^{p_n},\qquad
 \mathcal C_n=A^{q_n}-3^{r_n}
\]
have the same logarithmic error and satisfy
\begin{align}
 M^{q_n}&=2^{r_n}+2^{aq_n}\mathcal B_n,&
 A^{q_n}&=3^{r_n}+\mathcal C_n,\notag\\
 L(M^{q_n})&=3^{r_n}+3^{aq_n}L(\mathcal B_n),&
 R(A^{q_n})&=2^{r_n}+R(\mathcal C_n).
 \label{gapjet:eq-radix-gap-square}
\end{align}
Consequently the digit defects from Section~\ref{carry:digit-lifts} obey
\begin{equation}
 D_{q_n}=\mathcal C_n-3^{aq_n}L(\mathcal B_n),\qquad
 E_{q_n}=R(\mathcal C_n)-2^{aq_n}\mathcal B_n.
 \label{gapjet:eq-radix-gap-defects}
\end{equation}
The square is exact but not contractive:
$3^{aq_n}L(\mathcal B_n)/\mathcal C_n=O(\epsilon_n^{\log_2 3-1})\to0$ and
$2^{aq_n}\mathcal B_n/R(\mathcal C_n)=O(\epsilon_n^{1-\log_3 2})\to0$.
Thus $D_{q_n}\sim\mathcal C_n$ and $E_{q_n}\sim R(\mathcal C_n)$; digit transfer discards rather than
amplifies the small relative gap.

\subsection{Rational secants and separated denominators}
\label{gapjet:secants}

For positive $p,q$ with $3^q\ne2^p$, define
\[
 Q_{p,q}=\frac{N^q-M^p}{3^q-2^p}.
\]
Under a hypothetical solution $x>1$ this is positive rational and the fundamental theorem
of calculus gives
\begin{equation}
 Q_{p,q}=x\int_0^1\bigl((1-t)2^p+t3^q\bigr)^{x-1}\,dt.
 \label{gapjet:eq-secant-integral}
\end{equation}
Its reduced denominator is exactly
$|3^q-2^p|/\gcd(|3^q-2^p|,|N^q-M^p|)$.  Thus adjacent convergents give coprime reduced
denominators.  After setting
\[
 T_j=\frac{2^{p_j}}{M^{p_j}}Q_{p_j,q_j},\qquad
 \delta_j=q_j\log3-p_j\log2,
\]
one has
\[
 T_j=\Phi_x(\delta_j),\qquad
 \Phi_x(\delta)=\frac{e^{x\delta}-1}{e^\delta-1},\qquad
 T_j-x=\frac{x(x-1)}2\delta_j+O_x(\delta_j^2).
\]
The integral representation of $\Phi_x$ makes it strictly increasing, so the rational
$T_j$ alternate above and below $x$.  Away from primes dividing $M$, consecutive reduced
denominators remain coprime.  This is exact arithmetic separation, not an irrationality
measure: the error is only $O(1/q_{j+1})$ while the rational heights can be exponential in
$p_j$.

Symmetrization gives arbitrary fixed contact order without fixing the height problem.  For a
positive $3$-smooth rational $r\ne1$, define
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal J_x(r)=\frac{r^x-r^{-x}}{r-r^{-1}}.
 \label{gapjet:eq-symmetric-secant}
\end{equation}
Under a hypothetical solution $\mathcal J_x(r)\in\Q$, and
$\mathcal J_x(e^h)=\sinh(xh)/\sinh h$ is an even power series
$x+\sum_{j\ge1}a_j(x)h^{2j}$.  For $m\ge1$ put
\begin{equation}
 c_{m,k}=(-1)^{k-1}\frac{2(m!)^2}{(m-k)!(m+k)!},\qquad1\le k\le m.
 \label{gapjet:eq-richardson-coefficients}
\end{equation}
These are the Lagrange weights at zero for the nodes $1^2,\ldots,m^2$; hence
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{k=1}^mc_{m,k}=1,\qquad
 \sum_{k=1}^mc_{m,k}k^{2j}=0\ (1\le j<m),\qquad
 \sum_{k=1}^mc_{m,k}k^{2m}=(-1)^{m-1}(m!)^2.
 \label{gapjet:eq-richardson-moments}
\end{equation}
The rational extrapolant
\begin{equation}
 R_{m,x}(r)=\sum_{k=1}^mc_{m,k}\mathcal J_x(r^k)
 \label{gapjet:eq-richardson-extrapolant}
\end{equation}
therefore satisfies
\begin{equation}
 R_{m,x}(e^h)=x+(-1)^{m-1}(m!)^2a_m(x)h^{2m}
 +O_{x,m}(h^{2m+2}).
 \label{gapjet:eq-richardson-contact}
\end{equation}
Taking $r=3^q/2^p$ along convergents to $\log_2 3$ produces explicit rational
approximations to $x$ with error $O_{x,m}(q^{-2m})$ for every fixed $m$.  This does not
approach an irrationality-measure contradiction: the unreduced denominators remain
exponential in $p+q$, and increasing $m$ increases their coefficient and product costs.

\subsection{Finite signatures and the entrywise jet ceiling}
\label{gapjet:finite-barriers}

No finite list of strict monomial comparisons identifies the special slope.  For every
finite $F\subset\Z^2\setminus\{0\}$ there are infinitely many coprime multiplicatively
independent pairs $(M,N)$ such that
\[
 \operatorname{sgn}(a\log M+b\log N)
 =\operatorname{sgn}(a\log2+b\log3)\qquad((a,b)\in F).
\]
Choose a large prime $M=P$ and an integer $N$ nearest $P^{\log_2 3}$ but not divisible by
$P$; the log slope lies in the same finite sign chamber.  This rules out only finite strict
order signatures, not congruence, valuation, or uniform infinite information.

There is a complementary determinant ceiling.  For an $R\times R$ integer decoration
matrix $C$, let $\Sigma(C)$ be the set of permutations whose Leibniz products are nonzero
and assume $\Sigma(C)\ne\varnothing$.  Let $\tau_p(C)$ be the minimum $p$-valuation over
$\Sigma(C)$ and put
$T(C)=\prod_pp^{\tau_p(C)}$.  If every nonzero $|c_{ij}|\le B$, then for every integral $E$,
\begin{equation}
 T(C)\mid\det(E\circ C),\qquad \log T(C)\le R\log B.
 \label{gapjet:eq-decoration-budget}
\end{equation}
For Euler or Hasse multipliers of order at most $J$ on exponent scale $L$, this standalone
guaranteed divisor contributes at most $RJ\log L$.  It need not be coprime to, or additive
with, existing determinant divisors.  Therefore only the entrywise/termwise multiplier
contribution is $o(R^2)$ when $J\log L=o(R)$; global confluence, cancellation, or
factorization remains outside the theorem.  The gap, secant, signature, and decoration
results are \statusnew{} paper arguments and do not prove the conjecture.

\begin{statusbox}{The determinant-distance collision core is \statuslean{} in
\lean{UnimodularGapCollision}; the
continued-fraction gcd, radix gap square, transported and symmetric secants, fixed-order
Richardson extrapolants, finite-signature, and entrywise jet packages are paper proofs.
Existing transcendence reductions are cross-referenced, and no fixed-order
jet statement is promoted to a claim about global determinant cancellation.}
\end{statusbox}

\section{Exact orbit heights and Farey entropy}
\label{sec:orbit-height-entropy}

The compact-orbit, recurrence, contact-rigidity, and Four Exponentials inputs are established
earlier.  The new contribution is quantitative: it computes every reduced orbit
height exactly, converts Farey counting into a simultaneous two-coordinate denominator
lower bound, and compares Baker recurrence with a fixed analytic contact order.

\subsection{Exact reduced orbit law}
\label{orbitheight:orbit}

Condition on a nonintegral counterexample and write $x=B+\alpha$ with $0<\alpha<1$.
In lowest terms put
\[
 2^\alpha=\frac{W}{2^r},\qquad 3^\alpha=\frac{Z}{3^s},
 \qquad W>1\text{ odd},\quad 3\nmid Z.
\]
Thus $r+\alpha=\log_2W$ and $s+\alpha=\log_3Z$.  For $k\ge0$ let
$(R_k,S_k)=(2^{\{k\alpha\}},3^{\{k\alpha\}})$, and for a reduced rational $a/b$ set
$H(a/b)=\max(|a|,b)$.  For every $k\ge1$ the exact reduced expressions are
\begin{equation}
 R_k=\frac{W^k}{2^{\lfloor k\log_2W\rfloor}},\qquad
 S_k=\frac{Z^k}{3^{\lfloor k\log_3Z\rfloor}},
 \label{orbitheight:eq-exact-orbit}
\end{equation}
so
\begin{equation}
 H(R_k)=W^k,\quad H(S_k)=Z^k,\qquad
 \frac{W^k}{2}<\den(R_k)<W^k,\quad
 \frac{Z^k}{3}<\den(S_k)<Z^k.
 \label{orbitheight:eq-height-law}
\end{equation}
The floor identity behind this is
$rk+\lfloor k\alpha\rfloor=\lfloor k(r+\alpha)\rfloor$; coprimality makes the displayed
fractions reduced.  Consequently, with $C_0=\max(W,Z)$,
\begin{equation}
 \#\{k\ge0:\max(H(R_k),H(S_k))\le H\}
 =1+\left\lfloor\log_{C_0}H\right\rfloor\qquad(H\ge1).
 \label{orbitheight:eq-exact-count}
\end{equation}
The floor and finite simultaneous-denominator cores are \statuslean{} in
\lean{OrbitHeightEntropy}; the reduced-fraction and height specialization is the
\statusnew{} paper layer.

\subsection{Worst-case Farey-to-orbit distortion}
\label{orbitheight:farey}

Fix a nondegenerate closed interval $I\subset(0,1)$ and let $\mathcal F_I(Q)$ be its
reduced rationals with denominator at most $Q$.  The classical estimate
\[
 \#\mathcal F_I(Q)=\frac{3|I|}{\pi^2}Q^2+O_I(Q\log Q)
\]
combines with~\eqref{orbitheight:eq-height-law} as follows.  If
\[
 \Phi:\Q\cap I\longrightarrow\{(R_k,S_k):k\ge0\}
\]
is injective and $D_2(Q),D_3(Q)$ are the maximum first- and second-coordinate
denominators over $\mathcal F_I(Q)$, then
\begin{equation}
 \liminf_{Q\to\infty}\frac{\log D_2(Q)}{Q^2}
 \ge\frac{3|I|}{\pi^2}\log W,\qquad
 \liminf_{Q\to\infty}\frac{\log D_3(Q)}{Q^2}
 \ge\frac{3|I|}{\pi^2}\log Z.
 \label{orbitheight:eq-farey-entropy}
\end{equation}
Indeed $N$ distinct nonnegative orbit indices include one index at least $N-1$; the
\emph{same} image therefore has denominators exceeding $W^{N-1}/2$ and $Z^{N-1}/3$.
The argument also permits fibers of a fixed integer multiplicity $M\ge1$, dividing the two
constants by $M$.  The finite injective engine is \statuslean{} in
\lean{OrbitHeightEntropy}; the Farey asymptotic and limiting constants are
\statusnew{} paper mathematics.

This is a maximum-envelope theorem: for each large cutoff it forces at least one badly
distorted input, not every input.  It excludes polynomially tame injective, or uniformly
bounded-multiplicity, relabelings of the existing orbit.  It does not exclude an arithmetic
operation that creates new rational graph points.  A denominator-tame thickening with
polynomially many genuinely new points is therefore a research target, not a consequence of
the entropy theorem.

\subsection{Baker recurrence versus fixed contact}
\label{orbitheight:contact}

Let $p_j/q_j$ run through the convergents below $\alpha$, so
$0<\delta_j=q_j\alpha-p_j<q_j^{-1}$.  A two-logarithm Baker estimate~\cite{Baker1975} gives constants
$c,\kappa>0$ with $\delta_j\ge c q_j^{-\kappa}$.  If
$0\ne P\in\Q[X,Y]$, $P(1,1)=0$, and
\[
 \sigma(P)=\ord_{t=0}P(2^t,3^t),
\]
then eventual nonvanishing and Taylor comparison give
\begin{equation}
 c_Pq_j^{-\kappa\sigma(P)}
 \le |P(R_{q_j},S_{q_j})|
 \le C_Pq_j^{-\sigma(P)}.
 \label{orbitheight:eq-contact-window}
\end{equation}
The separate elementary height estimate
$|F(R_k,S_k)|\ge e^{-C_Fk}$ applies when $F\in\Q(X,Y)$ is regular near the compact arc,
$k\ge1$, and $F(R_k,S_k)\ne0$; this corrects the source statement, which fails at $k=0$
for constants of absolute value below one.  The contact-multiplicity core is already stronger in
\lean{RationalContactRigidity}; the new paper contribution here is its two-sided composition
with the Baker return scale.

There is also an exact primitive-height calculation.  Write
\[
 M=2^mM_0,\quad 2\nmid M_0,
 \qquad A=3^aA_0,\quad 3\nmid A_0,
\]
and let $r_j/s_j\to x$ be convergents with
$\varepsilon_j=r_j-s_jx$.  For
\[
 u_j=\frac{2^{r_j}}{M^{s_j}}=2^{\varepsilon_j},\qquad
 v_j=\frac{3^{r_j}}{A^{s_j}}=3^{\varepsilon_j},
\]
one has, for all sufficiently large $j$,
\begin{equation}
 h(1:u_j:v_j)
 =s_j\log\operatorname{lcm}(M_0,A_0)
  +\max\{0,\varepsilon_j\log2,\varepsilon_j\log3\}.
 \label{orbitheight:eq-projective-secant-height}
\end{equation}
The coefficient $\log\operatorname{lcm}(M_0,A_0)$ is positive for a nonintegral
candidate.  Corvaja--Zannier's rational-function height theorem
\cite{CorvajaZannier2005} then gives
\begin{equation}
 h\!\left(\frac{u_j-1}{v_j-1}\right)
 =s_j\log\operatorname{lcm}(M_0,A_0)+o(s_j),
 \qquad
 \frac{u_j-1}{v_j-1}\longrightarrow\log_3 2.
 \label{orbitheight:eq-secant-height-zero}
\end{equation}
The analytic error is only polynomial in $s_j$, so its exponent relative to the reduced
height tends to zero.  More generally, every fixed nonconstant rational observable outside
the exceptional torus cosets has height $\gg s_j$.  Fixed Richardson order or fixed rational
contact therefore cannot repair the exponential height loss; a successful transfer must
have growing complexity or output-specific cancellation.
For the cross-multiplied residuals
\[
 X_j=A^{s_j}|2^{r_j}-M^{s_j}|,\qquad
 Y_j=M^{s_j}|3^{r_j}-A^{s_j}|,
\]
the same calculation gives
\begin{equation}
 \log\gcd(X_j,Y_j)
 =\bigl(m\log2+a\log3+\log\gcd(M_0,A_0)\bigr)s_j+o(s_j).
 \label{orbitheight:eq-cross-residual-gcd}
\end{equation}
The part supported away from the fixed primes dividing $6MA$ is only $\exp(o(s_j))$ by
Corvaja--Zannier.  Hence every linear common-divisor contribution is structural, not a
reservoir of new auxiliary primes.

More abstractly, if nonzero rational certificates satisfy
\[
 \den(\Xi_N)\le e^{A_NN},\qquad |\Xi_N|\le C_NN^{-d_N},
\]
with $A_N,d_N\ge0$ and $C_N>0$, the elementary denominator lower bound can contradict the
analytic estimate only if
\begin{equation}
 d_N\log N>A_NN+\log C_N.
 \label{orbitheight:eq-jet-budget}
\end{equation}
Here ``subexponential'' means $\log C_N=o(N)$.  This is a necessary scale benchmark, not a
construction and not a proof of the conjecture.

\begin{statusbox}{The exact floor identities and finite worst-case entropy mechanism are
\statuslean{} in \lean{OrbitHeightEntropy}.
The exact rational heights, Farey limits, and Baker--contact comparison are \statusnew{}
paper results.  The entropy theorem concerns relabelings of the existing cyclic orbit; a
genuine arithmetic thickening and every closing jet construction remain open.}
\end{statusbox}

\section{Projective Pad\'e defect and rational-transfer no-go}
\label{sec:projective-pade}

This section tests the weight-two polylogarithmic criterion of
Kawashima~\cite{Kawashima2026} against the logarithm determinant.  Its tensor-rank
reduction is subsumed by the stronger rank geometry in Section~\ref{sec:rank-geometry}; the
separate directed-rounding computation is not used here.  The new contribution is an optimized,
representation-independent height defect and the no-go theorem it forces for rational
polylogarithm points.

\subsection{The projective defect bound}
\label{pade:projective}

For $m\ge1$ put $D_m=(m+1)^2-1$ and
\[
 C_m=D_m\log2+3\log(m+1)+2+2D_m.
\]
Let $K$ be a number field, $v$ a place, let
$\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_m\in K^\times$ be pairwise distinct, and suppose
$\beta\in K$ satisfies
$|\beta|_v>H_v(\boldsymbol\alpha):=\max(1,\max_i|\alpha_i|_v)$.  Set
$z_i=\alpha_i/\beta$ and write
\[
 a_v(\mathbf z)=-\log\max_i|z_i|_v,\qquad
 \overline h(\mathbf z)=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m h(z_i).
\]
Kawashima's weight-two defect $\mathcal V_v(\boldsymbol\alpha,\beta)$ obeys the exact
projective upper bound
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal V_v(\boldsymbol\alpha,\beta)
 \le (D_m+1)a_v(\mathbf z)-D_m\overline h(\mathbf z)-C_m.
 \label{pade:eq-projective-defect}
\end{equation}
The proof writes $t=h_v(\beta)$ and optimizes
\[
 (D_m+1)t-(D_m+1)\max(0,t-a_v)-D_m\max(t,\overline h)-C_m.
\]
Since $a_v\le\overline h$, the maximum is attained throughout
$a_v\le t\le\overline h$ and equals the right side of
\eqref{pade:eq-projective-defect}.  This piecewise optimization and its abstract height-budget
wrapper are \statuslean{} in \lean{ProjectiveDefect}; the number-field height
specialization and Kawashima's theorem are respectively \statusnew{} and \statusknown{}.

If the defect is positive, then necessarily
\begin{equation}
 a_v>C_m,\qquad
 \frac{a_v}{\overline h}>\frac{D_m}{D_m+1}
 =1-\frac1{(m+1)^2},\qquad
 \overline h<\left(1+\frac1{D_m}\right)a_v.
 \label{pade:eq-efficiency}
\end{equation}
These implications are also \statuslean{} in \lean{ProjectiveDefect}.  Thus mere
archimedean proximity to one is insufficient: the local depth must consume almost all of the
global height.  Direct points $1-1/q$, high-root splittings, and ordinary unit-fraction
telescoping all fail this necessary condition.  A common integral rescaling is strictly
harmful, decreasing the affine defect by $2D_m\log t$.

\subsection{No rational transfer of the prime direction}
\label{pade:rational-transfer}

Let distinct $z_1,\ldots,z_m\in\Q\cap(0,1)$ admit a positive-defect specialization at the
real place, and put $\ell_i=-\log(1-z_i)$.  Then
\begin{equation}
 \log2\notin\operatorname{span}_{\Q}\{\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_m\}.
 \label{pade:eq-no-transfer}
\end{equation}
The same proof applies to a fixed $q\in\Q_{>0}\setminus\{1\}$ with a changed constant.
Indeed~\eqref{pade:eq-efficiency} makes every $\ell_i=O(e^{-a_v})$ while bounding all prime
valuations of $(1-z_i)^{-1}$ by $O(ma_v)$.  If the fixed prime direction lay in their
rational span, Cramer's rule and Hadamard's inequality would supply integer coefficients of
size polynomial in $a_v$; exponentiation would then force the nonzero constant $\log2$ below
an exponentially decaying bound.  The final elementary comparison is uniform in $m$ (with
the logarithm taken of the ratio of that bound to $\log2$ and with the endpoint derivative
checked explicitly).  This is a \statusnew{} paper theorem.

Consequently a positive-defect rational tuple cannot reproduce the counterexample's formal
four-log tensor.  The range of that tensor contains the prime directions by
Section~\ref{sec:rank-geometry}, whereas every tensor built from these rational logarithms has
range inside their forbidden valuation span.  This rules out the factor-by-factor rational
$\operatorname{Li}_1$ transfer; it does not rule out algebraic points, varying fields, or a
genuinely mixed-denominator determinant construction.

For a fixed number field $K$, place $v$, finitely generated
$\Gamma<K^\times$, and fixed cardinality $m$, the effective approximation theorem of
Calegari--Dimitrov--Tang~\cite{CDTHolonomy} further implies that only finitely many tuples
$z_i=1-\gamma_i$, $\gamma_i\in\Gamma$, can have positive defect, with effective height
bounds.  The fixed-$m$ qualification is essential; this is not uniform over constructions
with $m\to\infty$.

Finally, let $p_n/q_n$ be the continued-fraction convergents to $\log_2 3$ and choose
$\varepsilon_n\in\{\pm1\}$ so that the units
$r_n=(2^{p_n}3^{-q_n})^{\varepsilon_n}>1$; then $r_n\to1$ and
\[
 \frac{-\log(1-r_n^{-1})}{h(1-r_n^{-1})}\longrightarrow0,
\]
and the output units have the same low-efficiency behavior.  The present Pad\'e criterion
requires efficiency tending to one.  This identifies an arithmetic-efficiency gap, not a
closing theorem.  A proposed cross-row, mixed-denominator cancellation remains only a
schematic research target because its exceptional ``zero coefficient after rational
changes'' alternative has not yet been defined precisely.

\begin{statusbox}{The finite projective optimization and efficiency implications are
\statuslean{} in \lean{ProjectiveDefect}; the
number-field specialization, rational-transfer no-go, and fixed-cardinality group finiteness
are \statusnew{} paper results using the cited external theorems.  No mixed-denominator
construction or proof of the conjecture is claimed.}
\end{statusbox}

\section{Carry languages and fixed-target entropy}
\label{sec:carry-languages}

The logarithmic cone, one-orbit equivalence, one/two/three-base threshold, $3$-smooth lattice
count, and residual compact orbit are already part of the accepted corpus.  The distinct
contribution here is additive: a hypothetical
counterexample forces a distinguished-descendant carry language whose words give many
equal-arity representations of one fixed target.  Character balancing explains why these
families lie in algebraic parts rather than contradicting functional transcendence.

\subsection{Carry paths and finite alphabets}
\label{carry:carry-path}

Let $U,V\ge2$ be multiplicatively independent integers and write
$e_{a,b}=U^aV^b$.  A step decreasing the first exponent replaces one distinguished copy by
$U$ copies, freezes $U-1$, and continues with the remaining copy; the second-coordinate
step does the same with $V$.  A monotone word with $r$ first steps and $s$ second steps
therefore yields a multiset representation
\begin{equation}
 U^rV^s=\sum_{j=1}^{K_{r,s}} e_{a_j,b_j},\qquad
 K_{r,s}=1+r(U-1)+s(V-1).
 \label{carry:eq-path-representation}
\end{equation}
The frozen terms telescope to the initial monomial.  At every intermediate total degree the
multiset records the unique visited vertex; multiplicative independence then reconstructs
the word.  Hence there are at least
\begin{equation}
 \binom{r+s}{r}
 \label{carry:eq-binomial-fiber}
\end{equation}
distinct representations of the fixed target.  Under a hypothetical counterexample this
applies to $(U,V)=(M,N)=(2^x,3^x)$ and every term is itself
$(2^a3^b)^x$.

The construction extends to a finite alphabet of distinct moves
$v_i=(\alpha_i,\beta_i)\in\mathbb N_0^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}$.  Put
\[
 D_i=U^{\alpha_i}V^{\beta_i},\qquad
 (r,s)=\sum_i n_iv_i,\qquad
 K=1+\sum_i n_i(D_i-1).
\]
Words with the same symbol counts then give at least
\begin{equation}
 \binom{\sum_i n_i}{n_1,\ldots,n_m}
 \label{carry:eq-multinomial-fiber}
\end{equation}
distinct $K$-term representations of $U^rV^s$.  The exact telescoping sum, term count,
strict suffix-degree descent, and reconstruction from the endpoint and ordered suffix list
are \statuslean{} in \lean{CarryPath}.  Recovering the word from the unordered
frozen multiset and the multinomial enumeration remain the \statusnew{} paper layer.

The two primitive counterexample carries $(2t)^x=Mt^x$ and $(3t)^x=Nt^x$ are also exactly
character-balanced.  More generally every finite sequence of such rewrites groups into
independently vanishing character classes.  Thus their positive-dimensional families are
compatible with, rather than forbidden by, the usual functional-transcendence
decomposition.

\subsection{Exact carry-language pressure}
\label{carry:pressure}

For a fixed finite alphabet $\mathcal S$ of at least two $3$-smooth integers
$d_i=2^{\alpha_i}3^{\beta_i}>1$, let
$D_i=d_i^x$ under the hypothetical solution.  Entropy maximization gives two exact
\emph{carry-language} rates.  They are the unique positive roots
\begin{equation}
 \sum_i d_i^{-\delta_{\mathcal S}}=1,\qquad
 \sum_i e^{-\tau_{\mathcal S}(D_i-1)}=1.
 \label{carry:eq-finite-pressure}
\end{equation}
For symbol proportions $\pi_i$, relative entropy proves
\[
 \sup_\pi\frac{H(\pi)}{\sum_i\pi_i\log d_i}=\delta_{\mathcal S},\qquad
 \sup_\pi\frac{H(\pi)}{\sum_i\pi_i(D_i-1)}=\tau_{\mathcal S}.
\]
The alphabet $\{2,3,6\}$ already gives ambient exponent one.  Exhausting all nonunit
$3$-smooth letters gives
\begin{equation}
 (1-2^{-\delta_*})(1-3^{-\delta_*})=\frac12,\qquad
 \delta_*=1.4352790836694176\ldots .
 \label{carry:eq-delta-star}
\end{equation}
This is an exact supremum over the finite-alphabet carry construction, not over all additive
representations.

There is also an unrestricted word pressure.  Let $\tau_x>0$ be the unique solution of
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{(a,b)\in\Nzero^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}}
 e^{-\tau_x(M^aN^b-1)}=1,
 \qquad g=\gcd(M-1,N-1).
 \label{carry:eq-global-pressure}
\end{equation}
For every sufficiently large positive multiple $n$ of $g$, some endpoint $(r_n,s_n)$ with
$r_n+s_n\le n$ receives
\begin{equation}
 \gg_x\frac{e^{\tau_x n}}{n^2}
 \label{carry:eq-fixed-target-fiber}
\end{equation}
distinct carry-language representations of the fixed target $M^{r_n}N^{s_n}$ as a sum of
$n+1$ values $a^x$, all with $a\le3^n$.  The word generating series is
\[
 \frac1{1-\Phi_x(z)},\qquad
 \Phi_x(z)=\sum_{(a,b)\ne(0,0)}z^{M^aN^b-1}.
\]
After factoring the period $g$, its unique dominant positive pole gives
$[z^n](1-\Phi_x)^{-1}\asymp_x e^{\tau_xn}$ along $g\mid n$; pigeonholing among
$O(n^2)$ endpoints yields~\eqref{carry:eq-fixed-target-fiber}.  The matching upper rate is
only for fibers generated by this unrestricted carry language, not for the full additive
representation fiber.

These are \statusnew{} exact paper theorems.  They do not conflict with Harrison's
fixed-arity and fixed-target bounds~\cite{Harrison2026}: here the arity grows linearly with
the logarithm of the input cutoff.  A closing
theorem would need uniform fixed-target bounds through that growing-arity range, strong
enough to beat $e^{\tau_xn}$; no such estimate is known.  Compact-orbit and point-counting
reformulations do not supply it.

\subsection{Multiplicative floor-carry rectangles}
\label{carry:floor-rectangles}

There is a second, genuinely different carry language on the multiplicative orbit itself.
For integers $a,b\ge2$, put
\[
 T_a(t)=\{at\},\qquad c_a(t)=\lfloor at\rfloor\qquad(0\le t<1).
\]
Then $T_aT_b=T_bT_a$ and the two carry decompositions of $ab,t$ give
\begin{equation}
 b\,c_a(t)+c_b(T_a t)=a\,c_b(t)+c_a(T_b t).
 \label{carry:eq-floor-plaquette}
\end{equation}
On an $R\times S$ rectangle, the potentials
$P_{ij}(t)=\lfloor a^ib^jt\rfloor$ therefore give horizontal digits
$h_{ij}=P_{i+1,j}-aP_{ij}\in\{0,\ldots,a-1\}$, vertical digits
$v_{ij}=P_{i,j+1}-bP_{ij}\in\{0,\ldots,b-1\}$, and the local law
\[
 b h_{ij}+v_{i+1,j}=a v_{ij}+h_{i,j+1}.
\]
Conversely, after fixing $P_{00}=0$, the bounded edge labels and these plaquette laws
reconstruct the potentials path-independently.  If $Q=a^Rb^S$, the half-open cylinders
$[k/Q,(k+1)/Q)$ give an exact bijection
\begin{equation}
 \{0,\ldots,Q-1\}\ \longleftrightarrow\
 \{\text{compatible $R\times S$ floor-carry rectangles}\};
 \label{carry:eq-floor-rectangle-count}
\end{equation}
in the cylinder indexed by $k$ one has
$P_{ij}=\lfloor k/(a^{R-i}b^{S-j})\rfloor$.  Thus there are exactly $a^Rb^S$
rectangles, an aggregate fraction $(ab)^{-RS}$ of all unrestricted edge labelings.
The four digit bounds and the local identity~\eqref{carry:eq-floor-plaquette} are
\statuslean{} in \lean{MixedRadixCarryFinite}; the finite reconstruction and count are a
\statusnew{} paper argument.

Closed inverse-limit cylinders require the usual radix-endpoint convention.  A nonsmooth
point has one field, while every rational in $(0,1)$ whose reduced denominator divides
some $a^Rb^S$ has both the floor and left-limit fields.  In particular $t=1/2$ already has
two distinct compatible $(2,3)$ fields.  No uniqueness assertion at those endpoints is
used below.

For multiplicatively independent $a,b$, the Furstenberg--Boshernitzan density theorem
implies that every compatible finite rectangle occurs arbitrarily far out in the orbit of
every irrational $t$~\cite{Boshernitzan1994}.  In particular, for $Q=2^R3^S$,
\begin{equation}
 \{\lfloor2^r3^s t\rfloor\bmod Q:r\ge R, s\ge S\}=\mathbb Z/Q\mathbb Z.
 \label{carry:eq-complete-smooth-residues}
\end{equation}
This rules out arguments based only on a forbidden finite floor-carry word.  Frequencies,
first-occurrence scales, heights, and arithmetic labels are not universal and remain
available.

For a hypothetical nonintegral exponent $x$, a smooth anchor $q=2^r3^s$ with
$\nu=\lfloor qx\rfloor$ and $t=\{qx\}$ satisfies
\[
 \lfloor2^i3^jqx\rfloor=2^i3^j\nu+\lfloor2^i3^jt\rfloor.
\]
An all-zero $R\times S$ block, equivalently $0<t<1/Q$, therefore synchronizes both
denominator-depth residues modulo $Q$ and gives paired leading gaps
\[
 M^q=2^\nu+\Delta_2,\qquad 0<\Delta_2<2^{\nu-G_2(Q)},\qquad
 A^q=3^\nu+\Delta_3,\quad 0<\Delta_3<3^{\nu-G_3(Q)},
\]
where
$G_b(Q)=\max\{0,\lfloor-\log_b(b^{1/Q}-1)\rfloor\}=\log_bQ+O_b(1)$.
This is stronger than either one-base leading-gap statement because the smooth index and
leading exponent are shared.

The quantitative wall can be stated by the one-sided hitting time
\[
 H_x(Q)=\min\{2^r3^s:r,s\in\Nzero,\ 0<\{2^r3^sx\}<1/Q\}.
\]
Baker's two-logarithm estimate gives $H_x(Q)\gg_x Q^{\eta_x}$ for a counterexample.
Combining its polynomial Diophantine consequence with the effective coprime-base orbit
theorem of Bourgain--Lindenstrauss--Michel--Venkatesh and its explicit refinement by
Gayfulin--Moshchevitin gives, for every $\varepsilon>0$,
\begin{equation}
 Q^{\eta_x}\ll_x H_x(Q)
 \le \exp\!\exp\!\exp\bigl(C_{x,\varepsilon}Q^{8+\varepsilon}\bigr)
 \label{carry:eq-hitting-corridor}
\end{equation}
for large $Q$~\cite{Baker1975,BLMV2009,GayfulinMoshchevitin2023}.
The parameter map uses the coprime bases $2,3$ and the polynomial Diophantine estimate;
it is not a uniform statement for arbitrary bases.  Any bound
$H_x(Q)=Q^{o(1)}$ along an unbounded sequence would contradict the Baker lower bound and
settle the conjecture, but finite-language universality alone gives no such acceleration.

\subsection{Base-change digit lifts and integral carry defects}
\label{carry:digit-lifts}

Write $m=\sum\varepsilon_j2^j$ and $n=\sum d_j3^j$, and evaluate the same digit strings in
the other base:
\[
 L(m)=\sum\varepsilon_j3^j,\qquad R(n)=\sum d_j2^j.
\]
With $\theta=\log_2 3$ and $\rho=\theta^{-1}$, elementary carry normalization gives
\begin{equation}
 L(m)\le m^\theta,\qquad n^\rho\le R(n),\qquad
 R(L(m))=m,\qquad L(R(n))\ge n.
 \label{carry:eq-digit-lift-orders}
\end{equation}
Equality in the first two inequalities occurs only at zero and at a pure power of the
source base.  If $m=2^B+r$ with $0<r<2^B$, then the sharper bound
$m^\theta-L(m)\ge(3/2)^Br$ holds.  The exact valuation transfer is
\[
 v_3(L(m))=v_2(m),\qquad v_2(R(n))\ge v_3(n),
\]
with equality in the second formula when the least nonzero ternary digit is one.
More sharply, for distinct $m,n$,
\begin{equation}
 v_3(L(m)-L(n))=v_2(m-n).
 \label{carry:eq-radix-valuation-index}
\end{equation}
Thus $L$ extends from $\mathbb Z_2$ to the closed $\{0,1\}$-digit subset of
$\mathbb Z_3$ as a homeomorphism preserving the first-differing-digit index.  It is not an
isometry for the standard $p$-adic metrics: the two distances are respectively $2^{-r}$ and
$3^{-r}$.  The finite congruence form of~\eqref{carry:eq-radix-valuation-index} is
\statuslean{} in \lean{RadixShadow}.

All addition and multiplication formulas are instances of one normalization identity.  If
a finite coefficient string $r$ is normalized in base $b$, and $q$ records the elementary
carry counts, then evaluation in another base $c$ satisfies
\begin{equation}
 \operatorname{ev}_c(\operatorname{norm}_b r)
 =\operatorname{ev}_c(r)+(c-b)\operatorname{ev}_c(q).
 \label{carry:eq-generic-normalization}
\end{equation}
This gives the sign of every forward or reverse carry without conflating positional radix
carries with the exponent-rewrite paths of Section~\ref{carry:carry-path}.

Multiplication has a signed carry expansion:
\begin{equation}
 L(ab)-L(a)L(b)=\sum_j\kappa_j(a,b)3^j\ge0,\qquad
 R(a)R(b)-R(ab)=\sum_j\lambda_j(a,b)2^j\ge0,
 \label{carry:eq-digit-multiplication}
\end{equation}
where the coefficients count elementary base-$2$ and base-$3$ carries.  For a hypothetical
nonintegral solution define
\[
 D_n=A^n-L(M^n),\qquad E_n=R(A^n)-M^n.
\]
Both are positive integers; at genuine integral exponents they vanish, so nonintegrality is
essential.  They have the same exponential rates as the outputs, but their exact carry
recurrences retain additional combinatorics:
\begin{align}
 L(M^{m+n})-L(M^m)L(M^n)
 &=A^mD_n+A^nD_m-D_mD_n-D_{m+n},\\
 R(A^m)R(A^n)-R(A^{m+n})
 &=M^mE_n+M^nE_m+E_mE_n-E_{m+n}.
 \label{carry:eq-digit-defect-recurrence}
\end{align}
When $t_n=\{nx\}<\rho$, the exact tail bounds further give
$D_n/A^n\asymp t_n$ and $E_n/M^n\asymp t_n^\rho$ on shrinking targets.  The signs,
valuation transfer, and recurrences are exact paper-level constraints, but their natural
heights grow with the outputs and currently yield no contradiction.

The forward defect has an exact mantissa gauge.  For the terminating binary fraction
$\xi_n=2^{t_n}-1$, define its Cantor reevaluation
$\mathcal C(\sum_{j\ge1}\varepsilon_j2^{-j})=\sum_{j\ge1}\varepsilon_j3^{-j}$.
Then
\begin{equation}
 \frac{L(M^n)}{A^n}=3^{-t_n}\bigl(1+\mathcal C(\xi_n)\bigr),
 \qquad
 \frac{t_n}{3}\le\frac{D_n}{A^n}\le(\log3)t_n.
 \label{carry:eq-mantissa-gauge}
\end{equation}
This couples the already-known Sturmian phase to a positional carry observable without
repeating its density or natural-boundary theory.

There is also an exact first collision.  If $m=2^au$ with $u>1$ odd, then
\begin{equation}
 v_3\bigl(L(m^2)-L(m)^2\bigr)=2a+v_2(u-1),\qquad
 \frac{L(m^2)-L(m)^2}{3^{2a+v_2(u-1)}}\equiv1\pmod3.
 \label{carry:eq-first-square-collision}
\end{equation}
Indeed the two lowest set bits of $m$ create the first raw square coefficient $2$, and no
earlier carry is possible.  Writing $M=2^aU$ therefore gives
\[
 v_3\bigl(L(M^{2n})-L(M^n)^2\bigr)=2an+v_2(U^n-1)
\]
for the non-power case $U>1$.  This supplies a precise structural-prime divisor of the
normalization carry, but no matching archimedean upper bound is known.

The individual increments of the two radix shadows are especially simple:
\begin{align}
 L(n)-L(n-1)&=\frac{3^{v_2(n)}+1}{2},&
 R(n)-R(n-1)&=2-2^{v_3(n)}.
 \label{carry:eq-radix-increments}
\end{align}
Hence
\begin{equation}
 L(N)=\frac N2+\frac12\sum_{n\le N}3^{v_2(n)},
 \qquad
 R(N)=2N-\sum_{n\le N}2^{v_3(n)}.
 \label{carry:eq-radix-summatory}
\end{equation}
For the defects above, put $C_n=L(M^n)=A^n-D_n$ and
$K_n=L(R(A^n))-A^n$.  Telescoping over the special endpoint intervals gives
\begin{align}
 E_n&=2D_n-\sum_{C_n<j\le A^n}2^{v_3(j)},\notag\\
 D_n+K_n&=\frac12\left(E_n+
   \sum_{M^n<j\le M^n+E_n}3^{v_2(j)}\right).
 \label{carry:eq-defect-intervals}
\end{align}
In particular $0<E_n\le D_n$ and $E_n\le R(D_n)\le2D_n^{\log_3 2}$.  This converts
the archimedean defect into an exact excess of valuation weights on consecutive intervals;
average-order estimates alone do not control their arithmetic endpoints.

There is also a rigid most-significant-digit description.  Write
\begin{equation}
 M^n=\sum_j\varepsilon_{n,j}2^j,\qquad
 A^n=\sum_j\delta_{n,j}3^j,\qquad
 P_n(Z)=\sum_j(\delta_{n,j}-\varepsilon_{n,j})Z^j.
 \label{carry:eq-digit-difference-polynomial}
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{equation}
 P_n(3)=D_n,\qquad P_n(2)=E_n.
 \label{carry:eq-two-word-evaluations}
\end{equation}
Its leading coefficient is $1$ or $2$.  More generally, if
$P(Z)=\sum_{i=0}^Jc_iZ^i$ has $c_i\in\{-1,0,1,2\}$, positive leading coefficient,
and $E=P(2)>0$, then
\begin{align}
 c_J=1&\Longrightarrow E=1+\sum_{i<J}(c_i+1)2^i,\notag\\
 c_J=2&\Longrightarrow E=2^J+1+\sum_{i<J}(c_i+1)2^i.
 \label{carry:eq-borrow-expansion}
\end{align}
Thus $E<2^s$ with $s\le J$ forces $c_J=1$ and
$c_i=-1$ for $s\le i<J$.  For $P_n$, every such position has the digit pair
$(\delta_{n,i},\varepsilon_{n,i})=(0,1)$.  This finite shifted-evaluation borrow step is
\statuslean{} in \lean{BorrowBlockCore}.  The ensuing paper argument converts an abnormally
small $E_n$ into
\begin{equation}
 M^n\equiv-u\pmod{2^J},\qquad A^n\equiv v\pmod{3^J},\qquad
 1\le u\le2^s,\qquad0\le v<3^s.
 \label{carry:eq-borrow-congruences}
\end{equation}

The common leading word has an explicit length.  Put
$\ell_n=\lfloor nx\rfloor$ and $u_n=\{nx\}$.  The leading binary and ternary positions of
$M^n$ and $A^n$ are both $\ell_n$.  For $0<u<\log_3 2$, compare the fractional digits of
$2^u$ in base $2$ and of $3^u$ in base $3$.  Their common prefix is exactly a leading $1$
followed by zeros; at the first mismatch the ternary digit is larger.  Indeed
\begin{equation}
 (1+2^{-t})^{\log_2 3}>1+2\,3^{-t}\qquad(t\ge1),
 \label{carry:eq-cylinder-separation}
\end{equation}
so a binary $1$ at the first nonzero fractional position forces the ternary digit to be $2$.
If
\begin{equation}
 t(u)=\left\lceil\log_3\frac1{3^u-1}\right\rceil,
 \label{carry:eq-prefix-depth}
\end{equation}
then $P_n$ has degree $\ell_n-t(u_n)$ when $u_n<\log_3 2$, and degree $\ell_n$ otherwise.
Two-logarithm bounds give $t(u_n)=O_M(\log n)$, hence
\begin{equation}
 D_n\gg_{M,A}\frac{A^n}{n^C}
 \label{carry:eq-prefix-defect-lower}
\end{equation}
for an effective $C$.  The direct digit defect is therefore exponentially large even when
long borrowing makes the return defect small.  Finally, normalizing the ternary digits of
$A^n$ in base $2$ with carry bits $c_j$ gives the exact mask
\begin{equation}
 K_n=\sum_{j\ge0}c_j3^j.
 \label{carry:eq-return-carry-mask}
\end{equation}
These identities expose a rigid cross-base word, but its two evaluations remain at
incompatible scales and provide no contraction.

\begin{statusbox}{The bounded carry-word sum, length, suffix-degree, and ordered reconstruction
identities are \statuslean{} in
\lean{CarryPath}; the mixed-radix local floor-carry identity is \statuslean{} in
\lean{MixedRadixCarryFinite}; the finite radix-shadow congruence and valuation-index
bridge are \statuslean{} in \lean{RadixShadow}; and finite borrow-block rigidity is
\statuslean{} in \lean{BorrowBlockCore}.  Multiset injectivity, multinomial fibers,
character balancing, the finite and unrestricted pressure laws, finite floor-carry
reconstruction, smooth-language consequences, hitting corridor, normalization carries,
mantissa gauge, square-collision formula, interval-valuation identities, prefix separation,
and carry-mask formula are \statusnew{} paper results.  Every
``exact rate'' is explicitly scoped to the carry-language construction; no contradiction
with fixed-arity theorems or proof of Alaoglu--Erd\H{o}s is claimed.}
\end{statusbox}

\section{Critical entire interpolation, canonical products, and exact closure barriers}
\label{sec:critical-interpolation}

This section studies the power function on the universal cover of $\C^\times$ and the
arithmetic sampling set $\{2^a3^b:a,b\ge0\}$.  Its Six Exponentials monodromy and
algebraic-multiplier inputs are established in Sections~\ref{mc:counting-monodromy} and
\ref{sec:spectrum}.  The first new core is an exact analytic growth
threshold for the $3$-smooth lattice and an infinite boundary-defect identity at that
threshold.

\subsection{Regularity ladder for a power branch}
\label{crit:regularity}

On the universal cover, a holomorphic function satisfying
\[
 F(w+\log2)=2^xF(w),\qquad F(w+\log3)=3^xF(w),\qquad F(0)=1
\]
is necessarily $F(w)=e^{xw}$: after division by $e^{xw}$, the two incommensurable real
periods have a dense subgroup, so continuity makes the quotient constant.  The corresponding
branch $z^x$ descends to a single-valued holomorphic function on $\C^\times$ exactly when
$e^{2\pi i x}=1$, hence exactly when $x\in\Z$.  Throughout the algebraic, Puiseux, and
D-finite discussion, $z^x$ means a branch on a simply connected punctured neighborhood or
on this universal cover, not an ordinary analytic germ at zero.

Finite ramification makes the monodromy a root of unity and forces $x\in\Q$, after which the
elementary rational-exponent argument closes the conjecture.  A further exact criterion is
arithmetic D-finiteness.  If a branch $z^\lambda$ satisfies a nonzero linear differential
equation with coefficients in $\overline\Q[z]$, of order $r$ and leading coefficient
$p_r\ne0$, then clearing powers of $z$ gives
\begin{equation}
 Q(z,\lambda)=\sum_{j=0}^r p_j(z)(\lambda)_jz^{r-j}=0.
 \label{crit:eq-dfinite-relation}
\end{equation}
The polynomial $Q(z,X)$ is nonzero because $[X^r]Q=p_r(z)$, so $\lambda$ is algebraic.
The coefficient identity and noncancellation are \statuslean{} in
\lean{DfiniteExponentCore}; the differential-equation specialization is the
\statusnew{} paper layer.  This would force integrality for the conditional power branch,
whose nonintegral exponent is already known transcendental.  Allowing coefficients that
depend on $x$ makes differential algebraicity vacuous: $zy'-xy=0$.  Even without admitting
$x$ as a coefficient, every power branch satisfies the coefficient-free nonlinear identity
\[
 zyy''-z(y')^2+yy'=0,
\]
so unrestricted nonlinear differential algebraicity still does not isolate the arithmetic
exponents.

Integer samples accumulating at a puncture are also insufficient.  The entire product below
makes $1+E(1/z)$ holomorphic on $0<|z|<\varepsilon$, essential at zero, yet equal to $1$ at
every $z=2^{-a}3^{-b}$.  Exact dilation information, not sampling alone, is indispensable.

\subsection{The sharp cubic logarithmic type}
\label{crit:canonical-product}

Define the locally uniformly convergent entire product
\begin{equation}
 E(z)=\prod_{a,b\ge0}\left(1-\frac{z}{2^a3^b}\right).
 \label{crit:eq-canonical-product}
\end{equation}
Its zeros are simple and exactly the positive $3$-smooth integers.  Factorwise equality at
$z=-R$ gives $M_E(R)=E(-R)$, and lattice integration yields the exact leading growth
\begin{equation}
 \log M_E(R)=\frac{(\log R)^3}{6\log2\log3}+O((\log R)^2).
 \label{crit:eq-cubic-growth}
\end{equation}
Indeed, for $T=\log R$,
\[
 \sum_{a,b\ge0}(T-a\log2-b\log3)_+
 =\frac{T^3}{6\log2\log3}+O(T^2).
\]
For an entire $F$, set
\[
 \tau_3(F)=\limsup_{R\to\infty}
 \frac{\log^+M_F(R)}{(\log R)^3},\qquad
 \tau_*:=\frac1{6\log2\log3}.
\]
Jensen's formula gives the matching lower bound
\begin{equation}
 F\not\equiv0,\quad F(2^a3^b)=0\ (a,b\ge0)
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \tau_3(F)\ge\tau_*.
 \label{crit:eq-jensen-threshold}
\end{equation}
The constant is sharp by~\eqref{crit:eq-cubic-growth}.  These self-contained statements are
\statusnew{} to this corpus; no claim of priority in the literature is made.

The threshold gives a sharp sufficient analytic interface.  More generally, let $p,q>1$
be multiplicatively independent, $P,Q\in\C^\times$, and suppose an entire $H$ satisfies
\[
 H(p^aq^b)=P^aQ^b\qquad(a,b\ge0).
\]
If
\begin{equation}
 \limsup_{R\to\infty}\frac{\log^+M_H(R)}{(\log R)^3}
 <\frac1{6\log p\log q},
 \label{crit:eq-subcritical}
\end{equation}
then $H(z)=z^n$, $P=p^n$, and $Q=q^n$ for some $n\in\Nzero$.  To prove this, the defect
$H(pz)-PH(z)$ vanishes on the whole lattice and remains subcritical, so
\eqref{crit:eq-jensen-threshold} annihilates it; coefficient comparison then leaves a single
monomial.  Thus a subcritical interpolant of the hypothetical data would prove the
conjecture.  At equality, $1+E$ is transcendental entire and integer-valued on every node,
while $z^n+cE(z)$ interpolates the same integral-exponent data as $z^n$.  These examples show
failure of uniqueness at critical type; they do not prove that every more structured
critical-type criterion is incapable of forcing exponent integrality.

\subsection{The critical boundary cocycle}
\label{crit:cocycle}

The product has exact edge factorizations
\begin{equation}
 E(2z)=E(z)B_2(z),\qquad E(3z)=E(z)B_3(z),
 \label{crit:eq-edge-factorization}
\end{equation}
where
\[
 B_2(z)=\prod_{b\ge0}\left(1-\frac{2z}{3^b}\right),\qquad
 B_3(z)=\prod_{a\ge0}\left(1-\frac{3z}{2^a}\right).
\]
Their second-order growth is
\begin{equation}
 \log M_{B_2}(R)=\frac{(\log R)^2}{2\log3}+O(\log R),\qquad
 \log M_{B_3}(R)=\frac{(\log R)^2}{2\log2}+O(\log R).
 \label{crit:eq-edge-growth}
\end{equation}
For an entire interpolant $H(2^a3^b)=M^aA^b$, set
$D_2(z)=H(2z)-MH(z)$ and $D_3(z)=H(3z)-AH(z)$.  Their lattice zeros and the simplicity of
$E$ give unique entire quotients $D_2=EU$ and $D_3=EV$.  Commutativity of the two dilations
is exactly the cocycle
\begin{equation}
 B_3(z)U(3z)-AU(z)=B_2(z)V(2z)-MV(z).
 \label{crit:eq-defect-cocycle}
\end{equation}
This is an infinite analytic analogue of \lean{BoundaryDilationDefect}, not a replacement
for its finite algebra.

If $U$ and $V$ are polynomials, the strict quadratic gap in
\eqref{crit:eq-edge-growth}, evaluated on the negative real axis, first forces $U=0$ and
then $V=0$.  Both dilation equations are exact, so coefficient comparison gives
$H(z)=z^n$, $M=2^n$, and $A=3^n$.  This polynomial-boundary-quotient closure and the cocycle
are \statusnew{} paper theorems.  Critical type alone does not establish the polynomial
quotient hypothesis; manufacturing that finite-dimensional boundary regularity is the new
open target.

The one-axis connection formalism in Section~\ref{arithinterp:qconnection} gives a useful
gauge for the same cocycle without introducing another compatibility equation.  Abbreviate
$\mathcal N_2(z)=\mathcal N_{2,M}(z)$,
$\mathcal E_2(z)=(z;1/2)_\infty$, and $\varkappa_2=\varkappa_2(M)$.  Since an entire interpolant $H$ agrees with $\mathcal N_2$
on the dyadic axis, there is an entire $W$ with
\[
 H(z)=\mathcal N_2(z)+\mathcal E_2(z)W(z).
\]
Its normalized dyadic defect is
\begin{equation}
 K_2(z):=\frac{H(2z)-MH(z)}{\mathcal E_2(z)}
 =\varkappa_2+(1-2z)W(2z)-MW(z).
 \label{crit:eq-qnewton-gauge}
\end{equation}
Because $E(z)=\mathcal E_2(z)E(z/3)$ and $D_2=EU$, one also has
\begin{equation}
 K_2(z)=E(z/3)U(z).
 \label{crit:eq-qnewton-export}
\end{equation}
Thus $K_2$ vanishes on the shifted smooth grid and
\begin{equation}
 \limsup_{R\to\infty}\frac{\log^+M_{K_2}(R)}{(\log R)^3}
 <\frac1{6\log2\log3}
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad K_2=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x\in\Nzero,
 \label{crit:eq-qnewton-gauge-closure}
\end{equation}
with a symmetric triadic statement.  The scalar $\varkappa_2$ cannot by itself provide the
strict saving: at the origin the free value of $W$ absorbs it, and
$K_2(0)=(1-M)H(0)$.  Equation~\eqref{crit:eq-qnewton-export} also shows that this is exactly
the existing boundary quotient in a one-axis-normalized gauge, not a second cocycle.

\begin{statusbox}{The D-finite noncancellation core is \statuslean{} in
\lean{DfiniteExponentCore}.  The universal-cover
classification, sharp canonical-product/Jensen threshold, subcritical interpolation
rigidity, edge growth, critical cocycle, and polynomial-quotient closure are \statusnew{}
paper results.  Overlapping monodromy material is omitted, and neither critical-type sampling
nor the cocycle currently supplies the missing interpolant regularity.}
\end{statusbox}

\subsection{One-edge residual rigidity at quadratic type}
\label{crit:edge-residual}

The two-dimensional product has cubic logarithmic growth, but each exposed edge has a sharp
quadratic scale.  For an entire function $F$, put
\begin{equation}
 \sigma_2(F)=\limsup_{R\to\infty}
 \frac{\log^+M_F(R)}{(\log R)^2},
 \qquad M_F(R)=\max_{|z|\le R}|F(z)|.
 \label{crit:eq-quadratic-type}
\end{equation}
Jensen's formula gives the exact edge barrier
\begin{equation}
 F\not\equiv0,\quad F(q^n/c)=0\ (n\ge0)
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \sigma_2(F)\ge\frac1{2\log q}
 \qquad(q>1,\ c>0).
 \label{crit:eq-edge-jensen}
\end{equation}
Indeed, the zeros through radius $R$ contribute
$(\log R)^2/(2\log q)+O(\log R)$ to Jensen's sum.  Equality is attained by
$\prod_{n\ge0}(1-cz/q^n)$; this is the one-dimensional version of the canonical-product
calculation above \cite{LevinEntire}.

The cocycle admits two asymmetric residuals
\begin{align}
 R_2(z)&=A U(z)+B_2(z)V(2z)-M V(z),\\
 R_3(z)&=M V(z)+B_3(z)U(3z)-A U(z).
 \label{crit:eq-edge-residuals}
\end{align}
Using~\eqref{crit:eq-defect-cocycle} once gives the exact factorizations
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{R_2(z)=B_3(z)U(3z),\qquad R_3(z)=B_2(z)V(2z).}
 \label{crit:eq-edge-residual-factorization}
\end{equation}
Thus $R_2$ vanishes at every $2^a/3$, and $R_3$ at every $3^b/2$.  Consequently
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{
 \sigma_2(R_2)<\frac1{2\log2}\quad\text{or}\quad
 \sigma_2(R_3)<\frac1{2\log3}
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad x\in\Nzero.}
 \label{crit:eq-edge-residual-closure}
\end{equation}
For example, the first inequality and~\eqref{crit:eq-edge-jensen} force $R_2=0$;
then~\eqref{crit:eq-edge-residual-factorization} gives $U=0$.  Comparing coefficients in
$H(2z)=MH(z)$ leaves one monomial, and evaluation at $3$ identifies the same integral
exponent.  In particular a counterexample forces both residuals to be nonzero and to meet or
exceed their respective critical edge scales.  The deliberately stronger separated hypothesis
\[
 \sigma_2(U)<\frac1{2\log2},\qquad
 \sigma_2(V)<\frac1{2\log2}-\frac1{2\log3}
\]
implies the first inequality in~\eqref{crit:eq-edge-residual-closure}, but the residual itself
is the more flexible target because it retains cancellation among its three terms.

There is a matching coefficient-space criterion.  Euler's $q$-binomial identity gives
\begin{equation}
 [z^j]B_2=\frac{(-6)^j}{\prod_{k=1}^j(3^k-1)},\qquad
 [z^j]B_3=\frac{(-6)^j}{\prod_{k=1}^j(2^k-1)}.
 \label{crit:eq-edge-coefficients}
\end{equation}
If $r_n=[z^n]R_2$, then any estimate
\begin{equation}
 |r_n|\le C\exp\!\left[-\left(\frac{\log2}{2}+\varepsilon\right)n^2\right]
 \quad(n\gg1)
 \label{crit:eq-edge-gaussian-certificate}
\end{equation}
makes $\sigma_2(R_2)<1/(2\log2)$ by completing the square in
$\sum_n|r_n|R^n$, and therefore closes the conjecture.

Arithmetic supplies a second sharp coordinate.  For
$F(z)=\sum_{n\ge0}a_nz^n\in\Q[[z]]$ entire, define
\begin{equation}
 \delta_2(F)=\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log\den(a_n)}{n^2}.
 \label{crit:eq-coefficient-denominator-type}
\end{equation}
A Cauchy estimate at $R=\exp(n/(2\sigma'))$ proves the elementary uncertainty theorem
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{4\sigma_2(F)\delta_2(F)<1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad F\text{ is a polynomial}.}
 \label{crit:eq-coefficient-uncertainty}
\end{equation}
Indeed, a nonzero rational coefficient is at least the reciprocal of its reduced
denominator, while Cauchy's bound is
$|a_n|\le\exp(-n^2/(4\sigma'))$; strict separation of the two quadratic constants forces all
large coefficients to vanish.  It follows that
\begin{equation}
 R_2\in\Q[[z]],\quad
 \sigma_2(R_2)\le\frac1{2\log2},\quad
 \delta_2(R_2)<\frac{\log2}{2}
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad x\in\Nzero,
 \label{crit:eq-critical-arithmetic-closure}
\end{equation}
with the symmetric triadic statement as well.  The constants are exact: the edge product
$B_3$ has the two values $1/(2\log2)$ and $(\log2)/2$, so their uncertainty product is one.
In checking its reduced denominators, primes dividing the base $q$ are separated from primes
dividing the fixed numerator parameter; LTE on the remaining progressions shows that only
$O(n\log n)$ can cancel from the quadratic denominator logarithm.

This arithmetic interface is nonempty.  Expanding the two-dimensional product formally gives
\begin{equation}
 ne_n=-\sum_{k=1}^n
 \frac{e_{n-k}}{(1-2^{-k})(1-3^{-k})},
 \qquad E(z)=\sum_{n\ge0}e_nz^n,
 \label{crit:eq-rational-product-recurrence}
\end{equation}
so $E\in\Q[[z]]$.  Moreover the smooth nodes can be enumerated as
$\lambda_0<\lambda_1<\cdots$ with $\lambda_n/n\to\infty$.  Successively correcting a
rational interpolation polynomial by
\[
 d_n\left(\frac z{\lambda_n}\right)^{k_n}
 \frac{\prod_{j<n}(z-\lambda_j)}{\prod_{j<n}(\lambda_n-\lambda_j)},
 \qquad k_n\ge n,
\]
and choosing $k_n$ to make the correction at most $2^{-n}$ on $|z|\le n$ constructs an
entire rational-coefficient interpolant.  The same construction works verbatim for any
prescribed rational values at the nodes: the correction $d_n$ remains rational, and
$k_n\ge n$ ensures that each Taylor coefficient receives only finitely many corrections.
Formal division by $E\in1+z\Q[[z]]$ then makes
$U,V,R_2,R_3$ rational-coefficient entire functions.  This construction gives no useful
growth or denominator bound; rather, it isolates the exact missing simultaneous estimate.

\begin{statusbox}{\statusnew{} --- the edge Jensen barrier, residual factorization and
closure, coefficient uncertainty, rational-coefficient interpolation, and the sharp
type--denominator gauge target are paper theorems.  Jensen's formula and the elementary
$q$-product identities are classical; no priority claim is made.  The strict inequalities
are essential, since the canonical edge product realizes equality in both coordinates.}
\end{statusbox}

The critical analysis can be sharpened further.  The strongest positive result is an explicit
entire interpolant at the exact critical type, together with a
strict second-order criterion that would force it to be a monomial.  The same audit closes
several tempting shortcuts negatively: low Hermite jets, Lambert cocycles, reciprocal Hankel
rank, fixed-prime denominator support, and pure-$2/3$ convergent denominators all stop at
quantified barriers.  None of the statements below is advertised as a proof of the
Alaoglu--Erd\H{o}s conjecture.

\subsection{The canonical critical interpolant and the quadratic threshold}
\label{crit:critical-interpolant}

Put
\[
 \alpha=\log2,\qquad \gamma=\log3,\qquad
 \tau=\frac1{6\alpha\gamma},\qquad
 c_E=\frac1{4\alpha}+\frac1{4\gamma},\qquad
 \delta_{\mathrm{quad}}=\frac1{4\alpha}-\frac1{4\gamma}>0.
\]
For the canonical product $E$ from~\eqref{crit:eq-canonical-product}, irrational-rotation
equidistribution sharpens the lattice count to
\begin{equation}
 \#\{(a,b)\in\Nzero^2:a\alpha+b\gamma\le T\}
 =\frac{T^2}{2\alpha\gamma}
  +\left(\frac1{2\alpha}+\frac1{2\gamma}\right)T+o(T).
 \label{crit:eq-refined-count}
\end{equation}
Integrating this formula and comparing
$\log(1+e^u)$ with $u_+$ in unit-width boundary shells gives
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{\log M_E(e^T)=\tau T^3+c_ET^2+o(T^2).}
 \label{crit:eq-refined-product}
\end{equation}
The same Jensen argument as in Section~\ref{crit:canonical-product} now says that every
nonzero entire function vanishing on all $2^a3^b$ has maximum-modulus logarithm at least the
right side of~\eqref{crit:eq-refined-product}, up to $o(T^2)$.

There is a canonical entire function attaining this refined scale for \emph{every}
nonintegral $x>0$.  On the slit plane use the principal branch and define
\begin{equation}
 w_x(t)=\frac{t^x}{E(-t)},\qquad
 J_x(z)=\int_0^\infty\frac{w_x(t)}{t+z}\,dt,\qquad
 H_x(z)=z^x+\frac{\sin\pi x}{\pi}E(z)J_x(z).
 \label{crit:eq-stieltjes-interpolant}
\end{equation}
All moments of $w_x$ are finite.  Across the negative axis the Plemelj jump of $J_x$ is
$-2\pi i r^x/E(-r)$, exactly cancelling the jump of $z^x$; the remaining singularity at
zero is removable.  Hence $H_x$ is entire and
\begin{equation}
 H_x(2^a3^b)=(2^a3^b)^x\qquad(a,b\ge0).
 \label{crit:eq-exact-interpolation}
\end{equation}
Moreover, polynomial interpolation on any nested finite exhaustion of the smooth nodes
converges locally uniformly to $H_x$.  To see convergence across the cut as well, order the
nodes as $s_0,s_1,\ldots$, put $F_j=\{s_0,\ldots,s_j\}$, and write $P_j$ for the
interpolating polynomial.  Its Newton increment is
\[
 P_j(z)-P_{j-1}(z)=[F_j](t^x)\prod_{i<j}(z-s_i).
\]
After discarding finitely many terms, choose $j_0>x$.  The positivity formula below gives,
for $j\ge j_0$ and uniformly on $|z|\le R$,
\[
 |P_j(z)-P_{j-1}(z)|
 \le \frac{C_{F_j}E(-R)}{s_j}
 \le \frac{C_{F_{j_0}}E(-R)}{s_j}.
\]
Since $\sum_j s_j^{-1}=\sum_{a,b\ge0}2^{-a}3^{-b}<\infty$, the Weierstrass test gives
local uniform convergence to an entire function.  Off the negative cut, the finite
keyhole-contour remainder and dominated convergence identify that limit with $H_x$.

The Cauchy transform in~\eqref{crit:eq-stieltjes-interpolant} is bounded in the two
half-planes, while on the negative ray
\[
 R\operatorname{PV}\!\int_0^\infty\frac{w_x(t)}{t-R}\,dt
 \longrightarrow-\mu_0,\qquad
 \mu_0:=\int_0^\infty w_x(t)\,dt>0.
\]
Thus
\begin{equation}
 |H_x(-R)|\sim\frac{|\sin\pi x|\mu_0}{\pi R}E(-R),
 \qquad
 \log M_{H_x}(e^T)=\tau T^3+c_ET^2+o(T^2).
 \label{crit:eq-interpolant-type}
\end{equation}
The positive Stieltjes moment is the first exact obstruction: it disappears precisely when
$\sin\pi x=0$.  Cancelling finitely many moments only replaces $E(z)/z$ by $E(z)/z^k$ and
does not change the quadratic coefficient.

For an entire interpolant $H$, set
\[
 c_2(H):=\limsup_{T\to\infty}
 \frac{\log M_H(e^T)-\tau T^3}{T^2}.
\]
The defect $D_2(z)=H(2z)-MH(z)$ vanishes at all smooth nodes.  Dilation raises the quadratic
coefficient by $3\alpha\tau=1/(2\gamma)$, whereas refined Jensen requires $c_E$ if
$D_2\ne0$.  Therefore
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{c_2(H)<\delta_{\mathrm{quad}}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 H(z)=z^n,\quad M=2^n,\quad A=3^n.}
 \label{crit:eq-quadratic-rigidity}
\end{equation}
This is strictly sharper than merely assuming that the boundary quotients are polynomials.
Indeed, if $D_2=EU$ and $D_3=EV$, and
\[
 u=\limsup_{r\to\infty}\frac{T(r,U)}{(\log r)^2},\qquad
 v=\limsup_{r\to\infty}\frac{T(r,V)}{(\log r)^2},
\]
then the cocycle~\eqref{crit:eq-defect-cocycle} and the global Nevanlinna inequalities give
\begin{equation}
 U,V\ne(0,0)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad u+v\ge\delta_{\mathrm{quad}}.
 \label{crit:eq-nevanlinna-gap}
\end{equation}
There are no exceptional radii in this estimate.  If $U=0$, zeros of $B_2$ propagate under
halving to zero and force $V=0$.  Thus $u+v<\delta_{\mathrm{quad}}$ is another exact sufficient condition.
The explicit $H_x$ proves that ordinary residue interpolation lands on the wrong side of the
gap: $c_2(H_x)=c_E>\delta_{\mathrm{quad}}$.

\subsection{A four-value positivity closure and the canonical obstruction}
\label{crit:positive-closure}

There is a remarkably short sufficient condition at the opposite analytic extreme.  Let
\[
 H(z)=\sum_{n\ge0}c_nz^n,
 \qquad c_n\ge0,
 \qquad H(1)=1.
\]
Absolute convergence at $6$ and Tonelli's theorem give the exact covariance identity
\begin{equation}
 H(6)-H(2)H(3)
 =\frac12\sum_{m,n\ge0}c_mc_n
   (2^m-2^n)(3^m-3^n).
 \label{crit:eq-positive-covariance}
\end{equation}
Every summand is nonnegative, and it is strictly positive for two distinct indices carrying
positive mass.  Consequently
\begin{equation}
 c_n\ge0,\quad H(1)=1,\quad H(6)=H(2)H(3)
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad H(z)=z^N
 \label{crit:eq-positive-closure}
\end{equation}
for one $N\in\Nzero$.  An absolutely monotone entire interpolant of the smooth table would
therefore prove the conjecture from the four values at $1,2,3,6$.  The finite covariance and
single-support core is \statuslean{} in \lean{PositiveCoefficientClosure}; the passage to an
infinite nonnegative series is the displayed paper argument.

This rigidity is quantitatively stable.  If $(p_n)$ is a probability distribution with
$\mathcal M(t)=\sum_np_nt^n$ and $\mathcal M(6)<\infty$, then
\begin{equation}
 \Delta:=\mathcal M(6)-\mathcal M(2)\mathcal M(3)
 \ge1-\sum_np_n^2\ge1-\sup_np_n.
 \label{crit:eq-positive-concentration}
\end{equation}
Indeed the kernel in~\eqref{crit:eq-positive-covariance} is at least $2$ off the diagonal.
Thus $\Delta\le\varepsilon<1$ forces one atom to carry mass at least $1-\varepsilon$.
If every $p_n$ is an integral multiple of $1/D$, then $D^2\Delta$ is a nonnegative integer;
either $\Delta=0$ or $\Delta\ge D^{-2}$.  A positive rational approximation can therefore
close only if its covariance error beats the square of its weight mesh.

The three values at $1,2,3$ already suffice analytically.  For a probability distribution
with $\mathcal M(3)<\infty$, strict Jensen convexity gives
\begin{equation}
 \sum_np_n3^n\ge\left(\sum_np_n2^n\right)^{\log_2 3},
 \label{crit:eq-discrete-jensen}
\end{equation}
with equality only for a point mass.  The four-value identity is more useful arithmetically
because its defect is rational or integral.

\paragraph{Geometric curvature, sums of squares, and the positivity tax.}
There is a broader three-value closure that does not refer to Taylor coefficients.

\begin{proposition}[Three-value geometric-curvature closure]
\label{crit:prop-geometric-curvature}
Let $H$ be real entire, positive on $[1,3]$, and suppose
\[
 H(1)=1,\qquad H(2)=2^x,\qquad H(3)=3^x
\]
for some $x\in\R$.  If $u\mapsto\log H(e^u)$ is convex or concave on
$[0,\log3]$, then $x=N\in\Nzero$ and $H(z)=z^N$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Put $a=\log2$, $b=\log3$, and
$\phi(u)=\log H(e^u)-xu$.  Then $\phi(0)=\phi(a)=\phi(b)=0$, with
$0<a<b$.  Equality at the interior point of the endpoint chord forces a convex or concave
function to be affine on the whole segment, so $\phi=0$ on $[0,b]$.  Hence
$zH'(z)-xH(z)$ vanishes on $(1,3)$ and therefore identically.  Comparing coefficients in
$H(z)=\sum_nc_nz^n$ gives $(n-x)c_n=0$ for every $n$; since $H(1)=1$, exactly one
coefficient survives, at an index $N=x\in\Nzero$, and it equals one.
\end{proof}

Equivalently, monotonicity of the elasticity $tH'(t)/H(t)$ on $[1,3]$ already closes the
problem.  The proposition includes positive Mellin mixtures, for which log convexity follows
from H\"older's inequality.  It also includes a positive $H$ whose multiplicative Hankel
kernel $K(s,t)=H(st)$ is positive semidefinite on $[1,\sqrt3]$: its $2\times2$ Gram
inequalities give midpoint log convexity.  The corresponding $\mathrm{TP}_2$ condition gives
