convexity, and reverse $\mathrm{TP}_2$ gives concavity.  Likewise, complete monotonicity of
$t\mapsto H(3e^{-t})$ makes its logarithm convex, while a Bernstein log-coordinate is
concave.

Pointwise positivity itself is completely flexible.

\begin{proposition}[Positive rational sum-of-squares interpolation]
\label{crit:prop-positive-sos}
For every pair $M,A\in\N_{>0}$ there is an entire
$H_+\in\Q[[z]]$ such that
\[
 H_+(t)\ge1\quad(t\in\R),\qquad
 H_+(2^a3^b)=M^aA^b\quad(a,b\in\Nzero).
\]
Indeed $H_+$ can be the diagonal of a positive semidefinite kernel on $\R$ of rank at most
five.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
For each smooth node $s=2^a3^b$, Lagrange's four-square theorem supplies integers
$r_{1,s},\ldots,r_{4,s}$ with
$M^aA^b-1=\sum_{j=1}^4r_{j,s}^2$.  Apply the arbitrary-rational-value interpolation
construction above separately to the four data sequences, obtaining entire
$F_j\in\Q[[z]]$ with $F_j(s)=r_{j,s}$.  Then
\[
 H_+(z)=1+\sum_{j=1}^4F_j(z)^2
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 K_+(s,t)=1+\sum_{j=1}^4F_j(s)F_j(t)
\]
have the asserted properties.  The construction supplies no useful growth or denominator
bound.
\end{proof}

Global positivity nevertheless has an exact growth cost.

\begin{proposition}[Elasticity oscillation and refined positivity tax]
\label{crit:prop-positive-growth-tax}
Let $x\notin\Nzero$, and let $H$ be an entire interpolant of
$H(2^a3^b)=(2^a3^b)^x$ that is positive on $[1,\infty)$.  If
$\lambda_0<\lambda_1<\cdots$ are the smooth nodes and
\[
 L_xH(z):=zH'(z)-xH(z),
\]
then $L_xH$ has a zero in every interval
$(\lambda_j,\lambda_{j+1})$, and
\begin{equation}
 \log M_H(e^T)\ge \tau T^3+c_ET^2+o(T^2).
 \label{crit:eq-positive-growth-tax}
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Writing $\chi(t)=tH'(t)/H(t)$, consecutive interpolation values give
\[
 \int_{\lambda_j}^{\lambda_{j+1}}(\chi(t)-x)\,\frac{dt}{t}=0.
\]
The integrand cannot vanish identically on one gap, since the identity theorem would then
give $L_xH\equiv0$ and Proposition~\ref{crit:prop-geometric-curvature} would force
$x\in\Nzero$.  It therefore takes both signs and has a zero in the gap.  Jensen's formula,
the interlacing, and~\eqref{crit:eq-refined-count} give, after removing a possible zero at
the origin,
\[
 \log M_{L_xH}(e^T)
 \ge\sum_{\lambda_{j+1}\le e^T}\log\frac{e^T}{\lambda_{j+1}}-O_H(T)
 =\tau T^3+c_ET^2+o(T^2).
\]
For $\delta=T^{-2}$, Cauchy's estimate on the concentric disks of radii $e^T$ and
$e^{T+\delta}$ gives
\[
 M_{L_xH}(e^T)
 \le(2T^2+|x|)M_H(e^{T+\delta})
\]
for large $T$.  Replacing $T+\delta$ by the outer logarithmic radius preserves both displayed
leading terms and proves~\eqref{crit:eq-positive-growth-tax}.
\end{proof}

Thus positivity, real zero-freeness, rational Taylor coefficients, and even a finite-rank
kernel diagonal can all be imposed without resolving the conjecture.  The rigid extra input
is one-signed geometric curvature; absent that curvature, a positive representative must
oscillate in elasticity at every node scale and pay at least the full refined critical
growth.

There is an explicit linear separator for the discrete moment cone.  If $k<x<k+1$, put
\begin{equation}
 \psi_k(t)=(2^t-2^k)(3^t-3^{k+1}).
 \label{crit:eq-moment-separator}
\end{equation}
Then $\psi_k(n)\ge0$ for every integer $n\ge0$, whereas
\begin{equation}
 \psi_k(x)=-(M-2^k)(3^{k+1}-A)\in\Z_{\le-1}.
 \label{crit:eq-integral-separation}
\end{equation}
Consequently any normalized positive mixture of
$(1,2^n,3^n,6^n)$ stays at sup-norm distance at least
$(3^{k+1}+2^k+1)^{-1}$ from the target four-vector.  More generally, a finite signed
representation $\sum_nc_n(1,2^n,3^n,6^n)=(1,M,A,MA)$ must satisfy
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{c_n<0}|c_n|\psi_k(n)
 \ge(M-2^k)(3^{k+1}-A)\ge1.
 \label{crit:eq-weighted-negativity}
\end{equation}
Thus every exact interpolant needs a quantifiable negative component; moving a very small
negative coefficient to a very large exponent can still pay the separator, so ordinary
negative mass alone has no degree-independent lower bound.

The canonical Stieltjes representative cannot satisfy this condition.  Write
$m=\lfloor x\rfloor$ and $H_x(z)=\sum_{k\ge0}h_kz^k$.  The sign in
\eqref{crit:eq-stieltjes-divdiff}, together with the signs of the elementary symmetric
coefficients in the Newton basis and the locally uniform interpolation limit, gives
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{(-1)^{k-m-1}h_k>0\qquad(k\ge m+1).}
 \label{crit:eq-alternating-tail}
\end{equation}
This obstruction survives every finite positive-scale diagonal filter.  If
$0<s_1<\cdots<s_J$ and $p_j\in\R[T]$, then for the Euler operator
$\mathcal D=z\,d/dz$ the coefficient of $z^k$ in
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal T H_x(z)=\sum_{j=1}^Jp_j(\mathcal D)H_x(s_jz)
 \quad\text{is}\quad
 h_kR(k),\qquad R(k)=\sum_{j=1}^Jp_j(k)s_j^k.
 \label{crit:eq-dilation-tail-filter}
\end{equation}
If $\mathcal T\ne0$, choose the largest scale with nonzero combined polynomial.  After
division by that scale to the $k$th power and by the leading power of $k$, $R(k)$ tends to
the nonzero leading coefficient.  Hence $R(k)$ has a fixed sign eventually, so the filtered
coefficients still alternate strictly.  Adding a polynomial changes only finitely many
coefficients.  Thus no nonzero finite linear combination of positive smooth dilations---even
with Euler multipliers---turns the canonical representative into the nonnegative-coefficient
interpolant required by~\eqref{crit:eq-positive-closure}.  The constant-multiplier finite
core, including arbitrary signed weights with a unique largest active scale, is
\statuslean{} in \lean{FiniteDilationAlternation}; the Euler extension is a paper argument.
Infinite filters, arbitrary nonlinear operations, and arbitrary representatives $H_x+EG$
remain outside this linear result.

The most direct nonlinear node-preserving corrections also miss by an exact cubic margin.
For every integer $r\ge2$,
\begin{equation}
 V_r(z):=H_x(z)^r-H_x(z^r)
 \label{crit:eq-nonlinear-node-defect}
\end{equation}
vanishes at every smooth node.  Moreover $V_r\equiv0$ if and only if $H_x$ is a monomial:
factoring $H_x=z^du$ at the origin and taking the local logarithm of $u/u(0)$ reduces the
identity to $L(z^r)=rL(z)$, whose least nonzero Taylor term is impossible.  Since
$H_x(1)=1$, the monomial is $z^d$.  For $r,s\ge2$, the composition identity
\[
 V_{rs}=V_r\sum_{j=0}^{s-1}H_x^{r(s-1-j)}H_x(z^r)^j+V_s(z^r)
\]
also shows that the dyadic tower is generated recursively by $V_2$ and its substitutions;
it supplies no independent compatibility conditions.  For a nonzero finite combination
$W=\sum_{r=2}^Rc_rV_r$ with $c_R\ne0$, maximum-modulus comparison gives
\begin{equation}
 \log M_W(e^T)=\tau R^3T^3+c_ER^2T^2+o(T^2).
 \label{crit:eq-nonlinear-node-defect-growth}
\end{equation}
Indeed, $H_x(z^R)$ has that growth and exponentially dominates $H_x(z)^R$ and every lower
index.  Since $W=EG$ for an entire $G$,
\[
 \log M_G(e^T)\ge (R^3-1)\tau T^3+(R^2-1)c_ET^2+o(T^2).
\]
Thus every nonzero finite correction of this form is strongly supercritical.  The
interpolant $H_x+W$ also cannot have nonnegative coefficients for nonintegral $x$, by the
four-value closure theorem.

Infinite scalar combinations have an exact convergence threshold.  Put
$a_r=-\log|c_r|$, with $a_r=+\infty$ when $c_r=0$.  The maximum-modulus comparison
\[
 M_{H_x}(e^{rT})-M_{H_x}(e^T)^r
 \le M_{V_r}(e^T)
 \le M_{H_x}(e^{rT})+M_{H_x}(e^T)^r
\]
gives, for every fixed $T>0$, as $r\to\infty$,
\[
 \log M_{V_r}(e^T)=\tau r^3T^3+O_T(r^2).
\]
Consequently
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{r\ge2}c_rV_r\ \hbox{converges normally (absolutely locally uniformly)}
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \frac{a_r}{r^3}\longrightarrow+\infty.
 \label{crit:eq-nonlinear-normal-series}
\end{equation}
An infinite support therefore has an absolute maximum-modulus majorant of infinite cubic
type.  Cancellation in an arbitrary normally convergent signed series remains open, but one
large class is rigid: if such a series has infinite support, all its indices have one fixed
$2$-adic valuation $k$, and all nonzero $c_r$ lie on one complex ray, evaluation at
$z=e^T\exp(i\pi/2^k)$ sends every $z^r$ to $-e^{rT}$.
The asymptotic $H_x(-t)\sim\mathfrak c_xE(-t)/t$, $\mathfrak c_x\ne0$, puts all dominant terms in
one shrinking cone and proves that the sum itself has infinite cubic type.

Nor does multiplicative renormalization help.  For integers $q,s\ge2$, the quotients
\[
 \mathfrak A_q(z)=\frac{H_x(z^q)}{H_x(z)^q}
\]
obey
\begin{equation}
 \mathfrak A_{qs}(z)=\mathfrak A_s(z^q)\mathfrak A_q(z)^s
 =\mathfrak A_q(z^s)\mathfrak A_s(z)^q.
 \label{crit:eq-power-substitution-cocycle}
\end{equation}
With a local logarithm at the origin, their natural rooted tower telescopes:
\[
 \prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\mathfrak A_q(z^{q^j})^{q^{-j-1}}
 =\frac{H_x(z^{q^n})^{q^{-n}}}{H_x(z)}\longrightarrow\frac1{H_x(z)}.
\]
Globally each unrooted factor $\mathfrak A_q$ equals one at every smooth node.  On the other
hand, the pointwise modulus ratio
\[
 \frac{|H_x(z^{q^n})|^{q^{-n}}}{|H_x(z)|}
\]
has supremum on $|z|=e^T$, for every $T>0$, whose logarithm grows at least like
$\tau q^{2n}T^3$.  Hence the local rooted telescope cannot extend to a globally
normally convergent holomorphic product.  The dyadic and triadic towers are the same
coboundary rather than independent constraints.

Finite Prouhet cancellation also fails beyond the polynomial asymptotic.  For distinct
finite multisets $\mathcal U,\mathcal V$ of positive substitution indices in one $2$-adic
class, assume $\sum_{r\in\mathcal U}r=\sum_{r\in\mathcal V}r$ and set
\[
 \mathcal W_{\mathcal U,\mathcal V}(z)
 =\prod_{r\in\mathcal U}H_x(z^r)-\prod_{r\in\mathcal V}H_x(z^r).
\]
This function vanishes on the smooth nodes, but
\begin{equation}
 \tau_3(\mathcal W_{\mathcal U,\mathcal V})
 =\tau\max\left\{\sum_{r\in\mathcal U}r^3,\sum_{r\in\mathcal V}r^3\right\}.
 \label{crit:eq-prouhet-composition-type}
\end{equation}
Indeed Mellin inversion and Baker separation~\cite{Baker1975} write $\log E(-e^T)$ as a
cubic polynomial plus two absolutely convergent Fourier series with frequencies in
$2\pi(\log2)^{-1}\Z$ and
$2\pi(\log3)^{-1}\Z$, up to an exponentially small remainder.  If the polynomial moments tie,
the least index whose multiplicities differ contributes a nonzero frequency that no larger
index can reproduce; the two frequency lattices cannot collide because $\log_2 3$ is
irrational.  Hence the product ratio stays away from one along an unbounded sequence.  Even
an eight-against-eight Thue--Morse pair matching power sums through degree three retains
type $65408\tau$.

There is a complementary defect using only smooth dilations:
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal R_x(z)=H_x(z)H_x(6z)-H_x(2z)H_x(3z)=E(z)\mathcal G_x(z).
 \label{crit:eq-four-dilation-defect}
\end{equation}
The rank-one table law gives the node zeros and hence the entire quotient $\mathcal G_x$.
The exact product identity
\[
 E(z)E(6z)=(1-6z)E(2z)E(3z)
\]
and the negative-axis Stieltjes asymptotic give
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal R_x(-R)\sim
 \frac{\mathfrak c_x^2}{R}E(-2R)E(-3R),
 \qquad
 \log|\mathcal G_x(-e^T)|
 =\tau T^3+3c_ET^2+o(T^2).
 \label{crit:eq-four-dilation-growth}
\end{equation}
The Stieltjes formula supplies the matching global upper bound, so
$\tau_3(\mathcal G_x)=\tau$: the most elementary four-dilation determinant produces another
exactly critical multiple of $E$, not a subcritical one.  At every integral control
$x\in\Nzero$, all the nonlinear and dilation defects above vanish identically.  General
signed infinite cancellation and mixed
$2$-adic supports remain outside these results.

In particular infinitely many Maclaurin coefficients are negative.  Similarly,
\[
 H_x(t)-t^x=\frac{\sin\pi x}{\pi}E(t)J_x(t),\qquad J_x(t)>0,
\]
alternates sign between consecutive smooth nodes.  This is the canonical sign-level
manifestation of the general curvature and elasticity obstruction in
Propositions~\ref{crit:prop-geometric-curvature} and~\ref{crit:prop-positive-growth-tax}.

The miss is also quantitative at the boundary.  For the canonical quotients
$H_x(2z)-2^xH_x(z)=E(z)U_x(z)$ and
$H_x(3z)-3^xH_x(z)=E(z)V_x(z)$, put
\[
 K_x=\frac{\sin\pi x}{\pi}\int_0^\infty\frac{t^x}{E(-t)}\,dt\ne0.
\]
The signed principal-value asymptotic yields
\[
 U_x(-R)\sim-\frac{K_x}{2R}B_2(-R),\qquad
 V_x(-R)\sim-\frac{K_x}{3R}B_3(-R).
\]
The maximum-modulus/Poisson comparison, with the outer-to-inner radius ratio subsequently
sent to infinity, therefore gives
\begin{equation}
 u_x\ge\frac1{2\log3},\qquad
 v_x\ge\frac1{2\log2},\qquad
 u_x+v_x\ge2c_E>\delta_{\mathrm{quad}}.
 \label{crit:eq-canonical-quotient-lower}
\end{equation}
These are canonical-only lower bounds, not an improvement of the arbitrary-interpolant
cocycle gap.  The surviving positive direction is correspondingly precise: construct a
\emph{different} arithmetic representative in the nonnegative-coefficient cone.  Ordinary
Stieltjes/Newton interpolation provably does not do so.

The most natural positive measure attached to $E$ also fails in an exact way.  Normalize
\begin{equation}
 d\nu_x(t)=\frac{t^{x-1}}{I_xE(-t)}\,dt,
 \qquad I_x=\int_0^\infty\frac{t^{x-1}}{E(-t)}\,dt,
 \qquad
 \mathcal A_s(t)=\frac{E(-t)}{E(-t/s)}.
 \label{crit:eq-stieltjes-transfer-measure}
\end{equation}
For every suitable $f$ and $r,s>0$, substitution gives the exact quasi-invariance and
cocycle
\begin{equation}
 \int f(t)\mathcal A_s(t)\,d\nu_x(t)
 =s^x\int f(st)\,d\nu_x(t),
 \qquad
 \mathcal A_{sr}(t)=\mathcal A_s(t)\mathcal A_r(t/s).
 \label{crit:eq-stieltjes-transfer}
\end{equation}
Thus for a smooth $s=2^a3^b$ the normalizing constant is exactly $s^x=M^aA^b$, but this is
only the original table written as a Radon--Nikodym identity.  In particular
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal A_6(t)=\mathcal A_2(t)\mathcal A_3(t/2),\qquad
 \mathcal A_2(t)\mathcal A_3(t)=(1+t)\mathcal A_6(t).
 \label{crit:eq-stieltjes-transfer-corner}
\end{equation}
If $m_1=\int t\,d\nu_x(t)>0$, then
\begin{equation}
 \int\mathcal A_2\mathcal A_3\,d\nu_x
 =6^x(1+6m_1)>6^x,\qquad
 \int\mathcal A_2(t)\mathcal A_3(t/2)\,d\nu_x=6^x.
 \label{crit:eq-stieltjes-transfer-gap}
\end{equation}
The shifted argument absorbs the whole positive covariance gap, so
\eqref{crit:eq-positive-covariance} cannot be applied to these transfer weights.

The same conclusion survives at every Hankel order.  If
$H_d=(\int t^{i+j}\,d\nu_x)_{0\le i,j\le d}$ and $H_d[\mathcal A_s]$ denotes the matrix with
the tilted moments, then
\begin{equation}
 H_d[\mathcal A_s]=s^x\operatorname{diag}(s^i)H_d\operatorname{diag}(s^i),
 \qquad
 \det H_d[\mathcal A_s]=s^{x(d+1)+d(d+1)}\det H_d.
 \label{crit:eq-stieltjes-transfer-hankel}
\end{equation}
After probability normalization this is merely dilation congruence, not an arithmetic
lattice floor.  Finally, normalizing the positive Taylor coefficients of
$\mathcal A_s$ against the moments of $\nu_x$ produces an entire probability generating
function $\Phi_s$, but it has infinitely many positive coefficients and hence a strict
four-value covariance defect.  As smooth $s\to\infty$, every fixed coefficient of
$\Phi_s$ tends to zero while $\Phi_s(1)=1$: all mass escapes to infinity, so there is no
locally uniform positive-coefficient interpolant in this family.  These identities hold for
every real $x>0$, including all integral controls; integrality changes only the displayed
normalizing constants.

\subsection{The positive Stieltjes denominator target}
\label{crit:denominator-target}

Fix a hypothetical nonintegral counterexample, and let
$F\subset\{2^a3^b:a,b\in\Nzero\}$ contain $N+1$ distinct nodes with $N>x$.
A keyhole contour gives
the exact divided difference
\begin{equation}
 [F](t^x)=(-1)^{N+1}\frac{\sin\pi x}{\pi}
 \int_0^\infty\frac{t^x\,dt}{\prod_{s\in F}(t+s)}.
 \label{crit:eq-stieltjes-divdiff}
\end{equation}
Consequently, along every nested exhaustion of the smooth semigroup,
\begin{equation}
 C_F:=\left(\prod_{s\in F}s\right)|[F](t^x)|
 \searrow
 C_x:=\frac{|\sin\pi x|}{\pi}\int_0^\infty\frac{t^x}{E(-t)}\,dt>0.
 \label{crit:eq-positive-residue}
\end{equation}
Under a counterexample all node values are integers, so $[F](t^x)$ is rational.  If
$\mathfrak d_F$ is its reduced positive denominator, nonvanishing and
\eqref{crit:eq-positive-residue} imply
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{
 \liminf_{F\nearrow\{2^a3^b\}}
 \frac{\mathfrak d_F}{\prod_{s\in F}s}\ge\frac1{C_x}>0.}
 \label{crit:eq-denominator-lower}
\end{equation}
Hence a single semigroup exhaustion satisfying
$\mathfrak d_F=o(\prod_{s\in F}s)$ would prove the conjecture.  This is a finite arithmetic
target with no unspecified analytic constant in its leading scale.

\paragraph{Successive Markov ratios.}
The real common-power relation gives a stronger output-sensitive statement, but in the
opposite direction.  Write
\[
 \mathcal D_F(z)=[F](t^z).
\]
For $|F|=N+1$, $N>x$, and a new smooth node $s\notin F$, the ratio of two successive divided
differences is
\begin{equation}
 \Phi_F(s):=-\frac{\mathcal D_{F\cup\{s\}}(x)}{\mathcal D_F(x)}
 =\int_0^\infty\frac{d\mu_F(t)}{s+t}\in\Q_{>0},
 \qquad
 d\mu_F(t)=
 \frac{t^x\,dt}{I_F\prod_{u\in F}(t+u)},
 \label{crit:eq-successive-markov-ratio}
\end{equation}
where $I_F$ normalizes the measure to mass one.  If $m\ge1$ and $2m<N-x$, its moments through order
$2m$ are rational:
\begin{equation}
 \mu_k:=\int_0^\infty t^k\,d\mu_F(t)
 =(-1)^k\frac{\mathcal D_F(x+k)}{\mathcal D_F(x)}
 \in\Q
 \qquad(0\le k\le2m).
 \label{crit:eq-direct-rational-moments}
\end{equation}
Let $Q_m\in\Q[t]$ be the monic degree-$m$ orthogonal polynomial for $\mu_F$, put
$h_m=\int Q_m^2\,d\mu_F$, and define
\[
 P_{m-1}(s)=
 \int_0^\infty\frac{Q_m(-s)-Q_m(t)}{s+t}\,d\mu_F(t)\in\Q[s].
\]
Orthogonality gives the exact Markov--Pad\'e remainder
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{
 \Phi_F(s)-\frac{P_{m-1}(s)}{Q_m(-s)}
 =\frac1{Q_m(-s)^2}
   \int_0^\infty\frac{Q_m(t)^2}{s+t}\,d\mu_F(t)>0.}
 \label{crit:eq-markov-pade-remainder}
\end{equation}

This identity has an integral floor.  For $u\in F$, put
\[
 D_{F,u}=\prod_{v\in F\setminus\{u\}}(u-v),\qquad
 L_F=\operatorname{lcm}_{u\in F}|D_{F,u}|.
\]
Then
\[
 R_k=L_F\mathcal D_F(x+k)\in\Z,\qquad
 \epsilon=\operatorname{sgn}(R_0),\qquad
 a_k=\epsilon(-1)^kR_k\in\Z_{>0}\quad(0\le k<N-x),
\]
and set
\[
 \Delta_j=\det(a_{r+s})_{0\le r,s<j}\in\Z_{>0}
 \qquad(1\le j\le m+1).
\]
The Hankel system shows that $\Delta_mQ_m\in\Z[t]$ and that
$a_0\Delta_mP_{m-1}\in\Z[t]$, while
\[
 h_m=\frac{\Delta_{m+1}}{a_0\Delta_m}.
\]
Thus $C_m=a_0\Delta_m$ is a simultaneous clearing and
$C_mh_m=\Delta_{m+1}$.  If $\mathfrak b_{F,s}$ is the reduced denominator of
$\Phi_F(s)$, rational separation in~\eqref{crit:eq-markov-pade-remainder}, together with
the fact that every zero of $Q_m$ is positive, yields
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{
 \mathfrak b_{F,s}>
 \frac{s|Q_m(-s)|}{\Delta_{m+1}}>
 \frac{s^{m+1}}{\Delta_{m+1}}.}
 \label{crit:eq-markov-denominator-repulsion}
\end{equation}
If $\mathcal D_F(x)=A_F/\mathfrak d_F$ and
$\mathcal D_{F\cup\{s\}}(x)=A_{F,s}/\mathfrak d_{F,s}$ are reduced, then
$\mathfrak b_{F,s}\le |A_F|\mathfrak d_{F,s}$, so the same estimate divided by
$|A_F|$ applies to $\mathfrak d_{F,s}$.  The strongest permitted choice has
$m<(N-x)/2$, whereas the elementary append denominator has degree $N+1$ in $s$.
The result therefore exposes an exact half-order barrier rather than the desired upper
bound.

The nonzero integer behind the floor is a useful sharper target.  Write both fractions in
lowest terms:
\[
 \Phi_F(s)=\frac{\mathfrak a_{F,s}}{\mathfrak b_{F,s}},\qquad
 \frac{P_{m-1}(s)}{Q_m(-s)}=\frac{p_s}{q_s},
 \qquad \mathfrak b_{F,s},q_s>0.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
 \begin{aligned}
 \delta_{m,s}
 &=\mathfrak a_{F,s}q_s-\mathfrak b_{F,s}p_s\in\Z_{>0},\\
 \frac{\delta_{m,s}}{\mathfrak b_{F,s}q_s}
 &=\frac1{Q_m(-s)^2}
   \int_0^\infty\frac{Q_m(t)^2}{s+t}\,d\mu_F(t),\\
 \delta_{m,s}
 &<\frac{\mathfrak b_{F,s}q_sh_m}{sQ_m(-s)^2}.
 \end{aligned}
 \label{crit:eq-markov-defect-integer}
\end{equation}
Thus a source-sensitive divisor of $\delta_{m,s}$ exceeding an independent upper bound for
the last quantity would give a contradiction.  No present cluster or Smith argument
supplies one.
For distinct new nodes $s,u$, the ratios also satisfy the exact resolvent recursion
\begin{equation}
 \Phi_{F\cup\{u\}}(s)
 =\frac{\Phi_F(u)-\Phi_F(s)}{(s-u)\Phi_F(u)}.
 \label{crit:eq-markov-resolvent-recursion}
\end{equation}
This is the cleanest finite identity through which such a divisor could propagate across
Newton levels.
For a finite calibration, not a global counterexample, take
$x=1/2$, $F=\{1,4,9,16\}$, and $s=36$.  Then
$\Phi_F(36)=1/40$, the primitive approximant $1/41$, and
$\delta_{1,36}=1$.

\paragraph{Smith saturation of the Pad\'e defect.}
Raw collision content disappears on passing to the primitive approximant.  Put
\[
 \mathsf H_m=(a_{i+j})_{\substack{0\le i<m\\0\le j\le m}},\qquad
 c_j=(-1)^{m+j}\det\mathsf H_m^{\widehat j}.
\]
Then
\[
 \sum_{j=0}^m c_jt^j=\Delta_mQ_m(t).
\]
Write $\Phi_F(s)=A/B$ in lowest terms, set
\[
 z_0=a_0A,\qquad z_j=Ba_{j-1}-sz_{j-1}\quad(1\le j\le m),
\]
and append this row to $\mathsf H_m$.  The moment identity
$z_j=Ba_0\int t^j(s+t)^{-1}\,d\mu_F(t)$ gives
\begin{equation}
 \begin{split}
 J_{m,s}:=\det\begin{pmatrix}\mathsf H_m\\z_0&\cdots&z_m\end{pmatrix}
 &=Ba_0\Delta_m
   \left(Q_m(-s)\Phi_F(s)-P_{m-1}(s)\right),\\
 \delta_{m,s}&=\frac{|J_{m,s}|}{g_{m,s}},
 \end{split}
 \label{crit:eq-pade-smith-saturation}
\end{equation}
where
\[
 \widehat p_{m,s}=a_0\Delta_m(-1)^mP_{m-1}(s),\qquad
 \widehat q_{m,s}=a_0\Delta_m(-1)^mQ_m(-s),\qquad
 g_{m,s}=\gcd(\widehat p_{m,s},\widehat q_{m,s}).
\]
If
\[
 \mathfrak s_m=\gcd(c_0,\ldots,c_m),
\]
then $\mathfrak s_m$ is the top Smith determinantal divisor of $\mathsf H_m$,
divides both safe Pad\'e coefficients, and
$J_{m,s}=\mathfrak s_m\langle z,c^{\rm sat}\rangle$.
Thus the relevant local quantity is
\[
 v_p(J_{m,s})-min\{v_p(\widehat p_{m,s}),v_p(\widehat q_{m,s})\},
\]
not $v_p(\mathfrak s_m)$.

This distinction is sharp at arbitrary collision depth.  If
$a_k=\sum_\nu w_\nu u_\nu^k$ with integral $w_\nu,u_\nu$ and
$u_\nu\equiv u\pmod {p^h}$ for every $\nu$, a unimodular Pascal translation gives
\begin{equation}
 p^{h m(m-1)}\mid\mathfrak s_m.
 \label{crit:eq-pade-cluster-smith-content}
\end{equation}
Indeed, after translation the $(i,j)$ entry is divisible by $p^{h(i+j)}$, and every
maximal minor contains at least $h m(m-1)$ powers of $p$.
Nevertheless, let
\[
 \widetilde M=5043,\qquad x_0=\log_2\widetilde M,\qquad
 K_h=4\cdot5^{h-1},\qquad q_h=2^{K_h},\qquad w_h=\widetilde M^{K_h},
\]
and take the finite one-axis table
\[
 F_h=\{1,q_h,\ldots,q_h^{19}\},\qquad s_h=q_h^{20},\qquad m=2.
\]
Here $12<x_0<13$ and $4<19-x_0$; every source node, the appended node, and every
output $w_h^j$ is congruent to $1$ modulo $5^h$.  This finite one-axis calibration neither
assumes nor addresses the condition $3^{x_0}\in\Z$.  The geometric divided-difference formula yields
\[
 \Phi_{F_h}(s_h)=
 \frac{q_h^{19}-w_h}{q_h^{19}(q_h^{20}-1)},\qquad
 \mu_k=q_h^{19k-k(k+1)/2}
 \prod_{r=1}^k\frac{q_h^rw_h-1}{q_h^{19-r}-w_h}.
\]
The congruence
\[
 \frac{a^{K_h}-1}{5^h}\equiv\frac{a^4-1}{5}\pmod5
\]
at the relevant unit bases gives
\[
 (\mu_1,\mu_2,\mu_3)\equiv(2,2,1)\pmod5.
\]
Hence $Q_2(-s_h)\equiv1$ and $P_1(s_h)\equiv3\pmod5$.  Moreover
\[
 v_5(q_h^{19}-w_h)=h,\qquad v_5(q_h^{20}-1)=h+1.
\]
After both fractions are reduced, the primitive defect $\delta_{2,s_h}$ is therefore a
$5$-adic unit for every $h$, although~\eqref{crit:eq-pade-cluster-smith-content} gives
$5^{2h}\mid\mathfrak s_2$.  Thus no divisor depending only on source/output collision
depths, append congruence, or unsaturated Hankel Smith factors can control
$\delta_{m,s}$.  This is only a no-go for common-collision and unsaturated-Smith arguments;
a surviving divisor must use two-generator exponent geometry and the saturated transverse
residue.

There is no hidden real cancellation behind these inequalities.  Hermite--Genocchi gives
\begin{equation}
 L_F\mathcal D_F(z)
 =L_F(z)_N\int_{\Delta_N}
   \left(\sum_{u\in F}\lambda_u u\right)^{z-N}\,d\lambda.
 \label{crit:eq-direct-circuit-real-factorization}
\end{equation}
Here $d\lambda$ is coordinate-simplex measure of total mass $1/N!$.  The second factor is
positive on the real axis and is a compactly supported bilateral Laplace transform whose
Hankel kernel is strictly totally positive.  Hence the restricted circuit has exactly the real zeros
$0,1,\ldots,N-1$, all simple.  Likewise, if
$0\le i_1<\cdots<i_r$, $0\le j_1<\cdots<j_r$, and $i_r+j_r<N-x$, then
$\det(a_{i_p+j_q})_{p,q=1}^r$ is a positive integer.  In particular
\begin{equation}
 R_0R_2-R_1^2\ge1\qquad(x+2<N).
 \label{crit:eq-shifted-circuit-hankel-floor}
\end{equation}

The safe Hankel clearing can itself be factored exactly.  Order
$F=\{s_1<\cdots<s_n\}$, put
$\Delta_F^{\mathrm V}=\prod_{i<j}(s_j-s_i)$, $y_i=s_i^x$, and let
$\mathcal B^{\rm dir}_{F,r}$ have $i$th row
\[
 (1,s_i,\ldots,s_i^{n-r-1},y_i,y_is_i,\ldots,y_is_i^{r-1}).
\]
Cauchy--Binet and complementary Vandermonde factorization give
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{
 \Delta_r
 =\epsilon^r(-1)^{\binom r2}
   \frac{L_F^r}{\Delta_F^{\mathrm V}}
   \det\mathcal B^{\rm dir}_{F,r}.}
 \label{crit:eq-direct-hankel-alternant}
\end{equation}
for $1\le r\le m+1$.
At Pad\'e degree $m$, the exact prefactor is
$L_F^{m+1}/\Delta_F^{\mathrm V}$.  The shifted exponent block is interlaced with the ordinary
block, so the shape-free HCIZ dominance from the reciprocal construction below is
unavailable.  The identity isolates primitive Cramer or Smith content as the part not
measured by the full determinant.

Node-only denominator theory cannot prove that saving.  For the size triangle
\[
 \mathcal J_T=\{(a,b)\in\Nzero^2:a\alpha+b\gamma\le T\},\qquad
 F_T=\{2^a3^b:(a,b)\in\mathcal J_T\},\qquad
 P_T=\prod_{s\in F_T}s,
\]
put
\[
 D_s=\prod_{t\in F_T\setminus\{s\}}(s-t),\qquad
 L_T=\operatorname{lcm}_{s\in F_T}|D_s|.
\]
The symbolic top divided difference has denominator exactly $L_T$.  Already the endpoint
$s=1$ gives, after removing the $2$- and $3$-parts,
\begin{equation}
 \log (L_T)_{(6)}\ge\log P_T-O(T)
 \ge\frac{T^3}{3\log2\log3}-O(T^2).
 \label{crit:eq-away-capacity}
\end{equation}
At the structural primes, the exact endpoint valuation comparison gives
\begin{equation}
 \log (L_T)_{\{2,3\}}=\log P_T-2T+O(1).
 \label{crit:eq-smooth-capacity}
\end{equation}
Thus both the away-prime and smooth-prime capacities can individually pay the leading
Stieltjes requirement.  Any proof of the needed $o(P_T)$ upper bound must exploit primitive
cancellation for the \emph{one fixed} rank-one value table $M^aA^b$; no Vandermonde,
$p$-ordering, or node-only Smith theorem can supply it.

There is a precise fixed-divisor ceiling on any argument using only the abstract rank-one
law.  For a finite $E\subset\Nzero^2$, put $s_{(a,b)}=2^a3^b$ and define $D_e,L_E$ as
above.  The top divided difference of the table $s_{(a,b)}\mapsto U^aV^b$ is
\begin{equation}
 [E]y=\frac{R_E(U,V)}{L_E},\qquad
 R_E(U,V)=\sum_{(a,b)\in E}\frac{L_E}{D_{(a,b)}}U^aV^b\in\Z[U,V].
 \label{crit:eq-rank-one-fixed-divisor}
\end{equation}
The coefficients of $R_E$ are primitive.  If $r_E=\max_Ea$, $s_E=\max_Eb$, and
$\delta_E=\gcd\{R_E(u,v):u,v\in\Z\}$, then the binomial-basis finite-difference formula
gives
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{\delta_E\mid r_E!s_E!.}
 \label{crit:eq-rank-one-fixed-divisor-bound}
\end{equation}
Indeed, $\delta_E$ divides every integral binomial-basis coefficient, while returning to
the monomial basis costs at most $r_E!s_E!$; primitivity proves the claim.  Conversely, for
every modulus $q$, local pairs attaining the $p$-adic minima defining $\delta_E$ can be
combined by the Chinese remainder theorem.  Thus arbitrarily large positive $U,V$ satisfy
\[
 \gcd(R_E(U,V),q)=\gcd(\delta_E,q).
\]
If $n=|E|-1$, the integral controls calibrate exactly:
$R_E(2^k,3^k)=0$ for $k<n$, while $R_E(2^n,3^n)=L_E$.
For the size triangles, take $q=L_T$ and combine
\eqref{crit:eq-away-capacity}--\eqref{crit:eq-smooth-capacity}.  Suitable rank-one integer
specializations then have
\begin{equation}
 \log\mathfrak d_T\ge2\log P_T-O(T\log T),
 \qquad \mathfrak d_T\ge P_T^{2-o(1)}.
 \label{crit:eq-rank-one-fixed-divisor-no-go}
\end{equation}
The pair $(U,V)$ here may vary with $T$ and need not lie on a common real power curve.
Accordingly no universal bound obtained from adjugate, Sylvester, subresultant, or rank-one
congruence identities can force $\mathfrak d_T=o(P_T)$ for all rank-one specializations; this
does not rule out exceptional root concentration for the one fixed
hypothetical pair $(M,A)$.  Such concentration would have to account for logarithmic mass
$\Theta(T^3)$, whereas universal fixed-divisor content contributes only $O(T\log T)$.

For one fixed hypothetical pair, ordinary gap synchronization is also too sparse.  Let
\[
 \mathrm{Dir}_T=(\mathcal J_T-\mathcal J_T)\setminus\{(0,0)\}.
\]
For $d=(r,s)\in\mathrm{Dir}_T$, write in lowest terms
\[
 2^r3^s=\frac{P_d}{Q_d},\qquad
 M^rA^s=\frac{R_d}{S_d},\qquad
 g_d=\gcd(|P_d-Q_d|,|R_d-S_d|).
\]
Then the uniform triangular estimate is
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{\sum_{d\in\mathrm{Dir}_T}\log g_d=o(T^3).}
 \label{crit:eq-triangular-gap-gcd}
\end{equation}
The point is that all directions lie in the one fixed finitely generated group
$\Gamma=\langle(2,M),(3,A)\rangle\subset\mathbb G_m^2(\Q)$.  For $d\ne0$, put
$u_d=2^r3^s$ and $v_d=M^rA^s=u_d^x$.  Since $u_d\ne1$ and $x$ is irrational, $u_d,v_d$
are multiplicatively independent.  Corollary~1 of the Corvaja--Zannier $S$-unit gcd
theorem~\cite{CorvajaZannier2005} says that, for every $\varepsilon>0$, all but finitely
many multiplicatively independent $(u,v)\in\Gamma$ have generalized gcd at most
$\varepsilon\max\{h(u),h(v)\}$.  The quantity $\log g_d$ is its finite-place part, so the
same bound holds for $g_d$.  There are $O(T^2)$ directions and every height is $O_x(T)$;
summing and then sending $\varepsilon$ to zero proves~\eqref{crit:eq-triangular-gap-gcd}.
In particular the endpoint sum
\[
 \sum_{(a,b)\in\mathcal J_T\setminus\{(0,0)\}}
 \log\gcd(2^a3^b-1,M^aA^b-1)=o(T^3).
\]

This has a precise local interpretation.  Put $y_e=M^aA^b$ for $e=(a,b)$ and
$\lambda_p=\max_e v_p(D_e)$.  For $p\nmid6MA$, choose a maximizing node $i_p$ and define
\begin{equation}
 \kappa_p=\sum_{j\ne i_p}
 \min\{v_p(s_{i_p}-s_j),v_p(y_{i_p}-y_j)\}.
 \label{crit:eq-pairwise-overlap-budget}
\end{equation}
Distinct $j$ give distinct directions, so~\eqref{crit:eq-triangular-gap-gcd} implies
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{p\nmid6MA}\kappa_p\log p=o(T^3).
 \label{crit:eq-pairwise-overlap-ceiling}
\end{equation}
Define the collision graph modulo $p$ to have the nodes as vertices and an edge $\{i,j\}$
exactly when $s_i\equiv s_j\pmod p$.  If this graph has exactly one edge $\{i,j\}$ and
$h_p=v_p(s_i-s_j)$, the two active barycentric coefficients are opposite modulo $p^{h_p}$ and
one has the exact isolated-collision formula
\begin{equation}
 \min\{h_p,v_p(R_{\mathcal J_T}(M,A))\}
 =\min\{h_p,v_p(y_i-y_j)\}.
 \label{crit:eq-isolated-collision-cancellation}
\end{equation}
Thus every cancellation at an isolated collision prime is already charged to the subcubic
budget.  The exact mechanism for multiple collisions can also be exposed.  For a general
finite exponent set $E$, retain $D_e,L_E,R_E$ from
\eqref{crit:eq-rank-one-fixed-divisor}; for an arbitrary output vector
$y=(y_e)_{e\in E}$ also write
$R_E(y)=\sum_e(L_E/D_e)y_e$, and define $\kappa_p$ by
\eqref{crit:eq-pairwise-overlap-budget} with $\mathcal J_T$ replaced by $E$.
Fix a prime $p$ and put
\[
 d_e=v_p(D_e),\qquad \lambda=\max_ed_e,\qquad
 \omega_p=p^{-\lambda}L_E\in\Z_{(p)}^\times,\qquad
 u_e=p^{-d_e}D_e\in\Z_{(p)}^\times.
\]
Then, exactly over $\Q_p$,
\begin{equation}
 R_E(U,V)=\omega_p\sum_{e=(a,b)\in E}
 p^{\lambda-d_e}u_e^{-1}U^aV^b,
 \qquad
 \overline{R}_E
 =\overline{\omega}_p\sum_{d_e=\lambda}\overline{u}_e^{-1}U^aV^b.
 \label{crit:eq-cluster-initial-form}
\end{equation}
There is no hidden sign: it is contained in $u_e$.

The coefficients in~\eqref{crit:eq-cluster-initial-form} are read directly from the
collision tree.  Let
\[
 C_k(e)=\{f\in E:s_f\equiv s_e\pmod {p^k}\},\qquad C_0(e)=E.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
 d_e=\sum_{k\ge1}(|C_k(e)|-1).
 \label{crit:eq-cluster-depth-sum}
\end{equation}
For a depth-$k$ cluster $C$, choose a common residue $\rho_C$ modulo $p^k$ and label each
child $B$ by
$\xi_B=(s_b-\rho_C)/p^k\bmod p$, $b\in B$.  The labels are defined up to common
translation.  If $B_k(e)$ is the child containing $e$, then
\begin{equation}
 \overline u_e
 =\prod_{k\ge0}\ \prod_{\substack{B\text{ child of }C_k(e)\\B\ne B_k(e)}}
   \bigl(\xi_{B_k(e)}-\xi_B\bigr)^{|B|}.
 \label{crit:eq-cluster-angular-unit}
\end{equation}
Each other node contributes its valuation to
\eqref{crit:eq-cluster-depth-sum} and its angular difference at the unique level where its
branch separates from $e$, which proves both formulas.

There is a useful transfer theorem for the simplest geometry.  Assume no pair that is
congruent modulo $p$ remains congruent modulo $p^2$.  For each residue class $C$, let
$m_C=|C|$, let $r_C$ be its residue, choose an integer lift $r_C^*$, and write
$t_e=(s_e-r_C^*)/p\bmod p$ for $e\in C$.  If $m=\max_Cm_C$, then
$\lambda=m-1$ and
\begin{equation}
 \overline\omega_p^{-1}\overline R_E(y)
 =\sum_{m_C=m}
 \left(\prod_{C'\ne C}(r_C-r_{C'})^{-m_{C'}}\right)
 \sum_{e\in C}\frac{\overline y_e}
 {\prod_{f\in C\setminus\{e\}}(t_e-t_f)}.
 \label{crit:eq-simple-cluster-confluent}
\end{equation}
These summands are precisely the top confluent coordinates of the largest local Smith
blocks; the $p$-primary Vandermonde factors within a class of size $m_C$ are
$1,p,\ldots,p^{m_C-1}$.

\begin{proposition}[Unique affine cluster transfer]
\label{crit:prop-affine-cluster-transfer}
Assume $p\nmid6MA$, the preceding simple-cluster hypothesis, and a unique largest class
$C=\{e_0+kd:0\le k<m\}$, where $2\le m\le p$ and $d=(r,s)\in\Z^2$.
Then the collective excess at $p$ is zero:
\[
 \left(\min\{\lambda,v_p(R_E(M,A))\}-\kappa_p\right)_+=0
\]
for every maximizing node used to define $\kappa_p$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Put $q=2^r3^s$ and $\varrho=M^rA^s$.  The source collision gives
$q\equiv1\pmod p$ and, by simplicity,
$c=(q-1)/p\in\Z_p^\times$.  With $s_k=s_0q^k$ and
$y_k=y_0\varrho^k$, the last sum in
\eqref{crit:eq-simple-cluster-confluent} is
\[
 \frac{\overline y_0(\overline\varrho-1)^{m-1}}
 {(\overline s_0\overline c)^{m-1}(m-1)!},
 \]
using the elementary $(m-1)$st divided difference of $T^k$; the factorial is a unit because
$m\le p$.  Since the largest class is unique, $p\mid R_E(M,A)$ exactly when
$\varrho\equiv1\pmod p$.  In that case all $m-1=\lambda$ source collisions from a maximizing
node transfer to the output, so $\kappa_p=\lambda$; otherwise the capped cancellation is
zero.
\end{proof}

The hypotheses are sharp.  The first complete size triangle,
\[
 \mathcal J_{\log8}
 =\{(0,0),(1,0),(0,1),(2,0),(1,1),(3,0)\},
\]
has $F=\{1,2,3,4,6,8\}$ and
\begin{equation}
 R_F(U,V)=U^3+35U^2+35U-7UV-56V-8.
 \label{crit:eq-first-collective-polynomial}
\end{equation}
At $p=5$, $\lambda=1$ and
\[
 \overline R_F=(U-2)(U^2+2U+4+3V).
\]
For the fixed specialization $(M,A)=(7,6)$,
$R_F(7,6)=1665$ has $5$-adic valuation one, while the two collision pairs
$\{1,6\}$ and $\{3,8\}$ have output gaps $41$ and $337$.  Hence
$\kappa_5=0$: even a full triangle has collective excess one.

The excess is unbounded on arbitrary smooth supports while keeping both the prime and the
rank-one pair fixed.  For $h\ge1$, put $n=2\cdot5^{h-1}$ and
\[
 E_h=\{(0,0),(0,n),(n,n),(n,2n)\},\qquad
 \{s_e:e\in E_h\}=\{1,b,q,bq\},
 \quad b=3^n,\quad q=6^n.
\]
LTE gives two collision pairs $\{1,q\}$ and $\{b,bq\}$, each of depth $h$, so
$\lambda_5=h$.  For $(M,A)=(7,6)$ the output vector is congruent modulo $5^h$ to
\[
 (1,-b,-q,bq).
\]
For arbitrary distinct $1,b,q,bq$, these four values lie on the quadratic
\[
 \frac{2X^2-(b+1)(q+1)X+2bq}{(b-1)(q-1)}.
\]
Their third divided difference is therefore zero, and the integral cleared numerator gives
$5^h\mid R_{E_h}(7,6)$.  On both colliding pairs the output ratio is $-1$ modulo $5$, so
$\kappa_5=0$ and the collective excess equals $h$.

Accordingly no bound from the collision tree, local Smith form, support size, rank-one law,
or a fixed multiplicatively independent output pair alone can improve the trivial
$\lambda_p$ ceiling for collective cancellation.  For the full triangles, call a prime
geometrically bad if it has a deeper
collision, tied largest classes, or a non-affine largest class.  The preceding proposition
reduces the remaining capacity exactly to
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{p\nmid6MA}\min\{\lambda_p,v_p(R_{\mathcal J_T}(M,A))\}\log p
 \le o(T^3)+\sum_{p\ {\rm geometrically\ bad}}\lambda_p\log p.
 \label{crit:eq-bad-cluster-capacity}
\end{equation}
No smallness of the last sum is asserted.  The four-node family shows that any such estimate
must use the downward-closed geometry of $\mathcal J_T$ or the real common-power relation,
not smoothness or cluster data alone.

Two global calibrations further delimit the remaining capacity.  For every fixed $p\ge5$,
elementary order lifting
gives $\lambda_p=O_p(T^2)$, so no fixed set of nonstructural primes carries cubic mass.
Also $R_{\mathcal J_T}$ is primitive of degree $O(T)$, whence
\[
 \#\{(u,v)\bmod p^e:R_{\mathcal J_T}(u,v)\equiv0\pmod{p^e}\}
 \le O(T)p^{2e-1};
\]
this is only a density bound and cannot exclude one fixed exceptional pair.  At every fixed
integral control $x\in\Nzero$, by contrast, the endpoint gcd sum has the full cubic scale and
$R_{\mathcal J_T}(2^x,3^x)=0$ once the table is large enough.  Thus
\eqref{crit:eq-triangular-gap-gcd} shows that, among nonstructural primes, any cancellation
beyond the subcubic pairwise ratio-gap budget must be collective.  The CRT specializations
above evade it because their group changes with $T$.

The raw bad-cluster capacity in~\eqref{crit:eq-bad-cluster-capacity} cannot itself be made
small.  For $d=(r,s)\in\Z^2$, set
\[
 H_\triangle(d)=\max\{r_+\log2+s_+\log3,
                         r_-\log2+s_-\log3\}.
\]
Here $r_\pm=\max\{\pm r,0\}$ and $s_\pm=\max\{\pm s,0\}$.

\begin{proposition}[Full capacity of the bad triangle geometry]
\label{crit:prop-bad-cluster-full-capacity}
For the complete size triangle, the primes that are not geometrically bad contribute only
\[
 \sum_{\substack{p\ge5\\p\ \mathrm{not\ geometrically\ bad}}}
 \lambda_p\log p=O(T^2\log(2+T)).
\]
Consequently, for every fixed hypothetical pair $(M,A)$,
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{\substack{p\nmid6MA\\p\ \mathrm{geometrically\ bad}}}
 \lambda_p\log p
 \ge \frac{T^3}{3\log2\log3}-O_{M,A}(T^2\log(2+T)).
 \label{crit:eq-bad-cluster-full-capacity}
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
A prime counted in the first sum has a unique simple affine maximal class
$C=\{e_0+kd:0\le k\le\lambda_p\}$.  Each of
$C-(1,0)$, $C-(0,1)$, and $C+(1,0)$, whenever it stays inside $\mathcal J_T$, is a congruent
subset contained in a distinct residue class of size at least $|C|$.  Uniqueness therefore
forces the two coordinate minima of $C$ to be zero and its top edge to lie within $\log2$ of
the boundary.  For
$v=\lambda_pd$, its endpoints are $v_-$ and $v_+$ in the same coordinatewise convention, so
\[
 T-\log2<H_\triangle(v)\le T.
\]
For fixed $\lambda$, this constant-width lattice shell contains $O(T/\lambda+1)$ possible
steps $d$; summing over $\lambda=O(T)$ gives $O(T\log(2+T))$ pairs $(\lambda,d)$.
Every prime assigned to one pair divides
\[
 2^{r_+}3^{s_+}-2^{r_-}3^{s_-},
\]
and hence the sum of $\lambda\log p$ over that pair is at most
$\lambda H_\triangle(d)\le T$.  This proves the first estimate.  Now
\eqref{crit:eq-away-capacity} gives the full nonstructural capacity, and the finitely many
primes dividing $MA$ contribute only $O_{M,A}(T^2)$ by the fixed-prime estimate above.
Subtracting proves~\eqref{crit:eq-bad-cluster-full-capacity}.
\end{proof}

Thus downward closure does not make the error term in
\eqref{crit:eq-bad-cluster-capacity} lower order: almost all source capacity is forced into
its bad side.  There is nevertheless one exact refinement.  Under the simple-cluster
hypothesis, if all maximal classes have the same affine step $d=(r,s)$ up to orientation,
then their confluent coordinates share the factor
\begin{equation}
 \overline R_E(U,V)=
 \bigl(U^{r_+}V^{s_+}-U^{r_-}V^{s_-}\bigr)^{m-1}
 Q_{p,E}(U,V)
 \label{crit:eq-parallel-cluster-factor}
\end{equation}
over $\mathbf F_p$, where $m$ is their common maximal size.  This is the ordinary
$(m-1)$st finite difference along each class.  The common binomial is charged to the
pairwise budget; the genuinely unresolved quantities are the vanishing and higher $p$-adic
lifts of the output-sensitive transverse factor $Q_{p,E}(M,A)$, together with nonparallel
and deeper clusters.

Finally, $E\in\Q[[z]]$: its reciprocal-zero power sums are
\[
 \sum_{a,b\ge0}2^{-ak}3^{-bk}
 =\frac1{(1-2^{-k})(1-3^{-k})}\in\Q,
\]
and Newton identities make every Taylor coefficient rational.  Therefore rational Taylor
coefficients and any finite collection of rational Hermite normalizations cannot select the
critical interpolant: adding $qz^LP(z)E(z)$ preserves all node values and any prescribed
finite jet while retaining critical growth.

\subsection{The reciprocal Stieltjes moment lattice}
\label{crit:reciprocal-moment-lattice}

The same transform has an output-sensitive dual.  Assume a hypothetical nonintegral
counterexample and put $\eta=1/x\in(0,1)$.  Choose distinct exponent pairs
$e_i=(a_i,b_i)\in\Nzero^2$ so that
\[
 u_i=M^{a_i}A^{b_i}\quad(0\le i\le n)
\]
are increasing, and put $v_i=2^{a_i}3^{b_i}=u_i^\eta$.  For
$P(T)=\prod_{i=0}^n(T-u_i)$ and $n\ge2d+1$, define
\begin{equation}
 h_r=\frac{\sin\pi\eta}{\pi}
 \int_0^\infty\frac{s^{\eta+r}}{\prod_{i=0}^n(s+u_i)}\,ds
 \qquad(0\le r\le2d).
 \label{crit:eq-reciprocal-moments}
\end{equation}
Residues give the exact rational formula
\begin{equation}
 h_r=(-1)^{n+r+1}\sum_{i=0}^n\frac{u_i^rv_i}{P'(u_i)}>0.
 \label{crit:eq-reciprocal-barycentric}
\end{equation}
Let
$\Delta=\prod_{i<j}(u_j-u_i)$ and $k_r=\Delta h_r$.  Since
$\Delta/P'(u_i)$ is, up to sign, the product of the gaps not incident to $u_i$, every
$k_r$ is a positive integer.  Consequently
\begin{equation}
 K_d=(k_{i+j})_{0\le i,j\le d}
 \quad\text{is integral and positive definite},
 \qquad \det K_d\ge1.
 \label{crit:eq-integral-hankel-lattice}
\end{equation}
After normalizing the measure in~\eqref{crit:eq-reciprocal-moments} by $h_0$, every
nonzero $Q\in\Z[s]$ of degree at most $d$ satisfies
\begin{equation}
 \int_0^\infty Q(s)^2\,d\mu(s)
 =\frac{\text{a positive integer}}{k_0}\ge\frac1{k_0},
 \qquad
 \det\left(\frac{h_{i+j}}{h_0}\right)_{0\le i,j\le d}
 \ge k_0^{-(d+1)}.
 \label{crit:eq-reciprocal-lattice-floor}
\end{equation}
The determinant has substantially more integral content than the unit floor shows.  Put
$N=n+1$, $m=d+1$, and form the $N\times N$ alternant whose $i$th row is
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal B_{i,\bullet}=
 (1,u_i,\ldots,u_i^{N-m-1},v_i,u_iv_i,\ldots,u_i^{m-1}v_i).
 \label{crit:eq-reciprocal-alternant}
\end{equation}
Cauchy--Binet followed by complementary Vandermonde factorization gives the exact identity
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{
 \det K_d=(-1)^{mN+\binom m2}\Delta^{m-1}\det\mathcal B.}
 \label{crit:eq-reciprocal-alternant-identity}
\end{equation}
Since positivity fixes the sign of the right side and $\det\mathcal B$ is a nonzero integer,
\begin{equation}
 \det K_d\ge\Delta^d,
 \qquad
 \det\left(\frac{h_{i+j}}{h_0}\right)_{0\le i,j\le d}
 \ge\frac1{\Delta h_0^{d+1}}
 =\frac{\Delta^d}{k_0^{d+1}}.
 \label{crit:eq-reciprocal-strong-floor}
\end{equation}
There is an entrywise refinement as well.  If
\[
 L_F=\operatorname{lcm}_i|P'(u_i)|,
 \qquad G_F=\gcd_i\left|\frac{\Delta}{P'(u_i)}\right|=\frac{\Delta}{L_F},
\]
then $G_F$ divides every $k_r$.  The normalized quadratic floor in
\eqref{crit:eq-reciprocal-lattice-floor} can therefore be strengthened from $1/k_0$ to
$G_F/k_0=1/(L_Fh_0)$.

In fact no choice of nodes or matrix size can make the residual alternant small.  Let
$q_0<\cdots<q_{N-1}$ be the increasing rearrangement of
\[
 \{xk:0\le k<N-m\}\cup\{1+xk:0\le k<m\},
 \qquad G(N+1)=\prod_{r=1}^{N-1}r!.
\]
For every $x\ge2$, $1\le m<N$, and distinct integers
$1\le v_0<\cdots<v_{N-1}$, the HCIZ identity gives the shape-free estimate
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{
 |\det\mathcal B|
 \ge \frac{\prod_{i<j}(q_j-q_i)}{G(N+1)}
       \prod_{i<j}(v_j-v_i)
 \ge \prod_{i<j}(v_j-v_i)
 \ge G(N+1).}
 \label{crit:eq-reciprocal-shape-free}
\end{equation}
Indeed, the sorted exponent list begins with the pairs $kx,kx+1$ and then continues with
the unused tail of the longer block.  Thus $q_j-j$ is nonnegative and nondecreasing, so
$\prod_{i<j}(q_j-q_i)\ge G(N+1)$.  Put $a_i=\log v_i$.  In the HCIZ integral the diagonal
matrices $\operatorname{diag}(a_i)$ and
$\operatorname{diag}(q_j-j)$ are positive semidefinite; hence every integrand for the
$q$-spectrum is at least the corresponding integrand for $0,1,\ldots,N-1$.  Dividing the
two HCIZ identities proves the first inequality.  The last follows from
$v_j-v_i\ge j-i$.  This proof uses real exponents, so it applies directly to a hypothetical
nonintegral $x>12$; it also covers $m>N/2$, where the Stieltjes integrals themselves cease
to converge.

There is a matching free-energy law for arbitrary node geometries in the convergent range.
Let $t_{i,T}=\log v_{i,T}$ with $0\le t_{1,T}<\cdots<t_{N,T}\le CT$, let
$N=N_T\to\infty$ and $m=m_T$ satisfy $2m\le N$ for every $T$ and
$m/N\to\varrho\in(0,1/2]$, and suppose the empirical quantiles
$\mathcal Q_T(s)=T^{-1}t_{\lceil Ns\rceil,T}$, $0<s\le1$, converge in $L^1(0,1)$ to a nondecreasing
$\mathcal Q\ge0$.  With $\log^-y=\max\{0,-\log y\}$, assume also $\log(NT)=o(T)$ and the
microscopic separation condition
\[
 \sum_{i<j}\log^-|t_{j,T}-t_{i,T}|=o(TN^2).
\]
Writing
\[
 \mathsf M_{\mathcal Q}=\int_0^1\mathcal Q(s)\,ds,\qquad
 \mathsf A_{\mathcal Q}=\int_0^1s\mathcal Q(s)\,ds,
\]
Andr\'eief's identity and the HCIZ variational formula yield
\begin{align}
 \frac{\log\Delta_T}{xTN^2}&\longrightarrow\mathsf A_{\mathcal Q},
 &\frac{\log h_{0,T}}{xTN}&\longrightarrow-\mathsf M_{\mathcal Q},\nonumber\\
 \frac{\log\det G_d}{xTN^2}&\longrightarrow
 \frac12\int_0^{2\varrho}(2\varrho-s)\mathcal Q(s)\,ds,
 &\frac{\log|\det\mathcal B|}{xTN^2}&\longrightarrow
 \Phi_{\varrho}(\mathcal Q),
 \label{crit:eq-reciprocal-quantile-law}
\end{align}
where
\begin{equation}
 \Phi_{\varrho}(\mathcal Q)
 =\frac12\int_0^{2\varrho}s\mathcal Q(s)\,ds
  +\int_{2\varrho}^1(s-\varrho)\mathcal Q(s)\,ds.
 \label{crit:eq-reciprocal-quantile-functional}
\end{equation}
The particle optimizer has quantile $Z(r)=\mathcal Q(2r)$ for
$0\le r\le\varrho$.  Moreover
\begin{equation}
 \Phi_{\varrho}(\mathcal Q)
 \ge\left(\frac12-\varrho+\varrho^2\right)\mathsf M_{\mathcal Q}
 \ge\frac14\mathsf M_{\mathcal Q};
 \label{crit:eq-reciprocal-quantile-positive}
\end{equation}
it decreases with $\varrho$ and equals $\mathsf A_{\mathcal Q}/2$ at
$\varrho=1/2$.  Hence every noncollapsed limiting shape has a strictly positive residual
exponent.  A collapsed scale cannot help either, by the exact superfactorial bound
\eqref{crit:eq-reciprocal-shape-free}.

For calibration, take the complete input triangle
\[
 \mathcal S_T=\{v=2^a3^b:\log v\le T\},\qquad u=v^x,
 \qquad \mathcal L=\log2\log3.
\]
Here $N\sim T^2/(2\mathcal L)$ and $\mathcal Q(s)=\sqrt s$, so
\eqref{crit:eq-reciprocal-quantile-law} becomes
\begin{align}
 \log\Delta_T&=\frac{x}{10\mathcal L^2}T^5+o(T^5),
 &\log h_{0,T}&=-\frac{x}{3\mathcal L}T^3+o(T^3),\nonumber\\
 \log\det G_d&=\frac{2\sqrt2}{15}\,
   \frac{x\varrho^{5/2}}{\mathcal L^2}T^5+o(T^5),
 \label{crit:eq-reciprocal-triangle-asymptotics}
\end{align}
and
\begin{equation}
 \log|\det\mathcal B|
 =\frac{xT^5}{\mathcal L^2}
 \left(\frac1{10}-\frac{\varrho}{6}
       +\frac{2\sqrt2}{15}\varrho^{5/2}\right)+o(T^5).
 \label{crit:eq-reciprocal-alternant-growth}
\end{equation}
The coefficient decreases to $1/20$ at $\varrho=1/2$.  At the exact endpoint $N=2m$,
$x=2$ makes $\mathcal B$ the ordinary input Vandermonde, while $x=3$ gives that
Vandermonde times a positive Schur factor.  Thus the triangle calculation is the sharp
$x=2$ calibration of the universal no-go, not a peculiarity of that exhaustion.

The finite cofactor, integral-Hankel, quadratic-lattice transport, node--LCM content
divisibility, and common-content amplification are \statuslean{} in
\lean{ReciprocalMomentLatticeFinite}; the gcd characterization, alternant identity,
Stieltjes representation, positivity, shape-free HCIZ comparison, and asymptotic audit are
paper results.

\subsection{Cyclotomic defect cascades and familywise private support}
\label{crit:cyclotomic-defects}

The exact logarithmic determinant acquires a positive multiscale decomposition after the
power values are shifted by $\pm1$.  Put $X=\log2$, $Y=\log3$, and define, for $n\ge1$,
\begin{align}
 \Delta_n^+&=Y\log(M^n+1)-X\log(A^n+1),\nonumber\\
 \Delta_n^-&=Y\log(M^n-1)-X\log(A^n-1),
 &E_n&=-\Delta_n^- .
 \label{crit:eq-shifted-defects}
\end{align}
Writing $u=M^{-n}$ and using $A^{-n}=u^{\thetaq}$ gives
\begin{align}
 \frac{\Delta_n^+}{X}
 &=\thetaq\log(1+u)-\log(1+u^{\thetaq}),\nonumber\\
 \frac{\Delta_n^-}{X}
 &=\thetaq\log(1-u)-\log(1-u^{\thetaq}).
 \label{crit:eq-shifted-u}
\end{align}
Strict convexity shows $\Delta_n^-<0<\Delta_n^+$.  Moreover
\[
 \frac{d}{du}\left(-\thetaq\log(1-u)+\log(1-u^{\thetaq})\right)
 =\frac{\thetaq(1-u^{\thetaq-1})}{(1-u)(1-u^{\thetaq})}>0,
\]
so $E_n$ strictly decreases to zero.  Taylor expansion and
$(T^n-1)(T^n+1)=T^{2n}-1$ give
\begin{align}
 E_n&=YM^{-n}-XA^{-n}+O(M^{-2n}),
 &\Delta_n^+&=YM^{-n}-XA^{-n}+O(M^{-2n}),\nonumber\\
 \Delta_n^+&=E_n-E_{2n},
 &E_n&=\sum_{j\ge0}\Delta_{2^jn}^+.
 \label{crit:eq-dyadic-defect-cascade}
\end{align}
The constants depend only on the fixed pair.  A bound without a hidden constant is
\begin{equation}
 YM^{-n}\frac{1-(M/A)^n}{(1+M^{-n})(1+A^{-n})}
 \le \Delta_n^+<YM^{-n}.
 \label{crit:eq-plus-defect-bound}
\end{equation}

For $Q_{k,n}(T)=(T^{kn}-1)/(T^n-1)$ normalize its $k$ monomials by
\[
 p_\ell=\frac{M^{\ell n}}{Q_{k,n}(M)}\qquad(0\le\ell<k).
\]
Additivity of the logarithmic determinant gives the quotient law
\begin{equation}
 Y\log Q_{k,n}(M)-X\log Q_{k,n}(A)
 =E_n-E_{kn}
 =X(\thetaq-1)H_{\thetaq}(p)>0,
 \label{crit:eq-renyi-quotient}
\end{equation}
where $H_{\thetaq}(p)=(1-\thetaq)^{-1}\log\sum p_\ell^{\thetaq}$.
For every prime $p$, the prime-power factors partition the same mass:
\begin{align}
 \mathcal C_{p^j,n}
 &:=
 Y\log\Phi_{p^j}(M^n)-X\log\Phi_{p^j}(A^n)
 =E_{p^{j-1}n}-E_{p^jn}>0,\nonumber\\
 E_n&=\sum_{j\ge1}\mathcal C_{p^j,n},
 &
 \prod_{j\ge1}
 \frac{\Phi_{p^j}(M^n)^{\thetaq}}{\Phi_{p^j}(A^n)}
 &=\frac{1-A^{-n}}{(1-M^{-n})^{\thetaq}}.
 \label{crit:eq-cyclotomic-partition}
\end{align}
The R\'enyi notation records a deterministic strict
$\ell^1$--$\ell^{\thetaq}$ inequality, not a probabilistic input.

The dyadic factors have additional arithmetic structure.  For $T>1$ and $j\ge1$, put
$W_j(T)=T^{2^j}+1$.  If $i\ne j$, then
\begin{equation}
 \gcd(W_i(T),W_j(T))=
 \begin{cases}1,&T\text{ even},\\2,&T\text{ odd}.\end{cases}
 \label{crit:eq-dyadic-private-gcd}
\end{equation}
Each $W_j(T)$ has an odd prime divisor $q_j$, and every such divisor satisfies
\begin{equation}
 \operatorname{ord}_{q_j}(T)=2^{j+1},
 \qquad 2^{j+1}\mid q_j-1.
 \label{crit:eq-dyadic-private-order}
\end{equation}
Thus $q_j$ is private to its level, $\{W_j(T):j\ge1\}$ is multiplicatively independent,
and
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{j\le J}\log q_j\ge\frac{\log2}{2}J^2+O(J).
 \label{crit:eq-private-support-budget}
\end{equation}
The order, congruence, and level-separation core is \statuslean{} in
\lean{DyadicPrivateSupport}; existence, the gcd law, and the finite valuation argument are
the elementary paper layer.

Apply this separately to
$U_j=M^{2^j}+1$ and $V_j=A^{2^j}+1$.  With
\[
 L_j=\begin{pmatrix}X&\log U_j\\Y&\log V_j\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad \Gamma_j=-\det L_j=\Delta_{2^j}^+,
\]
the second columns acquire one-sided private odd support while
\begin{equation}
 \Gamma_j\sim YM^{-2^j},
 \qquad
 \frac{-\log\Gamma_j}{\log V_j}\longrightarrow\frac XY,
 \qquad
 \frac{U_j^{\thetaq}}{V_j}-1\sim\thetaq M^{-2^j}.
 \label{crit:eq-private-critical-slope}
\end{equation}
The Euclidean distance from $(\log U_j,\log V_j)$ to $\R(X,Y)$ is exactly
$\Gamma_j/\sqrt{X^2+Y^2}$.  Yet the absolute power error grows like
$\thetaq M^{(\thetaq-1)2^j}$, and every integral pair $(2^m,3^m)$ has the same normalized
critical slope.  Privacy is only within each ladder: no disjointness between the $U$- and
$V$-supports follows.

This extremality is also a contact ceiling for fixed transfers.  Let $P$ be a fixed monic
polynomial of degree $d\ge1$, suppose its coefficients in degrees
$d-1,\ldots,d-r+1$ vanish, and let the coefficient in degree $d-r$ be the fixed nonzero
$c$.  Then
\begin{equation}
 Y\log P(M^n)-X\log P(A^n)
 =cYM^{-rn}-cXA^{-rn}+O(M^{-(r+1)n}),
 \label{crit:eq-fixed-polynomial-contact}
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}
 \frac{-\log|Y\log P(M^n)-X\log P(A^n)|}{\log P(A^n)}
 \longrightarrow\frac{r}{d\thetaq}\le\frac1{\thetaq}.
 \label{crit:eq-fixed-polynomial-ceiling}
\end{equation}
Equality forces $P(T)=T^d+c$.  For a fixed cyclotomic polynomial the slope is
$1/(\thetaq\varphi(\operatorname{rad}m))$; among prime-power ladders it is
$1/(\thetaq(p-1))$, so only the dyadic ladder is critical.  This theorem is deliberately
fixed-polynomial and gives no uniform bound for degrees or coefficients varying with $n$.

Reciprocity gives a complementary sharp ceiling.  Let $P,Q\in\Z[T]$ be distinct monic
reciprocal polynomials of the same degree $D$, both with constant term $1$, and suppose
\[
 \frac{P(T)}{Q(T)}=1+cT^{-K}+O(T^{-K-1}),\qquad c\ne0.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
 2K\le D,
 \label{crit:eq-reciprocal-half-contact}
\end{equation}
with equality exactly when $D$ is even and $P-Q=cT^{D/2}$.  Indeed $P-Q$ is reciprocal,
so its smallest and largest nonzero exponents are paired about $D/2$.  Under a hypothetical
counterexample, the integer
\[
 P(A^s)Q(M^s)-Q(A^s)P(M^s)
\]
therefore has logarithmic size
\begin{equation}
 \bigl(D(1+\thetaq)-K\bigr)s\log M+O(1)
 \ge D\left(\thetaq+\frac12\right)s\log M+O(1).
 \label{crit:eq-reciprocal-filter-growth}
\end{equation}
Thus every fixed reciprocal or cyclotomic filter produces a rapidly growing nonzero integer.
The finite support and equality classification in~\eqref{crit:eq-reciprocal-half-contact}
are \statuslean{} in \lean{ReciprocalHalfContact}; the orbit asymptotic is a paper argument.

These formulas isolate a sharp open interface.  For an arbitrary fixed integer pair define
$\lambda_j=-\log_{V_j}|\det L_j|$ only on the eventually nonzero tail.  A theorem saying
that simultaneous power-primitivity and external support force
$\liminf\lambda_j<X/Y$ would prove the conjecture.  Integral controls show that no
one-sided private-support argument can establish it: cross-ladder synchronization is the
missing datum.

\subsection{Fresh-prime Newton synchronization}
\label{crit:fresh-prime}

The primitive-cancellation target in~\eqref{crit:eq-denominator-lower} has an exact local
form.  Let $s_0,\ldots,s_j$ be distinct positive integer nodes, let $y_i\in\Z$, and let
$P_{j-1}$ interpolate the first $j$ pairs.  With
\[
 W_{j-1}(X)=\prod_{i<j}(X-s_i),
\]
the Newton append coefficient is
\begin{equation}
 c_j=[s_0,\ldots,s_j]y
 =\frac{y_j-P_{j-1}(s_j)}{W_{j-1}(s_j)}.
 \label{crit:eq-newton-append}
\end{equation}
Suppose a prime $p$ divides no old difference $s_t-s_r$ but divides
$W_{j-1}(s_j)$.  There is a unique $i_p<j$ with $s_j\equiv s_{i_p}\pmod p$.  Put
$e_p=v_p(W_{j-1}(s_j))$.  Lagrange interpolation is integral at $p$, and hence
\begin{equation}
 y_j\not\equiv y_{i_p}\pmod p
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 v_p(c_j)=-e_p.
 \label{crit:eq-fresh-pole}
\end{equation}
Thus the entire fresh $p$-power survives in the reduced denominator.  Conversely, any
cancellation of its first power forces $y_j\equiv y_{i_p}\pmod p$; cancellation of higher
powers requires genuinely higher congruences.

For the smooth table $s_i=2^{a_i}3^{b_i}$ and $y_i=M^{a_i}A^{b_i}$, and for
$p\nmid6MA$, a canceled fresh pole transfers the one relation
\begin{equation}
 2^{\Delta a}3^{\Delta b}\equiv1,\qquad
 M^{\Delta a}A^{\Delta b}\equiv1\pmod p.
 \label{crit:eq-one-local-transfer}
\end{equation}
One relation is not a local common exponent.  The exact finite-group criterion is
\begin{equation}
 \ker\bigl((u,v)\mapsto2^u3^v\bmod p\bigr)
 \subseteq
 \ker\bigl((u,v)\mapsto M^uA^v\bmod p\bigr)
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \begin{cases}
 M\equiv2^{k_p}\pmod p,\\
 A\equiv3^{k_p}\pmod p
 \end{cases}
 \label{crit:eq-local-common-exponent}
\end{equation}
for some $k_p$ modulo the order of $\langle2,3\rangle\subset\mathbb F_p^\times$.  Indeed, full
relation transfer defines an endomorphism of that cyclic subgroup.  A single small top
denominator supplies neither the kernel inclusion nor an almost-all-prime family of such
exponents.

Two exact calibrations prevent false positives.  First, if an exponent pattern $\Omega$ has
$N+1$ nodes and top coefficient $q_\Omega=a/d$ in lowest terms, translating it by $(u,v)$,
with $c=2^u3^v$ and $R=M^uA^v$, gives
\begin{equation}
 q_{\Omega+(u,v)}=Rc^{-N}q_\Omega,\qquad
 \frac{d_{\Omega+(u,v)}}{P_{\Omega+(u,v)}}
 =\frac{d}{cP_\Omega\gcd(aR,dc^N)}.
 \label{crit:eq-translated-block}
\end{equation}
The apparent saving for a drifting block is automatic for every value table.  Such blocks
are not nested; adjoining them restores the omitted old--new cross-resultants.

Second, fix a smooth ray and put $q=2^u3^v$, $r=M^uA^v$.  Its order-$n$ coefficient is
\begin{equation}
 \frac{\prod_{i=0}^{n-1}(r-q^i)}
 {q^{n(n-1)/2}\prod_{k=1}^n(q^k-1)}.
 \label{crit:eq-ray-coefficient}
\end{equation}
Let $\ell$ be an odd prime, let $d_\ell$ be the reduced denominator in
\eqref{crit:eq-ray-coefficient}, and remove the $\ell$-primary part by writing
\[
 \Phi_\ell(q)^{[\ell]}=
 \frac{\Phi_\ell(q)}{\ell^{v_\ell(\Phi_\ell(q))}}.
\]
Prime-power bookkeeping at the first collision gives the exact divisor
\begin{equation}
 \frac{\Phi_\ell(q)^{[\ell]}}
 {\gcd(\Phi_\ell(q)^{[\ell]},r^\ell-1)}\mid d_\ell.
 \label{crit:eq-ray-fresh-divisor}
\end{equation}
For $p\mid\Phi_\ell(q)$, $p\ne\ell$, one has $\operatorname{ord}_p(q)=\ell$; any canceled
$p$-power in the unique numerator factor also divides $r^\ell-1$.  Under a hypothetical
nonintegral solution, $q$ and $r$ are multiplicatively independent, because a rational
exponent compatible with both original bases is integral.  The BCZ gcd estimate therefore
implies
\begin{equation}
 \log d_\ell\ge \ell\log q-o(\ell).
 \label{crit:eq-ray-bcz-lower}
\end{equation}
This is an uncanceled fresh denominator \emph{layer}; it need not be supported only on
value-mismatch primes, since a synchronized prime can cancel one power while higher powers
survive.  Fixed rays therefore make the desired denominator upper bound worse, not better.
The one-step append/evaluation and barycentric scaling identities are \statuslean{} in
\lean{NewtonCollisionCore}.  The localization, valuation, synchronization, translation,
and ray-divisor statements above are \statusnew{} paper arguments; BCZ is the cited
\statusknown{} input.

Fresh layers can in fact be made asymptotically as large as the whole node product, but this
strengthens the obstruction rather than overcoming it.  If a fixed pair $M,A>1$ is not
$(2^k,3^k)$, at least one of
\[
 (B,C)=(2,M),\qquad(3,A),\qquad(6,MA)
\]
is multiplicatively independent.  Given a finite smooth-node set $F$ containing $1$, choose
a sufficiently large prime $n$ so that $\Phi_n(B)$ is coprime to the old Vandermonde.  At the
new node $B^n\mapsto C^n$ every prime factor of $\Phi_n(B)$ gives a unique collision with
$1$, and the fresh-pole calculation yields
\begin{equation}
 R_n:=\frac{\Phi_n(B)}{\gcd(\Phi_n(B),C^n-1)}
 \mid \mathfrak d_{F\cup\{B^n\}},
 \qquad \log R_n=n\log B-o(n).
 \label{crit:eq-sparse-spike-divisor}
\end{equation}
The asymptotic is BCZ.  Recursively interleaving the next missing smooth node with a prime
spike whose height dominates all preceding nodes produces one nested exhaustion and a
subsequence along which
\begin{equation}
 \frac{\log\mathfrak d_F}{\log\prod_{s\in F}s}\ge1-o(1).
 \label{crit:eq-sparse-spike-scale}
\end{equation}
This construction works for every fixed off-curve integer pair and uses no real common
exponent.  More importantly, it has the wrong polarity for
\eqref{crit:eq-denominator-lower}: both results are lower bounds for the reduced denominator.
A larger denominator merely permits a larger reduced numerator, whereas closure requires an
upper bound $\mathfrak d_F=o(\prod F)$.  Likewise, even after combining a fixed-level
Kummer density with the generic $O(\sqrt p)$ short-relation estimate, the guaranteed
contribution in a $K\times K$ table reaches only $p\ll K^2$, hence has quadratic squarefree
logarithmic mass, while $\log\prod F_K=\Theta(K^3)$; residue-symbol depth is not a substitute
for gap valuation.
The missing statement is therefore an output-specific upper bound, or a theorem correlating
prime divisors of the sparse $S$-unit gaps with the detecting Frobenius classes.  Chebotarev
alone supplies neither.

\subsection{Support rigidity and Kummer defect primes}
\label{crit:support-defects}

The finite determinant has a primitive integral model.  For
$u\in\Q_{>0}^{\times}$ put
\[
 L_u(X)=\sum_pv_p(u)X_p,
 \qquad
 Q_{M,A}(X)=L_A(X)X_2-L_M(X)X_3.
\]
In the simultaneous normalization
\[
 M=2^aw^d,\qquad A=3^bv^e,
\]
where $w$ is odd, $3\nmid v$, and $w,v$ have primitive valuation vectors, one has
\begin{equation}
 \operatorname{cont}(Q_{M,A})=\gcd(d,e,|a-b|).
 \label{crit:eq-two-star-content}
\end{equation}
Least-output primitivity makes this content $1$.  Thus $Q_{M,A}$ remains nonzero modulo
every prime, while $Q_{M,A}=0$ over $\Z$ exactly for
$(M,A)=(2^n,3^n)$.  The coefficient-content identity, its least-output specialization, and
nonzero reduction modulo every nontrivial modulus are \statuslean{} in
\lean{TwoStarContent}; the formal zero criterion is \statuslean{} in
\lean{FormalPrimeDeterminant}.

The local kernel criterion has a sharp classical global counterpart.  A theorem of
Corrales--Rodr\'iguez and Schoof~\cite{CRS1997} states that if $u,v\in\Q^\times$ and, for
all but finitely many primes and every integer $n$,
\[
 u^n\equiv1\pmod p\quad\Longrightarrow\quad v^n\equiv1\pmod p,
\]
then $v=u^k$ for some $k\in\Z$.  Consequently, for positive integers $M,A$, the following
conditions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item $M=2^k$ and $A=3^k$ for some $k\in\Nzero$;
\item relation-kernel inclusion holds for almost every good prime;
\item a local common exponent $k_p$ exists for almost every good prime;
\item for almost every prime,
\begin{equation}
 \operatorname{ord}_p(M)\mid\operatorname{ord}_p(2),\qquad
 \operatorname{ord}_p(A)\mid\operatorname{ord}_p(3),\qquad
 \operatorname{ord}_p(MA)\mid\operatorname{ord}_p(6).
 \label{crit:eq-three-order-shadows}
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}
The last implication applies the support theorem to the three pairs and then uses unique
factorization.  For a fixed candidate even one of the three almost-everywhere divisibilities
forces $x\in\Z$.  This is an exact local--global reformulation, not a proof that a
counterexample supplies the local hypothesis.

The four Kummer coordinates give an exact finite density law.  For every sufficiently large
odd prime $\ell$ outside the saturation set, put $K_\ell=\Q(\zeta_\ell)$ and let
$V_\ell\subset K_\ell^\times/K_\ell^{\times\ell}$ be the space spanned by $2,3,M,A$.
Its dimension is the ordinary multiplicative rank, and its dual character space
$W_\ell=V_\ell^\vee$ embeds in $\mathbb F_\ell^4$ by evaluation on those four generators.
For an unramified prime ideal $\mathfrak p$ write
\begin{equation}
 (u_1,u_2,v_1,v_2)=
 (\kappa_{\mathfrak p}(2),\kappa_{\mathfrak p}(3),
  \kappa_{\mathfrak p}(M),\kappa_{\mathfrak p}(A)).
 \label{crit:eq-kummer-coordinate-vector}
\end{equation}
Exact local compatibility means that $(v_1,v_2)=t(u_1,u_2)$ for some
$t\in\mathbb F_\ell$; it is stronger than the determinant equation
$u_1v_2-u_2v_1=0$ when the source pair vanishes.  In the full space there are exactly
\begin{equation}
 1+\ell(\ell^2-1)=\ell^3-\ell+1
 \label{crit:eq-compatible-vector-count}
\end{equation}
compatible vectors.  Chebotarev therefore gives the relative prime-ideal densities
\begin{align}
 \operatorname{dens}_{\mathrm{rank},4}(\mathrm{compatible})
 &=\frac1\ell-\frac1{\ell^3}+\frac1{\ell^4},\notag\\
 \operatorname{dens}_{\mathrm{rank},3}(\mathrm{compatible})
 &=\frac1\ell-\frac1{\ell^2}+\frac1{\ell^3}.
 \label{crit:eq-exact-kummer-densities}
\end{align}
The second formula assumes that the rank-three Kummer hyperplane remains transverse modulo
$\ell$, which again excludes only finitely many primes.  For every fixed $t$,
compatibility has density exactly $\ell^{-2}$ in either rank.  Thus a nonintegral candidate
is locally incompatible on density $1-1/\ell+O(\ell^{-2})$, even though its real logarithm
matrix has rank one.  The exact existential-scalar count, including the zero-source case, is
\statuslean{} in \lean{KummerCompatibilityFinite}; the Kummer realization and Chebotarev
passage are classical paper inputs.

Compatibility at higher prime-power depth has an exact count.  Over
$\Z/\ell^e\Z$, the number of compatible four-coordinate vectors in full rank is
\begin{equation}
 N_4(\ell,e)
 =1+\ell(\ell^2-1)\frac{\ell^{3e}-1}{\ell^3-1},
 \qquad
 \operatorname{prop}_4=\frac{N_4(\ell,e)}{\ell^{4e}},
 \label{crit:eq-prime-power-compatible-rank-four}
\end{equation}
whereas a transverse rank-three hyperplane contains
\begin{equation}
 N_3(\ell,e)
 =1+\ell\frac{\ell^{2e}-1}{\ell+1},
 \qquad
 \operatorname{prop}_3=\frac{N_3(\ell,e)}{\ell^{3e}}.
 \label{crit:eq-prime-power-compatible-rank-three}
\end{equation}
At $e=1$ these recover~\eqref{crit:eq-exact-kummer-densities}; as $e\to\infty$ the
local proportions decay like $\ell^{-e}$.  Here transverse means that, for the primitive
rank-three relation $c=(c_1,c_2,c_3,c_4)$, the determinant
$c_1c_4-c_2c_3$ is an $\ell$-adic unit.  After Kummer realization these proportions are
relative densities inside the cyclotomic split layer; the corresponding absolute
rational-prime densities have the additional factor $1/\varphi(\ell^e)$.  The full-rank
compatibility count and the unit-transverse post-scalar normal-form count are \statuslean{}
in \lean{PrimePowerKummerCoherence}.  Identifying the latter normal form with compatible
vectors in the Kummer hyperplane, Kummer realization at depth $\ell^e$, and its Chebotarev
interpretation remain paper-level or classical inputs.
At depth one the rank-three relation also determines every zero/nonzero status pattern.
For its coefficient vector $c$, put
$J_\ell=\{i:c_i\not\equiv0\pmod\ell\}$.  If $s$ coordinates in $J_\ell$ and $h$
coordinates outside $J_\ell$ are prescribed nonzero, the count is
\[
 \frac{(\ell-1)^s+(\ell-1)(-1)^s}{\ell}\,(\ell-1)^h;
\]
in particular, a pattern with exactly one active nonzero coordinate is impossible.  Full
rank allows every pattern.  This gives a finite detector for the support of the unique
rank-three relation, but not an archimedean-to-local transfer theorem.

The determinant condition is weaker than compatibility at a zero source pair, but its
nonvanishing has a complementary density law.  Primitivity in
\eqref{crit:eq-two-star-content} and the finite quadratic-form bound give, for every odd
$\ell$, relative detecting density at least $(1-1/\ell)^2$ among primes splitting in the
cyclotomic layer, hence absolute density at least $(\ell-1)/\ell^2$.  Characteristic two
gives the absolute bound $1/4$.  Outside the finite saturation and rank-discriminant set,
the exact relative/absolute densities are
\begin{equation}
 \begin{array}{c|cc}
 &\text{relative}&\text{absolute}\\ \hline
 \text{rank three}&1-\ell^{-1}&\ell^{-1}\\[2pt]
 \text{rank four}&1-\ell^{-1}-(\ell-1)\ell^{-3}
                  &\ell^{-1}-\ell^{-3}.
 \end{array}
 \label{crit:eq-determinant-chebotarev-densities}
\end{equation}
In particular the cubic universal bounds are $4/9$ relative and $2/9$ absolute.  These
are determinant-transversality densities, not replacements for the stronger
common-scalar counts above.  Chebotarev and Kummer theory are the classical inputs; the
coefficient primitivity is the arithmetic hinge.
At the fixed quadratic and cubic levels the radical extensions have degrees at most $16$
and $162$, with logarithmic discriminant $O(\log(6MA))$.  Effective Chebotarev therefore
gives a detecting prime $\ll\log^2(6MA)$ under GRH for the relevant Dedekind zeta function,
and a fixed power of $6MA$ unconditionally.  These bounds are not uniform in a growing
torsion level.

The same coordinates localize common near-power divisors.  If at such a prime
\begin{equation}
 M^q\equiv2^p,\qquad A^q\equiv3^{p'}\pmod{\mathfrak p},
 \label{crit:eq-mixed-gap-congruences}
\end{equation}
then
\begin{equation}
 q(u_1v_2-u_2v_1)=(p'-p)u_1u_2\quad\text{in }\mathbb F_\ell.
 \label{crit:eq-mixed-gap-determinant}
\end{equation}
In particular, when $p=p'$ and $\ell\nmid q$, a nonzero determinant excludes simultaneous
division of the two gaps.  The finite determinant identity and same-residue obstruction are
\statuslean{} in \lean{MixedGapKummerFinite}.  Thus, for
\[
 D_2(r,s)=M^s-2^r,\qquad D_3(r,s)=A^s-3^r
 \quad(r\ge0, s>0),
\]
every eligible good common prime divisor at a level $\ell\nmid s$ lies on the
determinant-zero locus at that level.  If $s$ is odd this excludes a set of rational primes of density at least
$1/4$; if $3\nmid s$ the cubic exclusion has density at least $2/9$.
The same module verifies the abstract
retention bound
\[
 n_2=0\ \text{or}\ n_3=0
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \min(d_2,d_3)\le\max(d_2-n_2,d_3-n_3),
\]
where $d_2,d_3$ are denominator valuations and $n_2,n_3$ the corresponding numerator
valuations.  Hence, for some fixed $\ell$, common gaps
along every denominator $q$ prime to $\ell$ avoid a positive-density Chebotarev set.  This
does not upper-bound the gcd: one large integer can be supported entirely on the complementary
prime set.  It does turn the missing step into a precise Frobenius-distribution problem for
the prime divisors of the near-power gaps.

The direct ordinary $K_2$ encoding reaches a precise sign barrier.  In Milnor
$K_2(\Q)$~\cite{Milnor1971,Weibel2013} put
\begin{equation}
 \Xi(M,A)=\{M,3\}\{A,2\}.
 \label{crit:eq-steinberg-class}
\end{equation}
It is trivial on every standard pair, and its tame symbols are
\begin{equation}
 \partial_p\Xi=2^{-v_p(A)}3^{-v_p(M)}\pmod p\quad(p\ne2,3),
 \qquad
 \partial_3\Xi=(-1)^{v_3(M)+v_3(A)}
 \overline{M/3^{v_3(M)}}.
 \label{crit:eq-steinberg-tame-symbols}
\end{equation}
The standard-vanishing exterior class has the opposite sign from the symmetric logarithmic
determinant; retaining the symmetric sign makes the exterior class nonzero even on the
integer ray.  Thus the ordinary Steinberg symbol does not encode the required quadratic
period.  This rules out only the direct construction, not symmetric refinements or higher
cohomological operations.

Archimedean closeness does not reduce this local entropy.  With
$k_j=\lfloor jx\rfloor$, $\theta_j=\{jx\}$, the compact rational orbit
\[
 U_j=M^j2^{-k_j}=2^{\theta_j},\qquad
 V_j=A^j3^{-k_j}=3^{\theta_j}
\]
satisfies, for every interval $I\subset[0,1)$ and every residues $r,s\pmod\ell$,
\begin{equation}
 \operatorname{dens}\{j:\theta_j\in I,\ j\equiv r,\ k_j\equiv s\pmod\ell\}
 =\frac{|I|}{\ell^2}.
 \label{crit:eq-carry-phase-equidistribution}
\end{equation}
This is elementary equidistribution of an irrational rotation after restricting $j$ to one
residue class.  At $\mathfrak p$, the Kummer symbols of $(U_j,V_j)$ are the image of
$(j,k_j)$ under
\begin{equation}
 \begin{pmatrix}\kappa(M)&-\kappa(2)\\
                 \kappa(A)&-\kappa(3)\end{pmatrix}.
 \label{crit:eq-mantissa-symbol-map}
\end{equation}
Conditional on any real interval $I$, they are uniform on this matrix image.  A nonzero
Kummer determinant therefore gives all $\ell^2$ symbol pairs even on an arbitrarily short
real arc.  The real orbit is dense and nearly one-dimensional, while its generic finite
residue shadow remains fully two-dimensional.

Failure occurs on a quantitatively structured set.  For multiplicatively independent
$B,C>1$, choose two valuation coordinates with nonzero $2\times2$ minor and an odd prime
$\ell$ not dividing that minor.  Then $B,C$ are independent modulo $\ell$th powers, also
over $\Q(\zeta_\ell)$.  In
\[
 L=\Q(\zeta_\ell,B^{1/\ell},C^{1/\ell})
\]
the set of unramified primes satisfying
\begin{equation}
 p\equiv1\pmod\ell,\qquad
 B\in(\mathbb F_p^\times)^\ell,\qquad
 C\notin(\mathbb F_p^\times)^\ell
 \label{crit:eq-kummer-defect-set}
\end{equation}
has absolute natural density $1/\ell^2$ by Chebotarev.  Every such prime obeys
\[
 v_\ell(\operatorname{ord}_p(B))
 \le v_\ell(p-1)-1
 <v_\ell(\operatorname{ord}_p(C)),
\]
so the order loss is at least one.  For this fixed extension,
\begin{equation}
 \sum_{\substack{p\le X\\p\text{ satisfies }\eqref{crit:eq-kummer-defect-set}}}
 \log p=\frac{X}{\ell^2}+o(X).
 \label{crit:eq-kummer-weighted-primes}
\end{equation}
The witness $\ell$, field, and error term depend on $B,C$; no uniformity in the unknown
candidate is claimed.

These Frobenius defects enter interpolation denominators directly.  If an integral table
$(x_i,y_i)$ is interpolated by $Q\in\Q[X]$ and $\delta(Q)$ is least positive with
$\delta(Q)Q\in\Z[X]$, then
\begin{equation}
 v_p(\delta(Q))\ge
 \max\{0,v_p(x_i-x_j)-v_p(y_i-y_j)\}\qquad(i\ne j).
 \label{crit:eq-collision-valuation}
\end{equation}
Indeed $x_i-x_j$ divides $\delta(Q)(y_i-y_j)$.  On the ray
$B^j\mapsto C^j$, $0\le j\le N$, this yields
\begin{equation}
 \operatorname{lcm}_{1\le n\le N}
 \frac{B^n-1}{\gcd(B^n-1,C^n-1)}
 \mid\delta_N^{\mathrm{ray}}(B,C).
 \label{crit:eq-ray-lcm-divisor}
\end{equation}
For the Kummer witness, the squarefree product
\begin{equation}
 R_N(B,C;\ell)=
 \prod_{\substack{p\le\ell N+1\\p\text{ satisfies }\eqref{crit:eq-kummer-defect-set}}}p
 \quad\text{satisfies}\quad
 R_N\mid\delta_N^{\mathrm{ray}},
 \qquad
 \log R_N=\frac N\ell+o(N).
 \label{crit:eq-kummer-squarefree-divisor}
\end{equation}
It is supported on one Frobenius class, but remains too small by itself to close the
archimedean estimate.

For a good prime define the defect radius
\[
 \rho_p(M,A)=\min_{\substack{2^r3^s\equiv1\ (p)\\M^rA^s\not\equiv1\ (p)}}
 \max(|r|,|s|),
\]
with value $\infty$ if no relation defect exists.  In the square-grid notation of
Section~\ref{res:denominator-lattice}, $\rho_p(M,A)\le K-1$ forces
$p\mid\delta_K$.  Reducing relation exponents modulo $p-1$ gives
\begin{equation}
 \text{failure of a local common exponent at }p
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad p\mid\delta_{p-1}.
 \label{crit:eq-box-defect-detection}
\end{equation}
The index is $p-1$ because the live grid uses exponents $0,\ldots,K-1$.  Showing that many
Kummer defects have $\rho_p$ much smaller than $p$ is a concrete remaining target.

An additive reformulation has a sharp ceiling.  The semigroup homomorphism
\[
 \Phi(2^a3^b)=M^aA^b
\]
would force an integer exponent if it preserved all congruences away from the primes
dividing $6MA$, by the local common-exponent criterion and the support theorem above.
The primitive binary identities among $3$-smooth integers correspond, up to exchange, to
the four adjacent pairs listed in Section~\ref{mom:moments}; all other binary identities are
$3$-smooth scalings.  Their defects are
$M-2$, $A-M-1$, $M^2-A-1$, and $A^2-M^3-1$.  More generally,
\begin{equation}
 \bigl(P(M,A):P\in\Z[X,Y],\ P(2,3)=0\bigr)
 =\gcd(M-2,A-3)\Z.
 \label{crit:eq-additive-defect-ideal}
\end{equation}
At time $n$ the corresponding ideal is generated by
\begin{equation}
 C_n=\gcd(M^n-2^n,A^n-3^n),
 \qquad \log C_n=o(n)
 \label{crit:eq-dynamic-additive-defect}
\end{equation}
for a nonintegral candidate, by the $S$-unit gcd theorem.  Thus primitive binary relations
and same-time polynomial defects cannot supply the exponential congruence support required
by the local criterion; this does not exclude more elaborate, time-dependent additive data.

The support classification is the cited \statusknown{} input.  The finite exact-compatibility
counts are \statuslean{} in \lean{KummerCompatibilityFinite}, and their prime-power
extensions are \statuslean{} in \lean{PrimePowerKummerCoherence}.  The mixed-gap determinant
and same-residue obstruction are \statuslean{} in \lean{MixedGapKummerFinite}.  Chebotarev
densities, mantissa entropy, collision valuation, ray divisor, finite-box bridge, tame-symbol
calculation, and additive ceiling are \statusnew{} paper deductions.  They strengthen the
denominator lower bound without supplying the missing upper bound.

\subsection{Directional gap quotients and exact capture cost}
\label{crit:directional-capture}

The diagonal ray estimate has a homogeneous fixed-direction form.  Fix
$(u,v)\in\Z^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}$ and orient this direction so that
\[
 r=2^u3^v=P/Q>1,\qquad s=M^uA^v=R/S=r^x>1
\]
are in lowest terms.  The homogeneous Corvaja--Zannier gcd theorem gives, when $r$ and $s$
are multiplicatively independent,
\begin{equation}
 \log\gcd(P^n-Q^n,R^n-S^n)=o(n).
 \label{crit:eq-homogeneous-gap-gcd}
\end{equation}
Consequently the reduced directional quotient
\begin{equation}
 G_n(r,s)=\frac{R^n-S^n}{P^n-Q^n}
 \label{crit:eq-directional-gap-quotient}
\end{equation}
has
\begin{equation}
 \log\operatorname{den}G_n=n\log P+o(n),\qquad
 \log|\operatorname{num}G_n|=n\log R+o(n).
 \label{crit:eq-directional-gap-height}
\end{equation}
If $x=k\in\N$, by contrast, $s=r^k$ and $G_n$ is an integer.  Dependence of $r,s$
would make $x$ rational and therefore integral by the elementary rational-exponent
reduction.  Thus every fixed direction has an exact zero-versus-exponential denominator
dichotomy.  The fixed-group refinement in~\eqref{crit:eq-triangular-gap-gcd} sums the
corresponding gcd bounds over the triangular direction set; it still supplies denominator
mass, not the denominator upper bound required for closure.

There is also an exact group-theoretic measure of how far a source gap is from being
captured by a target gap.  Remove from $U_n=P^n-Q^n$ every prime power supported on $RS$,
calling the remaining modulus $\widetilde U_n$, and let
\[
 t_n=\operatorname{ord}_{\widetilde U_n}(RS^{-1})
\]
in the unit group.  The least positive multiplier $h$ for which
$\widetilde U_n\mid R^{hn}-S^{hn}$ is
\begin{equation}
 \boxed{\kappa(n)=\frac{t_n}{\gcd(t_n,n)}.}
 \label{crit:eq-capture-multiplier}
\end{equation}
Equivalently,
\begin{equation}
 \widetilde U_n\mid R^{hn}-S^{hn}
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \kappa(n)\mid h.
 \label{crit:eq-capture-divisibility}
\end{equation}
The finite-group identity behind~\eqref{crit:eq-capture-divisibility} is
\statuslean{} in \lean{CaptureMultiplier}.  For a fixed direction, $\kappa(n)=1$ in
the integral case, whereas in the nonintegral case $\kappa(n)\to\infty$: a bounded
subsequence would fix some $h$ infinitely often.  By LTE, the part removed from
$P^n-Q^n$ at the fixed primes dividing $RS$ has logarithm $O(\log n)$, so
$\widetilde U_n$ retains the full exponential scale.  Its divisibility into the fixed
target gap would then contradict the homogeneous Corvaja--Zannier theorem applied, after
fixing $h$ on that bounded subsequence, to the fixed pair $(r,s^h)$.  This qualitative
phase transition is external-derived and again nonuniform in the direction.

A recent preprint supplies a complementary one-base signature.  For integers $a,b>1$, the
sequence $\gcd(a^n-1,b^n-1)$ satisfies an integer-coefficient constant-recursion relation,
even eventually, exactly when $a,b$ are multiplicatively dependent
