$\sigma_\nu=M^aA^b=\rho_\nu^{\,x}$; for a convergent $p/q$ of $\thetaq$, $\nu=(-p,q)$ gives
the output near-unit $z_\nu=A^q/M^p=e^{x\delta_\nu}$ (note the contrast with
\eqref{ct:eq-germ}, which approximates $\beta$ rather than $\thetaq$).  Integer polynomials
in such near-units are ``masks.''  The finite core is \statuslean{} in
\lean{ExponentLatticeMask}; the barriers are \statusnew{} with classical inputs.

\subsection{Exact height and the two-direction uncertainty}
\label{masks:height}

With $L_{M,A}(\nu)=\sum_{p\mid MA}|av_p(M)+bv_p(A)|\log p$, a norm on $\R^2$ (the
valuation vectors of $M,A$ are independent because $M,A$ are multiplicatively independent),
the reduced $\sigma_\nu=R_\nu/S_\nu$ satisfies
\begin{equation}
 \log R_\nu+\log S_\nu=L_{M,A}(\nu),\qquad
 \log R_\nu-\log S_\nu=x\delta_\nu,
 \label{masks:eq-height-law}
\end{equation}
so both sides are exponentially large in $|\nu|$ even when $x\delta_\nu$ is tiny.  For two
vectors with determinant $D=ad-bc\ne0$ and $H=\|\nu\|_1+\|\omega\|_1$,
$d\delta_\nu-b\delta_\omega=D\log2$ and $a\delta_\omega-c\delta_\nu=D\log3$, so
$\max(|\delta_\nu|,|\delta_\omega|)\ge|D|\log3/H$; adjacent convergents ($D=\pm1$) are the
optimally conditioned basis, and even they cannot make both errors smaller than the
reciprocal exponent scale.

\subsection{Toric collapse and the gap-power theorem}
\label{masks:toric}

For a list $\nu_1,\dots,\nu_k$, the kernel of $T_i\mapsto U^{a_i}V^{b_i}$ on Laurent
polynomials is exactly the lattice ideal
$I_\nu=\langle T^\alpha-T^\beta:\sum\alpha_i\nu_i=\sum\beta_i\nu_i\rangle$ (group terms by
fibres), and every element of $I_\nu$ vanishes at \emph{both} $(\rho_{\nu_i})$ and
$(\sigma_{\nu_i})$.  Modulo $I_\nu$ every mask is a Laurent polynomial in two adjacent
near-units: adding convergent variables adds no formal degrees of freedom, and the
continued-fraction recurrence itself gives $T_{n+1}-T_n^{a_{n+1}}T_{n-1}\in I_\nu$, so
recurrence-only masks are identically zero, not small.  Any claimed high-contact mask must be
reduced modulo $I_\nu$ before its contact is credited.  (The numerical kernel at $(2,3)$ is
larger---$3-2-1=0$---but such additive identities do not transfer to arbitrary base pairs and
are the hard, candidate-specific part.)

For a mask $F\in\Z[U,V]$ the contact order at $(1,1)$ is the largest $r$ with
$F\in(U-1,V-1)^r$, equivalently the vanishing of the two-dimensional Prouhet moments
$\sum_\ell c_\ell a_\ell^ib_\ell^j$ for $i+j<r$; it is at most the total bidegree and at most
$(\#\text{monomials})-1$ (a generic linear functional reduces to a univariate exponential
sum with distinct frequencies).

\begin{theorem}[One-direction gap power]\label{masks:thm-gap-power}
If $P\in\Z[T]$ has a zero of multiplicity $\ge r$ at $1$ and $d\ge\deg P$, then for all
integers $R$, $S\ne0$ the cleared value $S^dP(R/S)=\sum_iP_iR^iS^{d-i}$ is divisible by
$(R-S)^r$; if nonzero it is at least $|R-S|^r$ in absolute value.
\end{theorem}

\statuslean{} (\lean{gap_pow_dvd_clearedEval}, \lean{abs_clearedEval_ge}): write
$P=(T-1)^rQ$ and clear.  For the Thue--Morse mask $P_r=\prod_{j<r}(1-T^{2^j})$ the cleared
value is exactly $\prod_{j<r}(S^{2^j}-R^{2^j})$.  This closes at once every one-dimensional
Prouhet partition, finite-difference mask, and sign pattern: high contact on a single
near-unit \emph{factorizes} into a power of the output gap.  Bivariately, contact $r$ places
$S_1^dS_2^eF(z_1,z_2)$ in the ideal $(G_1,G_2)^r$ of the two gaps, with the primewise Newton
floor $\tau_p(F)=\min_{\gamma_{ij}\ne0}(v_p(\gamma_{ij})+ig_{1,p}+jg_{2,p}+(d-i)s_{1,p}+(e-j)s_{2,p})$
as guaranteed divisor and the scalar product-formula criterion
$\prod_pp^{\tau_p}\le|J_F|\le\sum|\gamma_{ij}||G_1|^i|G_2|^jS_1^{d-i}S_2^{e-j}$.

\subsection{Stable structural support and the shared-pole Newton law}
\label{masks:stable}

For $\ell\mid MA$ write $m_\ell=v_\ell(M)$, $n_\ell=v_\ell(A)$ and
$u_{\ell,k}=v_\ell(z_k)=q_kn_\ell-p_km_\ell=q_k(n_\ell-\thetaq m_\ell)+m_\ell(q_k\thetaq-p_k)$.
The coefficient $n_\ell-\thetaq m_\ell$ is nonzero ($\thetaq\notin\Q$), so for large $k$ the
sign of $u_{\ell,k}$ is fixed: the reduced numerators and denominators of the adjacent
near-units are supported on the \emph{same} fixed sets
$\mathcal P_+=\{\ell:n_\ell>\thetaq m_\ell\}$ and $\mathcal P_-=\{\ell:n_\ell<\thetaq m_\ell\}$,
both nonempty because $\sum_\ell(n_\ell-\thetaq m_\ell)\log\ell=\log A-\thetaq\log M=0$,
with every depth linear in $q_k$.  Sufficiently deep adjacent pairs therefore have \emph{no
private denominator prime}; the near-cancellation $z_k\to1$ is a balance between two fixed,
linearly growing valuation profiles, not a matter of small valuations.  Adjacent depths are
coupled exactly (\statuslean{}, \lean{transport_q}, \lean{transport_p}):
\begin{equation}
 q_{k+1}u_{\ell,k}-q_ku_{\ell,k+1}=\varepsilon_km_\ell,\qquad
 p_{k+1}u_{\ell,k}-p_ku_{\ell,k+1}=\varepsilon_kn_\ell,\qquad
 \varepsilon_k=p_{k+1}q_k-p_kq_{k+1}=\pm1,
 \label{masks:eq-transport}
\end{equation}
i.e.\ $z_k^{q_{k+1}}/z_{k+1}^{q_k}=M^{\varepsilon_k}$ and $z_k^{p_{k+1}}/z_{k+1}^{p_k}=A^{\varepsilon_k}$.

At a private prime ($p\mid S_1$, $p\nmid S_2$) the leading $U$-face $f_d(V)$ of
$F=\sum f_i(V)U^i$ controls the first pole layer: if $v_p(S_2^ef_d(z_2))<s=v_p(S_1)$ then
$v_p(J_F)=v_p(S_2^ef_d(z_2))$ and the reduced denominator keeps $p^{ds-v_p(A_d)}$; a unit
or monomial top face keeps the full pole, and cancelling the first layer at all private primes
costs $\log P_1\le eh(z_2)+\log\|f_d\|_1$.  Cyclotomic faces $A_{\mathcal M}(V)=\prod_{m\in\mathcal M}\Phi_m(V)$
turn this into a finite order-cover condition
$\operatorname{ord}_p(z_2)\in\mathcal M$ (and fixed-order factors supply only logarithmic
depth).  Stable support shows this private-prime model is a finite diagnostic only.  The
asymptotic law is the shared one: for $\ell\in\mathcal P_-$ and
$F=\sum c_{ij}U^iV^j$,
\begin{equation}
 v_\ell(J_F)\ge\lambda_\ell:=\min_{c_{ij}\ne0}\bigl(v_\ell(c_{ij})+(d-i)s_{\ell,1}+(e-j)s_{\ell,2}\bigr),
 \label{masks:eq-shared-newton}
\end{equation}
with equality when the minimum is unique; when it ties, $v_\ell(J_F)>\lambda_\ell$ iff the
explicit initial form $\sum_{\text{face}}\overline{c_{ij}\ell^{-v_\ell(c_{ij})}}\,\overline{R_1}^i\overline{R_2}^j\overline{S_1'}^{d-i}\overline{S_2'}^{e-j}$
vanishes in $\mathbb F_\ell$, and deeper cancellation repeats this layer by layer.  A unit
top-right corner keeps the whole pole $\ell^{ds_{\ell,1}+es_{\ell,2}}$; the positive mask
$(U-1)^{2r}+(V-1)^{2r}$ keeps $\ell^{2r\max(s_{\ell,1},s_{\ell,2})}$ unless the depths tie.  A
nonzero binomial mask cannot vanish at both $(1,1)$ and $(z_1,z_2)$ (adjacent relation vectors
are a basis, so $z_1,z_2$ generate the rank-two group of $M,A$; \statuslean{} in the form
\lean{det_eq_zero_of_orthogonal}, \lean{not_dvd_of_dvd_reduced_gap}).

\subsection{Barriers and the reduced-denominator endgame}
\label{masks:endgame}

Along adjacent convergents, with $\Delta_n=\max(|x\delta_n|,|x\delta_{n+1}|)$ and the
effective two-logarithm bound $\log(1/\Delta_n)=O_x(\log q_n)$:

\begin{theorem}[Three barriers]\label{masks:thm-barriers}
(i) Full clearing cannot become subunit: for nonzero $F_n$ of bidegree $(d_n,e_n)$ and contact
$r_n$, $S_n^{d_n}S_{n+1}^{e_n}\|\widetilde F_n\|_1(2\Delta_n)^{r_n}>1$ for all large $n$,
uniformly in $F_n$, because $\log S\gg q(d+e)$ while $r\le d+e$ and $\log(1/\Delta)=O(\log q)$.
(ii) Structural primes are never shared by the reduced gaps of independent directions, and
$\gcd(G_\nu,G_\omega)\mid\gcd(M^D-1,A^D-1)$ with $D=|\det(\nu,\omega)|$ (the
gap-determinant transport of Section~\ref{crit:fresh-prime}); for adjacent directions the
shared gap is a fixed divisor of $\gcd(M-1,A-1)$, and for nonadjacent ones it is
$e^{o(H)}$ by Bugeaud--Corvaja--Zannier \cite{BCZ2003}, so contact-supplied shared divisors
are exponentially too small.  (iii) If the exact scalar criterion
$r\log(1/(2\Delta))>\log b_F+\log\|F(1+X,1+Y)\|_1$ (with $b_F$ the \emph{reduced}
denominator) succeeds infinitely often with subheight coefficients, then
$\log b_{F_n}=O_x((d_n+e_n)\log q_n)$: the compression index $\log(B_F/b_F)/\log B_F$ must
tend to one, and since $b_{F_n}=\prod_{\ell\in\mathcal P_-}\ell^{\rho_{\ell,n}}$ with
$\rho_{\ell,n}=(d_ns_{\ell,n}+e_ns_{\ell,n+1}-v_\ell(J_{F_n}))_+$, the mask must capture a
$1-o(1)$ fraction of the pole depth at \emph{every} stable denominator prime.
\end{theorem}

\begin{target}[Shared structural-face capture]\label{masks:target}
Construct non-toric masks $F_k$ on adjacent pairs with subheight shifted coefficients, certified
nonzero, whose successive initial forms \eqref{masks:eq-shared-newton} vanish deeply enough that
$\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal P_-}\rho_{\ell,k}\log\ell=O_x((d_k+e_k)\log q_k)$; or prove the
obstruction $\log b_F\ge c_x(d\log S_1+e\log S_2)-O_x(r\log H)$ for every such mask, which
would eliminate the architecture.  The supports should respect the transport relations
\eqref{masks:eq-transport}; the search is an integer program over shared Newton faces, not over
arbitrary high-contact coefficients.
\end{target}

\section{Rank-two rigidity: the pair-lattice defect and rational Hankel rays}
\label{sec:ranktwo}

This section integrates a further external report.  Its core — the canonical primitive
counterexample, the free monoid $\mathcal E_{\mathrm{int}}(2,3)=\N_0+\N_0\beta$ of common integral exponents,
the group $\mathcal E_{\mathrm{rat}}(2,3)=\Z+\Z\beta$ of common rational exponents, the uniqueness and leastness
of $\beta$, and the reciprocal duality $\mathcal E_{\mathrm{int}}(2^\beta,3^\beta)=\N_0+\N_0\beta^{-1}$ — is the
exact conditional structure already established in Sections~\ref{sec:conditional}
and~\ref{sec:radical} and kernel-verified in \lean{PrimitiveGenerator},
\lean{RationalPowerIndex}, and \lean{LeastSolution}; none of it is repeated here.  What is
new is a compact \emph{pair-lattice} packaging of the descent invariant, its local Kummer
form, and an exact classification of rational Hankel (three-term exponentiation) branches
inside the conditional orbit.  The finite algebra of the latter is \statuslean{} in
\lean{RationalHankelTriple}.

\subsection{The saturation defect of a pair}
\label{rt:defect}

For a counterexample pair $(A,B)=(2^x,3^x)$ write $a_p=v_p(A)$, $b_p=v_p(B)$ and define the
\emph{saturation defect}
\begin{equation}
 \delta_{\mathrm{sat}}(A,B)=\gcd\bigl(\{a_p:p\ne2\},\ \{b_p:p\ne3\},\ b_3-a_2\bigr).
 \label{rt:eq-defect}
\end{equation}
The valuation lattice spanned by the axis vector of $(2,3)$ and the vector of $(A,B)$ has
Smith normal form $\operatorname{diag}(1,\delta_{\mathrm{sat}})$, so $\delta_{\mathrm{sat}}$ is exactly the index of
the saturation; and $d\mid\delta_{\mathrm{sat}}$ holds iff there are a residue $r$ (unique mod $d$) and
integers $C,D$ with
\begin{equation}
 A=2^rC^d,\qquad B=3^rD^d,
 \label{rt:eq-root-extract}
\end{equation}
in which case $y=(x-r)/d$ is again a solution with outputs $(C,D)$.  Extracting the full
defect at once and then removing the axis content $\min(v_2(A),v_3(B))$ lands on the
canonical primitive pair in a single step --- no iterated descent is needed.  This is the
pair-lattice form of the rational-power index of Section~\ref{sec:conditional} and of the
ambient saturation index $d$ of Section~\ref{sec:lattice}; the three notions agree on a
counterexample orbit.  For a descendant $\alpha=n+k\beta$ the invariants are exact:
axis content $n$, defect $k$, localized pair $(A_0^k,B_0^k)$ --- so the coordinate $k$ is
\emph{intrinsic} (the Smith index of the pair lattice of $\alpha$), and a candidate pair
with defect $k>1$ is never primitive.  The change of basis from $(1,\beta)$ to
$(1,\alpha)$ lifts to the determinant lift $G\oplus\det G$ with Smith form
$\operatorname{diag}(1,k,k)$: the rank-three bookkeeping carries no third invariant.

\subsection{Local Kummer form and the defect-forcing criterion}
\label{rt:kummer}

The defect localizes prime by prime: $\ell^e\mid\delta_{\mathrm{sat}}(A,B)$ iff the two valuation
columns satisfy $g_1\equiv rg_0\pmod{\ell^e}$ for some residue $r$, iff
\[
 [A]=[2]^r,\qquad [B]=[3]^r
 \qquad\text{in }\Q_{>0}^{\times}/\Q_{>0}^{\times\ell^e}
\]
for one common $r$.  Hence for the \emph{canonical} pair the two valuation columns are
linearly independent over $\mathbb F_\ell$ for \emph{every} prime $\ell$: at least one of
\[
 \ell\nmid a_p\ (\text{some }p\ne2),\qquad
 \ell\nmid b_p\ (\text{some }p\ne3),\qquad
 a_2\not\equiv b_3\ (\mathrm{mod}\ \ell)
\]
holds for each $\ell$.

\begin{proposition}[Defect-forcing criterion]\label{rt:crit-defect}
If every counterexample pair necessarily satisfies $\delta_{\mathrm{sat}}(A,B)>1$ --- equivalently, if
some prime $\ell$ always carries a matched Kummer alignment $[A]=[2]^r$, $[B]=[3]^r$ modulo
$\ell$-th powers --- then the conjecture follows.
\end{proposition}

This is a clean endpoint for an ``archimedean-to-Kummer bridge'': the real relation would
have to force one congruence of valuation columns at one prime.  It is the mod-$\ell$
counterpart of the local common-exponent criterion of Section~\ref{crit:support-defects}
(via Corrales-Rodr\'iguez--Schoof, a common exponent at almost every prime characterizes
the integral case), and the same caution applies: nothing currently produces the bridge,
and the control principle of Section~\ref{log:control} is satisfied --- the criterion's
hypothesis genuinely fails for the controls, so it is not control-blind.  A cheap but
telling special case of the mod-$2$ statement: if $A\equiv B\ (\mathrm{mod}\ \text{squares})$
in the precise matched sense above, descent halves the exponent.

\subsection{Rational Hankel triples and the square valuation pattern}
\label{rt:hankel}

A three-term exponentiation orbit $U$, $V=U^{\xi}$, $W=U^{\xi^2}$ is encoded by the
logarithmic Hankel identity $(\log V)^2=\log U\log W$.  Two multiplicatively independent
initial values with a \emph{common} slope activate the six exponentials theorem: if both
triples $(U_i,V_i,W_i)$, $i=1,2$, satisfy the Hankel identity with the same
$\xi=\log V_i/\log U_i$, all six entries are algebraic, and $U_1,U_2$ are multiplicatively
independent, then $\xi\in\Q$.  (For algebraic $a,b$ this is the general-bases form of the
escape criterion of Section~\ref{sec:smooth}: simultaneous algebraicity of
$a,a^\xi,a^{\xi^2},b,b^\xi,b^{\xi^2}$ forces $\xi\in\Q$ via Gelfond--Schneider plus six
exponentials.)  The rational-slope case then has an exact integral classification:

\begin{theorem}[Square valuation pattern]\label{rt:thm-square}
Let $U,V,W$ be positive integers with $U^r=V^s$ and $V^r=W^s$ for coprime $r,s\ge1$ (the
monomial recurrences of the slope $\xi=r/s$).  Then there is a unique positive integer $T$
with
\[
 U=T^{s^2},\qquad V=T^{rs},\qquad W=T^{r^2};
\]
equivalently $(v_p(U),v_p(V),v_p(W))=d_p\,(s^2,rs,r^2)$ for every prime $p$.  Moreover the
positive solutions of $m_1^2=m_0m_2$ are exactly $(m_0,m_1,m_2)=d\,(u^2,uv,v^2)$ with
$u,v$ coprime.
\end{theorem}

Both statements are \statuslean{} (\lean{exists_common_base_of_recurrences} --- three
applications of the coprime-exponent common-base lemma, no factorization bookkeeping ---
and \lean{sq_eq_mul_parametrization}).  The exponent vector $(s^2,rs,r^2)$ is the primitive
integer kernel of the two recurrence rows $(r,-s,0)$, $(0,r,-s)$, whose $2\times2$ minors
$r^2,-rs,s^2$ have gcd $1$: the square pattern is lattice saturation in disguise.

Inside a conditional orbit the classification is global.  For
$t_i=n_i+k_i\beta\in\mathcal E_{\mathrm{rat}}(2,3)$, $t_i\ne0$, transcendence of $\beta$ turns the numerical
relation $t_1^2=t_0t_2$ into the coefficient identities
$n_1^2=n_0n_2$, $2n_1k_1=n_0k_2+n_2k_0$, $k_1^2=k_0k_2$, and these force all cross
determinants $n_ik_j-n_jk_i$ to vanish: the three exponents lie on one rational ray
$t_i=m_i\tau$ with $m_1^2=m_0m_2$, hence, for positive integral exponents,
\[
 (t_0,t_1,t_2)=d\,(s^2,rs,r^2)\,\tau ,
\]
and the localized solution pairs are $(\mathbf T^{s^2},\mathbf T^{rs},\mathbf T^{r^2})$ with
$\mathbf T=(A_0,B_0)^{d}$ after the axis factor is removed.  The determinant identity
\[
 (n_0k_1-n_1k_0)(n_2k_1-n_1k_2)=0
\]
and the full ray conclusion for nonzero forms, together with the transcendence bridge, are
\statuslean{} (\lean{crossDet_mul_crossDet_eq_zero}, \lean{hankel_ray},
\lean{coeff_identities_of_transcendental}).

\begin{corollary}[Quadratic closure inside the orbit is rational]\label{rt:cor-quadclosure}
Let $t\ne0$ lie in $\mathcal E_{\mathrm{rat}}(2,3)$ and $\theta\in\mathcal E_{\mathrm{rat}}(2^t,3^t)$.  If also
$\theta^2\in\mathcal E_{\mathrm{rat}}(2^t,3^t)$, then $\theta\in\Q$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
With $u=t\theta$, $v=t\theta^2$ in $\Z+\Z\beta$ one has $u^2=tv$; the ray classification
puts $t,u,v$ on one rational ray, so $\theta=u/t\in\Q$.
\end{proof}

This makes exact the reason fractional-linear manipulations cannot manufacture the missing
$\beta^2$ column: the orbit ratios $(m+\ell\beta)/(n+k\beta)$ with nonproportional
coefficient vectors are transcendental (Gelfond--Schneider), each changed base pair
$(2^t,3^t)$ again has the two-dimensional exponent group $(\Z+\Z\beta)/t$
(Section~\ref{sec:spectrum} in spectrum form), and any \emph{quadratic} closure collapses
to a rational slope.  The composable family of these base changes is a groupoid model of
every transformation obtainable without new arithmetic information --- all of it strictly
inside the six-exponentials ceiling of rank two.

\subsection{Near-axis remarks and cross-references}
\label{rt:nearaxis}

For the canonical pair, $\min(a_2,b_3)=0$ prevents simultaneous cancellation at the axis:
at least one of $A^q/2^p$, $B^q/3^p$ is already in lowest terms with denominator exactly
$2^p$ resp.\ $3^p$, giving the elementary bound $|q\beta-p|\ge1/(2^{p+1}\log2)$ (resp.\
base $3$) --- far weaker than the height laws of Sections~\ref{sec:orbit-height-entropy}
and~\ref{masks:height} but assumption-free.  The report's ``synchronized difference pairs''
$\Delta_2=2^p-A^q$, $\Delta_3=3^p-B^q$ with
$(\Delta_3/3^p)/(\Delta_2/2^p)\to\log3/\log2$ are precisely the synchronized germ gaps of
Section~\ref{sec:centeredtrace}; the two-channel theorem and the channel-descent
proposition (Theorem~\ref{ct:thm-channels}, Proposition~\ref{ct:prop-descent}) are the
sharpest known statements about coupling their prime divisors, and the reconnaissance of
Section~\ref{log:channel-recon} found no further exploitable coupling.  The report's
research programs map onto standing targets: its Kummer-alignment program is
Criterion~\ref{rt:crit-defect}; its nonlinear-orbit and functional-source programs are the
escape criterion (Section~\ref{sec:smooth}) and Section~\ref{primetop:remaining}; its
synchronized-primitive-divisor program is Target~\ref{ct:target}; its monoid-leakage
program packages the negative-coefficient contradictions already implicit in
Section~\ref{sec:conditional}.

\emph{Assessment.}  The merged material consolidates the conditional structure in a tighter
normal form and contributes two exact classifications (the local Kummer form of the defect
with its every-$\ell$ independence statement, and the Hankel-ray/square-pattern theorems,
now kernel-checked).  It does not move the four-exponentials barrier; its value is that the
defect-forcing criterion is a genuinely non-control-blind endpoint, and that quadratic
closure inside the orbit is now excluded exactly rather than heuristically.

\section{Bhargava factorials of the two--three semigroup}
\label{sec:bhargava}

The corpus has repeatedly normalized interpolation determinants by ad hoc Smith factors and
noted (Section~\ref{crit:positive-closure} environs) that Bhargava orderings remained an
undeveloped interface.  This section integrates a report that develops it completely for the
input semigroup
\[
 \mathcal B=\{2^a3^b:a,b\in\Nzero\},
\]
computing the \emph{exact} generalized factorial $k!_{\mathcal B}$ --- hence the optimal universal
denominator of integer-valued interpolation on the smooth nodes --- and reformulating the
conjecture as a subunit problem in the canonical lattice
$\operatorname{Int}(\mathcal B,\Z)=\{P\in\Q[T]:P(\mathcal B)\subset\Z\}$.  Status: the local formulas, the
cutoff, the normalized determinant, the defect theorems, and the localized no-go are
\statusnew{} paper proofs (with Bhargava's choice-invariance theorem \statusknown); the
tables are \statusexactcomp{} with source; two finite cores added here are \statuslean{}
(\lean{SmoothSemigroupCore}).

\subsection{The exact local factorial}
\label{bh:local}

For a prime $p$ let $\nu_{\mathcal B,p}(k)$ be Bhargava's minimal valuation of a $k$-th difference
product, so that $k!_{\mathcal B}=\prod_pp^{\nu_{\mathcal B,p}(k)}$ and a regular basis
$F_0,F_1,\ldots$ of $\operatorname{Int}(\mathcal B,\Z)$ has leading coefficients $1/k!_{\mathcal B}$.
Passing to $p$-adic closures and using that every closed subgroup of $\Z_p^\times$ ($p$ odd)
is procyclic, one gets, with
$h_p(e)=|\langle2,3\rangle\bmod p^e|=\operatorname{lcm}(\operatorname{ord}_{p^e}2,
\operatorname{ord}_{p^e}3)$:
\begin{equation}
 \nu_{\mathcal B,p}(k)=\sum_{e\ge1}\mathcal Bigl\lfloor\frac k{h_p(e)}\mathcal Bigr\rfloor\quad(p\ge5),
 \qquad
 \nu_{\mathcal B,3}(k)=v_3(k!),
 \label{bh:eq-local}
\end{equation}
the latter because $2$ is a primitive root modulo $3^e$, so $\mathcal B$ is dense in $\Z_3$ and the
prime $3$ gives \emph{no gain} over $\Z$.  At $p=2$ the closure splits self-similarly,
$K=\overline{\langle3\rangle}\sqcup2K$, giving an exact two-branch merge recursion for
$a_k=\nu_{\mathcal B,2}(k)$ (odd-branch costs $u_s=s+\lfloor s/2\rfloor+v_2(s!)$, even-branch costs
$r+a_r$; the multiset of values is the ordered merge of the two streams) with first values
$0,0,1,1,3,4,4,5,7,9,9,10,\ldots$ (independently reverified here) and, by a renewal
argument for self-similar merges,
\begin{equation}
 \lim_k\frac{\nu_{\mathcal B,2}(k)}k=\frac{\sqrt{11}-1}2=1.15831\ldots
 \label{bh:eq-slope}
\end{equation}
(the equation $1/c=1/(1+c)+2/5$ from the odd-branch slope $5/2$).  Every unramified prime
carries strict excess over the ordinary factorial:
$\alpha_p=\sum_e1/h_p(e)\ge p/(p-1)^2$.  A one-line pigeonhole \emph{cutoff} makes the
factorial finitely computable: for $p\ge5$ and $R=\lfloor\sqrt k\rfloor$, if
$h_p(e)\le k$ then two of the $(R+1)^2$ box elements $2^a3^b$ ($a,b\le R$) collide modulo
$p^e$, so $p^e$ divides a nonzero difference below $6^R$:
\begin{equation}
 h_p(e)\le k\ \Longrightarrow\ p^e<6^{\lfloor\sqrt k\rfloor}.
 \label{bh:eq-cutoff}
\end{equation}
The pigeonhole core of \eqref{bh:eq-cutoff} is \statuslean{}
(\lean{modulus_lt_of_card_image_lt}).  The resulting exact values (e.g.\
$k!_{\mathcal B}/k!=1,1,1,1,5,2,7,2,5,20,22,92,10465,\ldots$; first proper-orbit prime $23$ at
$k=11$ via $h_{23}(1)=11$; exceptional orbit primes like $431$ entering at degree
$43$) come with independent consistency checks.  The same calculus applies verbatim to any
two-generator semigroup --- in particular to the \emph{output} semigroup
$\{M^aN^b\}$ of a counterexample, whose ramified branches at primes dividing $MN$ obey
analogous rooted merge systems with closed renewal slopes.

\subsection{A counterexample as an isomorphism of factorial semigroups}
\label{bh:iso}

Under a hypothetical solution the power map $q\mapsto q^x$ is an order-preserving monoid
isomorphism from $\mathcal B$ onto the output semigroup, and both carry now-computable factorial
spectra $(k!_{\mathcal B})$ and $(k!_{\mathcal C})$.  The isomorphism controls all archimedean
ratios exactly, while the two local spectra are a priori unrelated --- Bhargava factorials
are invariants of the embedded sets, not of the abstract monoid.  \emph{Factorial-spectrum
rigidity} --- find a property of order-preserving power isomorphisms forcing a quantitative
relation between the two spectra --- is a genuinely new formulation of the missing
arithmetic--archimedean bridge, and it passes the control test of
Section~\ref{log:control}: for integer $x$ the two spectra coincide up to the explicit
change of generators.

\subsection{The optimally normalized determinant and the factorial defect}
\label{bh:determinant}

For nodes $E=(q_0,\ldots,q_{d+1})\subset\mathcal B$ and a regular basis, the determinant with
columns $F_0,\ldots,F_d,t^x$ is, under a counterexample, a \emph{nonzero integer} (each
$F_j(q_i)\in\Z$, each $q_i^x\in\Z$; nonvanishing because $1,t,\ldots,t^d,t^x$ is a Chebyshev
system on $\R_{>0}$), equal to the monomial determinant divided by $\prod_{j\le d}j!_{\mathcal B}$.
Every $m$-node Vandermonde is divisible by $\prod_{j<m}j!_{\mathcal B}$, so each node set has an
integer \emph{factorial defect} $Q_{\mathcal B}(E)=|V(E)|/\prod_{j<m}j!_{\mathcal B}$, and the master
archimedean inequality for a counterexample reads
\begin{equation}
 Q_{\mathcal B}(E)\,(d+1)!_{\mathcal B}\,\mathcal Bigl|\binom{x}{d+1}\mathcal Bigr|\,\xi^{x-d-1}\ \ge\ 1
 \qquad(\xi\in(\min E,\max E)).
 \label{bh:eq-master}
\end{equation}
The defect minima through eight nodes are exactly
\[
 1,\ 1,\ 1,\ 1,\ 1,\ 7,\ 7,\ 396 ,
\]
by exhaustive exact certificates.  The first failure is structural:

\begin{theorem}[First factorial defect]\label{bh:thm-defect7}
Every six-node subset of $\mathcal B$ has $Q_{\mathcal B}(E)\ge7$, with equality for
$E_6=\{1,2,3,4,6,8\}$.  Hence $\mathcal B$ admits no simultaneous $p$-ordering prefix of length
six, and the regular basis is not a Newton basis from degree $6$ on (the first non-Newton
basis element is explicit, glued by CRT from local orderings).
\end{theorem}

The proof reduces, via a translation-invariant span bound, to $792$ gap patterns, of which
only $(0,1,2,4,5,6)$ could beat $7$; that pattern would need two triples of consecutive
$3$-smooth integers four apart, and \emph{the only consecutive triples in $\mathcal B$ are
$\{1,2,3\}$ and $\{2,3,4\}$} --- this last, decisive fact is \statuslean{}
(\lean{consecutive_threeSmooth_triples}).  The verification $V(E_6)=7\cdot345600$ and the
denominator $\prod_{j\le5}j!_{\mathcal B}=345600$ are exact arithmetic.

The lattice reformulation is a closest-vector statement (\emph{Bhargava locking}): for a
counterexample, every $P\in\operatorname{Int}_{\le d}(\mathcal B,\Z)$ misses the integer vector
$(q_i^x)_i$ by at least $1$ in $\ell^\infty$ on any $d+2$ nodes; the primitive left-kernel
vector of the evaluation matrix is a dual certificate.  Four finite criteria result
(normalized determinant below $\prod j!_{\mathcal B}$; low-defect curvature
\eqref{bh:eq-master} reversed; regular-basis CVP; paired input--output determinants for
$t^x$ and $t^{1/x}$), each unconditional as an implication.

\subsection{Localization and the initial-form frontier}
\label{bh:localized}

Over $R_6=\Z[1/6]$ the full group $\{2^a3^b:a,b\in\Z\}$ is dense in $\R_{>0}$ and its
localized factorial keeps exactly the unramified part of \eqref{bh:eq-local}.  For a
counterexample the localized determinant is a nonzero element of $\Z[1/(6MN)]$: every
possible denominator is supported on the finitely many structural primes
$S=\{p:p\mid6MN\}$, so the conjecture follows from a single family of node sets with
\[
 |\Delta^\times|_\infty\cdot\mathfrak d_S(\Delta^\times)<1 .
\]
But the natural construction fails for the familiar reason, here in sharp form: for a
one-ratio geometric cluster $1,u,\ldots,u^{d+1}$ with $u=2^a3^{-b}\to1$, the archimedean
determinant decays only polynomially in $b$ (like $|\log u|^{\binom{d+2}2}$), while
termwise clearing at the structural primes costs exponentially in $b$.  This is the
Bhargava-normalized incarnation of the height mismatch of
Sections~\ref{sec:orbit-height-entropy} and~\ref{masks:endgame}, with all universal
denominators already removed; what survives is precisely a cancellation target: at each
$p\in S$, write $\Delta^\times=p^{m_p}(I_p+pJ_p)$ with $m_p$ the minimal term valuation ---
the \emph{initial-form bridge} asks for families where the archimedean logarithm is
$-A_d+o(A_d)$ while the initial forms $I_p$ vanish to weighted depth exceeding the termwise
budget by $A_d/\log p$.  This is the regular-basis twin of the shared-pole Newton endgame
(Target~\ref{masks:target} and \eqref{masks:eq-shared-newton}); the two formulations should
be attacked together, and the LP/Farkas methodology of Section~\ref{log:lp-experiment}
applies to both.

\subsection{Subquadratic growth and the two-prime synchronization gap}
\label{bh:sync}

A second, independently written report derives the same local calculus --- identical
formulas at every prime, the identical two-adic value stream, and the identical slope
$(\sqrt{11}-1)/2$ --- which functions as an external cross-check of
Section~\ref{bh:local}.  It adds three results that complete the picture.

First, the lifting depths are a gcd sequence: for $p\ge5$ with first orbit size
$d_p=h_p(1)$, the saturation depth satisfies $c_p=v_p(G_{d_p})$ where
$G_d=\gcd(2^d-1,3^d-1)$, so Bugeaud--Corvaja--Zannier \cite{BCZ2003} bounds the whole
factorial:
\begin{equation}
 \log\bigl(k!_{\mathcal B}\bigr)
 \le O(k)+2k\sum_{d\le k}\frac{\log G_d}{d}
 = o(k^2).
 \label{bh:eq-subquadratic}
\end{equation}
The intrinsic local denominator of the smooth semigroup is therefore \emph{subquadratic}:
small enough that exponential-height nodes would beat it.

Second, the \emph{conditional scalar bridge}: if there were simultaneous $p$-ordering
prefixes $A_j\subset\mathcal B$ of lengths $n_j\to\infty$ whose least node satisfies
$\log\min A_j\ge cn_j$, then the integer $n_j!_{\mathcal B}\,[A_j]\,t^x$ (integral by the
unit-triangular Newton basis) would have absolute value
$n_j!_{\mathcal B}\,|\binom{x}{n_j}|\,\xi^{x-n_j}\to0$ by
\eqref{bh:eq-subquadratic} --- proving the conjecture.

Third, and decisively, \emph{no such family exists}, for a reason more structural than the
six-node defect: the two structural primes impose incompatible equilibrium populations.  An
asymptotically optimal dyadic ordering must have odd-node proportion
$q_2=(\sqrt{11}-1)/5=0.4633\ldots$ (from the self-similar merge slopes), while an
asymptotically optimal triadic ordering must have $3$-unit proportion $2/3$; on
$\mathcal B\setminus\{1\}$ the odd nodes and the $3$-unit nodes are \emph{disjoint}
($2^a3^b$ is odd iff $a=0$, a $3$-unit iff $b=0$), and
\[
 q_2+\tfrac23=1+\tfrac{3\sqrt{11}-8}{15}>1 .
\]
Quantitatively, with pair energies
$\mathcal E_p(A)=\tfrac2{N^2}\sum_{s<t}v_p(s-t)$, every $N$-node set
$A\subset\mathcal B\setminus\{1\}$ pays
\begin{equation}
 \log2\,\bigl(\mathcal E_2(A)-\mathcal E_2^{\min}\bigr)
 +\log3\,\bigl(\mathcal E_3(A)-\mathcal E_3^{\min}\bigr)
 \ \ge\ \kappa+o(1),
 \qquad
 \kappa=\eta^2\frac{ab}{a+b}=0.0236\ldots,
 \label{bh:eq-quadratic-gap}
\end{equation}
($\eta=q_2-\tfrac13$, $a=\tfrac{\sqrt{11}+6}2\log2$, $b=\tfrac94\log3$): at least
$\tfrac12\kappa N^2$ extra logarithmic Vandermonde mass beyond the separated local minima.
This explains the defects $7,7,396$ of Section~\ref{bh:determinant} asymptotically and
closes the scalar-bridge route unconditionally --- another entry for the closed-routes
ledger of Section~\ref{sec:session-log}, with the same conclusion as always: the surviving
frontier is output-sensitive cancellation, not sharper counting.  A near-geometric chain
$s_j=2^{ju}3^{(n-j)v}$ makes the same point in exact form: its $2$- and $3$-adic
interpolation tax is $\tfrac{n(n-1)}2(u\log2+v\log3)$ against node heights $\asymp nu\log2$,
cancelling all but one power of the archimedean decay --- consistent with the one-ratio
cluster no-go of Section~\ref{bh:localized}.

\emph{Assessment.}  The Bhargava calculus settles, exactly and permanently, the universal
local-divisibility side of every interpolation attack on the smooth nodes: no future
determinant experiment needs to guess its denominator normalization again, node sets can be
scored by their exact defect $Q_{\mathcal B}$, and automatic output-prime mass is separated from
genuine signed cancellation.  It does not move the barrier --- its own no-gos show the
localized cluster route fails by the standard exponential-vs-polynomial margin, and the
simultaneous-ordering route fails by the two-prime equilibrium clash
\eqref{bh:eq-quadratic-gap} --- but it replaces ``try a larger determinant'' by two
canonical open interfaces: factorial-spectrum rigidity for the input--output isomorphism,
and structural-prime initial-form cancellation in the optimally normalized lattice.

\section{Additive isolation and the weighted smooth-support series}
\label{sec:additive-isolation}

A further external report develops three themes.  Its first --- an ``algebraic-orbit
filtration'' $\operatorname{Orb}_r(x)$ of bases whose first $r$ iterates under
$\alpha\mapsto\alpha^x$ stay algebraic, with ranks $2,\le1,0$ at $r=1,2,3$, the rank
identity $\operatorname{rank}\langle2,3,M,A\rangle=4-\operatorname{rank}
\operatorname{Orb}_2(x)\in\{3,4\}$, and the M\"obius form of the exponent in the dependent
branch --- is precisely the kernel-verified spectrum/kernel/tower chain of
Sections~\ref{sec:spectrum}, \ref{sec:kernel}, and the depth-three tower theorem
(\lean{TowerRigidity}), together with the rank-geometry M\"obius parametrization and its
height bound in Section~\ref{sec:rank-geometry}; it is not repeated.  The two remaining
themes are new to this report and are recorded here.

\subsection{Additive isolation}
\label{ai:isolation}

The spectrum theorem makes $u^x$ algebraic exactly for $3$-smooth positive rationals $u$.
Combining it with the classification of \emph{consecutive} smooth integers gives an exact
additive statement:

\begin{proposition}[Consecutive smooth pairs; additive isolation]\label{ai:prop-pairs}
The positive integers $u$ with $u$ and $u+1$ both $3$-smooth are exactly
$u\in\{1,2,3,8\}$ (pairs $(1,2),(2,3),(3,4),(8,9)$).  Consequently, under a hypothetical
counterexample, $(u+1)^x$ is algebraic for a smooth $u$ exactly when $u\in\{1,2,3,8\}$, and
transcendental otherwise; likewise $(u-1)^x$ is algebraic exactly for $u\in\{2,3,4,9\}$.
The longest run of consecutive smooth integers is $1,2,3,4$.
\end{proposition}

The external report proves the pair classification by invoking Mih\u{a}ilescu's theorem;
that is far more than needed.  The equations $2^a=3^b+1$ and $3^d=2^a+1$ are elementary
(reduce modulo $3$ resp.\ $8$, force an even exponent, and factor $y^2-1$ into two powers of
the other base differing by $2$), and the whole classification is \statuslean{} in
\lean{SmoothSemigroupCore} (\lean{pow_two_eq_pow_three_add_one},
\lean{pow_three_eq_pow_two_add_one}, \lean{consecutive_threeSmooth_pairs}), alongside the
triple classification used by the six-node defect.  Additive isolation sharpens the
``one more base'' picture of Section~\ref{sec:smooth}: a counterexample is multiplicatively
closed but additively barren --- any derivation of algebraicity of $5^x$, or of the
successor of any nonexceptional smooth integer, is already a complete proof, not an
auxiliary step.

\subsection{The weighted smooth-support series}
\label{ai:series}

The report encodes a hypothetical solution in the weighted series
\[
 H_{M,A}(z)=\sum_{a,b\ge0}M^aA^b\,z^{2^a3^b}\in\Z[[z]],
\]
whose coefficient at a smooth exponent $s$ is exactly $s^x$.  It satisfies an exact mixed
$2$--$3$ Mahler identity (inclusion–exclusion over the two dilations $z\mapsto z^2$,
$z\mapsto z^3$), extending the finite mixed-Mahler algebra of \lean{MixedMahlerFinite}.
Two quantitative results are proved about the automatic side: the number of binary and
ternary Cartier states of the unweighted support series grows exponentially (so the support
is far from $2$- or $3$-automatic --- quantifying the carry-language analysis of
Section~\ref{sec:carry-languages}), and the reductions of $H_{M,A}$ modulo a prime $\ell$ are
classified: they are algebraic over $\mathbb F_\ell(z)$ exactly according to the
$\ell$-divisibility geometry of $M$ and $A$.  The diagnosis matches the corpus: finite
characteristic sees the divisibility geometry of the outputs, while the conjecture is an
archimedean equality of two pole abscissae; the missing ingredient is a bridge between the
two layers, the same missing coupling as everywhere else in this report.  \statusnew{}
throughout this subsection; the elementary saturation and normalization layers of the
external report duplicate kernel-verified corpus modules and were not re-integrated.

\section{The external-prime Newton wall and nonarchimedean ray rigidity}
\label{sec:newtonwall}

A further external report opens the first genuinely $p$-adic \emph{analytic} layer of the
corpus: it works at an external prime of a hypothetical counterexample, where the sampled
input geometry acquires an accumulation point that the real picture lacks.  Its elementary
preliminaries (positivity, irrationality, and transcendence of a nonintegral $x$;
multiplicative independence of $2,M$ and of $3,A$; existence of an external prime $p\ge5$
dividing $MA$) are kernel-verified corpus facts (Sections~\ref{sec:smooth}
and~\ref{sec:spectrum}) and were not re-integrated.  Everything below consumes the external
prime itself, so the control principle of Section~\ref{log:control} is passed \emph{by
construction}: for an integer control $(2^d,3^d)$ no prime $p\ge5$ divides $MA$ and the
package cannot even be formed.

\subsection{Oriented data and nonarchimedean ray rigidity}
\label{nw:rigidity}

Orient the data at an external prime $p\ge5$: if $p\mid M$ set
$(Q,R;\alpha,\lambda)=(M,A;2,3)$, otherwise $(A,M;3,2)$; in both cases
\[
 m=\vpp p{Q}>0,\qquad a=\vpp p{R}\ge0,\qquad
 F(Q^k)=R^k,\qquad F(\alpha Q^k)=\lambda R^k
\]
are the two rows of sampling data that any local interpolation $F$ of the conditional grid
would have to satisfy near the $p$-adic accumulation point $Q^k\to0$.  Because $p\ge5$, the
numbers $2,3,\alpha,\lambda,\alpha-1$ are all $p$-adic units.  The report proves:

\begin{theorem}[Geometric-ray rigidity and the edge law]\label{nw:thm-rigidity}
Let $K$ be a complete nonarchimedean field of characteristic zero and $0<|t|<1$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item If an analytic germ $F$ at $0$ satisfies $F(t^k)=s^k$ for all large $k$, then
$s=t^d$ and $F(z)=z^d$ for a unique $d\in\Nzero$.  A meromorphic germ forces $s=t^d$ with
$d\in\Z$; a germ on a finite ramified cover $z=w^e$ forces $s^e=t^d$.
\item If $F$ is analytic on a disk $D$ with $qD\subseteq D$ and $F(qt^k)=\mu F(t^k)$ for
infinitely many $k$, then the Taylor support of $F$ lies in the spectrum
$\{n:q^n=\mu\}$; if the spectrum is empty, then $F\equiv0$.
\end{enumerate}
Consequently no nonzero analytic, meromorphic, or finite-Puiseux germ at $0$ can carry even
the single row $F(Q^k)=R^k$ (the forced relation $R=Q^d$ contradicts the kernel-verified
multiplicative independence of the outputs), and none can carry both rows: the edge pairs
$(\alpha,\lambda)=(2,3)$ and $(3,2)$ have empty spectrum.
\end{theorem}

The two arithmetic pivots are kernel-checked in the new module
\lean{ExternalPrimeNewtonWall}.  First, \emph{unit-convergence rigidity}: in any normed
division ring, a unit-norm element whose power sequence converges equals $1$
(\lean{eq_one_of_tendsto_pow}); this is the step that turns ``the powers of the unit
$R/Q^d$ converge to the nonzero leading coefficient'' into the exact equality $R=Q^d$.
Second, the \emph{formal edge law}: for formal power series over any commutative ring the
dilation-eigenvalue identity $F(qz)=\mu F(z)$ forces $(q^n-\mu)\cdot c_n=0$ for every $n$
(\lean{edge_spectrum}); over a field the support lies in the spectrum
(\lean{eq_zero_of_edge_law}); and for the Alaoglu--Erd\H{o}s edge pairs the spectrum is
empty over $\Q$ --- $2^n\ne3$ and $3^n\ne2$ --- so the only formal solution is zero
(\lean{no_formal_edge_realization}).  What remains of the analytic statements beyond these
cores is the classical nonarchimedean identity theorem for accumulating zeros
(Strassmann), \statusknown.

\subsection{The quantitative wall: exact valuations and last-term dominance}
\label{nw:wall}

Rigidity says that no exact local model exists; the report's central computation measures
\emph{how} every polynomial approximation fails.  Let
\[
 c_n(Q,R)=\frac{\prod_{j<n}(R-Q^j)}{Q^{\binom n2}\prod_{j=1}^n(Q^j-1)}
\]
be the $q$-Newton coefficients of the native row, so that
$P_N(z)=\sum_{n\le N}c_n\prod_{j<n}(z-Q^j)$ is the unique interpolant of degree at most $N$
through $(Q^k,R^k)_{0\le k\le N}$.  With the threshold $q_*=\lfloor(a-1)/m\rfloor$ and a
single tie excess $\varepsilon$ (nonzero only when $m\mid a$, where
$\varepsilon=\vpp p{R-Q^{a/m}}-a$), the report computes the valuation of \emph{every}
coefficient exactly: $\vpp p{c_n}=\vpp p{R-1}-m\binom n2$ when $a=0$, and
\[
 \vpp p{c_n}
 =m\binom{q_*+1}2+a(n-1-q_*)+\varepsilon-m\binom n2
 =-\frac m2\,n^2+\Bigl(a+\frac m2\Bigr)n+O(1)
 \qquad(n\ge q_*+2)
\]
when $a>0$.  Three consequences form the wall:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \emph{Universal quadratic denominator escape.}  The least $D_n$ with
$D_nc_n\in\Z_{(p)}$ has $\vpp p{D_n}=\frac m2n^2-O(n)$; and by a Gauss-norm division
argument this is not a Newton-basis artifact: \emph{every} rational polynomial of arbitrary
degree agreeing with the native values at $Q^0,\dots,Q^N$ has a coefficient of $p$-adic
denominator exponent at least $-\vpp p{c_N}=\frac m2N^2-O(N)$.
\item \emph{Off-ray explosion with last-term dominance.}  At an adjacent-row point
$z=uQ^k$ ($u\in\Z_p^\times$, $u\ne1$, fixed $k$) the Newton terms have exact eventual ratio
valuation $\vpp p{T_{n+1}/T_n}=a+mk-mn<0$, so the term valuations strictly decrease and the
partial sum inherits the valuation of its \emph{last} term --- the same ultrametric
unique-minimum mechanism as the coefficient tax of \lean{PrimeTopIsolation} --- giving
$\vpp p{P_N(uQ^k)}=-\frac m2N^2+\bigl(a+m(k+\tfrac12)\bigr)N+O(1)\to-\infty$.
\item \emph{Adjacent-row repulsion.}  Hence, for all large $N$,
$\vpp p{P_N(\alpha Q^k)-\lambda R^k}=\vpp p{P_N(\alpha Q^k)}$: the native interpolants are
not merely inaccurate at the second row, they are quadratically $p$-adically
\emph{repelled} from the prescribed integers.
\end{enumerate}
An exact rational audit (\texttt{fractions.Fraction}, no floating point; script with
pinned SHA-256 digest reproduced in the source report) confirms the formulas in three
exemplar regimes, including the delicate valuation-tie case.  \statusnew{} for the exact
ledger; the valuation layer is Lean-ready $q$-binomial bookkeeping and is recorded as a
pending target in Section~\ref{sec:formalization-inventory}.

\emph{Why the wall is not yet a contradiction.}  The wall shows that the canonical
archimedean completion of the native data has no $p$-adic convergence off the ray.  It does
not show that the complex value at an off-ray rational point equals a $p$-adic sum of the
same terms: a series of rationals may converge in two completions to different limits, and
at the adjacent row the series does not truncate, so equality is not place-independent.
The product formula does not close the gap either: a nonzero rational residual may carry a
$p$-denominator of size $p^{\Theta(N^2)}$ while being only geometrically small
archimedeanly, so the elementary denominator lower bound $\exp(-\Theta(N^2))$ sits far
below the archimedean error $\exp(-\Theta(N))$.  Quadratic escape therefore \emph{defeats}
naive unit-locking rather than helping it --- the shortcut ``the entire function has
rational data, so evaluate it $p$-adically'' is closed, and any repair needs a separate
overconvergence or algebraicity theorem.  This is the $p$-adic face of the coupling
problem diagnosed throughout this report.

\subsection{Tate edge operator, finite-strip defects, and overconvergence}
\label{nw:tate}

On polynomials the edge law is diagonal and quantitative.  For
$\LL_{\alpha,\lambda}P(z)=P(\alpha z)-\lambda P(z)$ the monomial eigenvalues are
$\alpha^n-\lambda$, so on degrees $\le d$ the operator has the finite spectral gap
\[
 \sigma_{p,d}(\alpha,\lambda)=\min_{0\le j\le d}|\alpha^j-\lambda|_p>0 ,
\]
positive precisely because $2^j\ne3$ and $3^j\ne2$ --- the same finite fact as the empty
edge spectrum, kernel-checked in \lean{ExternalPrimeNewtonWall}.  The report proves the
resulting weighted-Gauss-norm inequality
$\lVert\LL_{\alpha,\lambda}P\rVert_\rho\ge\sigma_{p,d}(\alpha,\lambda)\lVert P\rVert_\rho$,
extends it to Tate algebras on dilation-stable disks when the resonance statistic
$\mu_{p,d}=\max_{j\le d}\vpp p{\alpha^j-\lambda}$ stays bounded, and derives a
\emph{finite-strip defect theorem}: if a polynomial of degree $\le d$ satisfies the second-row
law on a strip $K\le k\le N$ and one native value, then in the forced factorization
$\LL_{\alpha,\lambda}P=\Phi_{K,N}S$ the quotient obeys
$\lVert S\rVert_\rho\ge\sigma_{p,d}(\alpha,\lambda)\,|R|_p^K\rho^{-(N-K+1)}$.  For the
canonical two-row interpolants the defect quotient thus grows at least geometrically at
nonresonant external primes: there is \emph{no tame defect quotient}.  A diagonal
compactness argument upgrades this to: no family $F_N$ analytic on one common disk of
radius $\rho>1$ can match even the one-row prefixes with bounded norms
(\emph{no uniformly overconvergent interpolation family}).  The report closes this layer
with two explicitly open interfaces --- a removable-singularity (Robba-to-Tate) bridge and
a coefficient-growth criterion --- either of which would convert the wall into a
contradiction; both are recorded as targets, \statusopen.

\subsection{The finite-rank two-dilation target}
\label{nw:qdiff}

A genuine interpolation of the conditional grid would satisfy two dilation laws at once,
\[
 F(2z)=3F(z),\qquad F(Mz)=AF(z),
\]
with multiplicatively independent dilation parameters.  The formal obstruction is the edge
law again: a Laurent series solving the first equation alone is already zero
($(2^n-3)c_n=0$), while on the universal cover of $\C^\times$ the nonzero solution
$z^{x}$ exists --- the gap is local regularity and monodromy, not consistency.  Rigidity
theorems for consistent pairs of independent $q$-difference systems
\cite{Bezivin1992,BezivinBoutabaa1992,SchaefkeSinger2019} reduce sufficiently regular
finite-rank systems to rational or constant normal forms, which the finite-Puiseux
rigidity of Theorem~\ref{nw:thm-rigidity} would then exclude; but the integer table is a
discrete semigroup of values, not a difference module over $\Qbar(z)$, and the geometric
Newton completion satisfies only a one-axis \emph{inhomogeneous} law with a $q$-product
defect.  The report therefore formulates the precise missing object as a target: a finite
vector $Y$ of arithmetic interpolation functions with rational transition matrices
$B_2(z),B_M(z)$ obeying the cocycle consistency $B_2(Mz)B_M(z)=B_M(2z)B_2(z)$, one
coordinate carrying the exact conditional grid, and regular-singular or overconvergent
behavior at an external prime.  \statusopen; the current defect family contains
nonrational infinite $q$-products and is not known to close in finite rank.

\subsection{Assessment}
\label{nw:assessment}

The external-prime report adds the corpus's first quantitative nonarchimedean analytic
layer, and it is control-clean by construction.  Its permanent content is threefold: the
ray-rigidity/edge-law pair, whose finite cores are now kernel-checked
(\lean{ExternalPrimeNewtonWall}) and whose analytic completions are classical; the exact
valuation ledger, which shows that every polynomial or overconvergent model of the
conditional data pays a quadratic $p$-adic price ($\frac m2N^2-O(N)$) precisely where the
archimedean models converge geometrically; and the sharpened statement of the obstruction
--- sampling is not regularity, and the two completions are decoupled at exactly the
quadratic-versus-geometric scale.  It does not advance the four-exponentials barrier: the
wall excludes local models but produces no equality between completions, and its author is
explicit that transferring the complex completion into a $p$-adic germ without a new
arithmetic compatibility theorem would be circular.  What it contributes to the frontier
of Section~\ref{sec:frontier-update} is a pair of well-posed interfaces (overconvergence
bridge, finite-rank edge cocycle) that are \emph{output-sensitive} in the required sense:
both consume the external prime, and both would, if closed, terminate the conjecture
through the kernel-verified rigidity layer rather than through counting.

\section{The global terminal-prime contraction: the factorial route is closed}
\label{sec:criticalwindow}

A further external report resolves the central open question of the factorial-cocycle
program (Section~\ref{sec:factorialcocycle}) --- and it resolves it \emph{negatively, in
full generality}.  Where the session log had emptied the constructive branch
(Corollary~\ref{log:cor-target-dead}) and the LP layer for the control
(Section~\ref{log:lp-experiment}), the new report closes the entire family in one stroke:
no nonzero integer polynomial with $P(M)=0$ ever makes the terminal factorial cocycle
integral, uniformly in degree, span, height, and sign pattern.

\subsection{The contraction theorem}
\label{cw:contraction}

Recall the objects of Section~\ref{sec:factorialcocycle}: $F_t=(A^t)_{\underline{M^t}}$ is
the terminal falling factorial, $\mathcal F_{P,n}=\prod_jF_{n+j}^{c_j}$ for
$P=\sum_jc_jT^j\in\Z[T]$, and $I_t=(A^t-M^t,A^t]$ is the terminal prime window, whose
relative length exponent $\log2/\log3=0.6309\ldots>7/12$ makes Huxley's theorem
applicable: $I_t$ contains $(1+o(1))M^t$ of logarithmic prime mass.  A prime $p\in I_t$
has $V_p(t):=v_p(F_t)=1$ and $V_p(s)=0$ for $s<t$ (both kernel-verified,
\lean{TerminalFactorialIndependence}), while at higher levels Legendre's interval formula
gives the uniform transport bound
\begin{equation}
 V_p(t+\ell)\le 2q^tM^\ell+2\Bigl(1+\frac\ell t\Bigr),
 \qquad q=\frac MA<1 .
 \label{cw:eq-transport}
\end{equation}

\begin{theorem}[Global terminal-prime contraction]\label{cw:thm-contraction}
Let $(M,A)$ arise from a hypothetical counterexample (so $M\ge2^{14}$ by the
kernel-verified region of Section~\ref{co:finite}).  There is $n_0(M,A)$ such that for
every $n\ge n_0$ and every nonzero $P\in\Z[T]$ with $P(M)=0$,
\[
 \mathcal F_{P,n}\notin\Z ;
\]
indeed for some negative coefficient index $k$ every prime of $I_{n+k}$ divides the reduced
denominator, so $\log\operatorname{den}(\mathcal F_{P,n})\ge(1-o(1))M^{n+k}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Write $c_j^\pm$ for the positive and negative parts and
$S_\pm=\sum_jc_j^\pm M^j$; the single archimedean input $P(M)=0$ is exactly the mass
balance $S_+=S_->0$.  Suppose $\mathcal F_{P,n}\in\Z$.  For each $k$ with $c_k<0$ pick
$p\in I_{n+k}$ (Huxley).  Since $V_p(n+k)=1$, lower levels vanish, and other negative
coefficients only help, integrality forces
\[
 c_k^-\le\sum_{j>k}c_j^+V_p(n+j)
 \le 2q^{n+k}\sum_{j>k}c_j^+M^{j-k}
 +2\sum_{j>k}c_j^+\Bigl(1+\frac{j-k}{n+k}\Bigr)
\]
by \eqref{cw:eq-transport}.  Multiply by $M^k$ and sum over all negative $k$.  The
transported-multiple kernel telescopes against the geometric series $\sum_kq^{n+k}$, and
the prime-power allowance kernel against $\sum_{\ell\ge1}M^{-\ell}$ and
$\sum_{\ell\ge1}\ell M^{-\ell}$:
\[
 S_-\;\le\;\Bigl(\frac{2q^n}{1-q}
 +\frac2{M-1}+\frac{2M}{n(M-1)^2}\Bigr)S_+ .
\]
With $S_+=S_-$ this is $1\le\kappa_n$, and $\kappa_n<0.008$ for $M\ge2^{14}$,
$q\le(2/3)^{14}$ --- a contradiction.  No factor of the degree or of the number of negative
coefficients ever appears: that is the decisive feature of the $M$-weighting.  For the
quantitative form, if the displayed inequality failed for every negative $k$ the same
summation would reproduce $1\le\kappa_n$; hence it fails for some $k$, and the transport
bound is uniform over $p\in I_{n+k}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Negative resolution of factorial feasibility]\label{cw:cor-closed}
Target~\ref{fc:target-linear} is closed unconditionally: for all large $n$ the conjunction
$P_n\ne0$, $P_n(M)=0$, $v_p(\mathcal F_{P_n,n})\ge0$ for every prime $p$ is impossible ---
the span condition, the near-unit condition, the further annihilations
$P_n'(M)=P_n(M^2/A)=0$, and any additional exact mode cancellations are all superfluous.
The binomial-cocycle and no-collision variants close identically.
\end{corollary}

The report also proves the sharp boundary statement \emph{before} the mass balance is
used: if the span satisfies $D_n\le(\log_23-1)\,t_n-h_n$ with $h_n\to\infty$
($t_n=n+k_n$), then the denominator retains
$(-c_{n,k_n})(\Delta_0-o(1))M^{t_n}$ of logarithmic prime mass with
$\Delta_0=1-8q/(\delta_0(1-q))\ge0.9337$, $\delta_0=2-\log_23$ (Brun--Titchmarsh at
relative thickness $\delta_0$; Huxley for the total) --- so an integral cocycle would need
$D_n\ge(\log_23-1)\,t_n-O(1)$, and canonical Hermite stencils at first appear to live in
exactly that bounded strip.  A complete-homogeneous remainder identity
($T^N-H_{\mathcal R}(T^N)=D_{\mathcal R}(T)h_{N-d}(T,\mathcal R)$, all tail coefficients
positive) then shows the stencils have a unique negative coefficient of the wrong
multiplicity, and the contraction supersedes the whole phase diagram anyway.  The
mesoscopic inequality $\tfrac12<\log2/\log3<\tfrac23$ (kernel-verified,
\lean{FactorialCocycle}) silently underlies both windows.

\subsection{Kernel verification of the contraction core}
\label{cw:kernel}

The new module \lean{CriticalWindowContraction} kernel-checks the complete finite skeleton
of Theorem~\ref{cw:thm-contraction} in division-free form:
\begin{itemize}
\item \lean{mass_balance}, \lean{sum_cpos_pos}: the sign-mass identity
$S_+=S_->0$ from $\sum_jc_jM^j=0$, $P\ne0$;
\item \lean{geom_mul_le_one}, \lean{geom_pow_mul_le}, \lean{weighted_geom_pow_mul_le}: the
two summable kernels $\sum_ku^k$ and $\sum_\ell\ell M^{-\ell}$ as exact polynomial
inequalities;
\item \lean{sum_Ioc_swap}: the exchange of window and coefficient summations;
\item \lean{contraction_mul}: the abstract contraction --- for any coefficient vector that
is $M$-balanced, nonzero, and obeys the transport inequalities with parameters
$(\varepsilon,u,\beta,\gamma)$, necessarily
$(1-u)(M-1)(M-2)\le\varepsilon(M-1)(M-2)+\beta(1-u)(M-2)+\gamma(1-u)(M-1)$;
\item \lean{kappa_mul_lt} and \lean{no_balanced_transport}: with the Legendre
parameters $\varepsilon=2q^n$, $\beta=\gamma=2$ the opposite strict inequality holds
whenever $M\ge2^{14}$ and $q\le(2/3)^{14}$, so \emph{no such coefficient vector exists};
\item \lean{exponent_gap_dvd}: the rational-root exponent-gap divisibility
$v^{N-b}\mid a$ used by the report's Hermite-stencil diagnostics.
\end{itemize}
The regime constants are exactly the corpus's kernel-verified zero-free region: a
counterexample has $x\ge14$, hence $M=2^x\ge2^{14}$ and $q=(2/3)^x\le(2/3)^{14}$
(\lean{FiniteCheck16384}).  What remains outside the kernel is the arithmetic instantiation
of the transport inequalities at window primes: $V_p(t)=1$ and vanishing below the window
are already kernel-verified (\lean{TerminalFactorialIndependence}); the Legendre-interval
upper bound \eqref{cw:eq-transport} is elementary and Lean-ready; Huxley's prime-window
theorem stays \statusknown.

\subsection{What survives: inflation-scale hybrids and two-dimensional transport}
\label{cw:survivors}

The contraction has four essential hypotheses: a one-parameter shift family, unit window
multiplicity, geometric transport, and the same-base balance $P(M)=0$.  The report
formulates the surviving interfaces as precise targets.  First, a \emph{two-dimensional
coefficient transport}: archimedean cancellations
$\sum_{ij}c_{ij}M^iA^j=0$ with a two-parameter terminal product, where the transport
kernel becomes a genuinely two-dimensional operator whose $M^iA^j$-weighted norm may or
may not contract --- either outcome is informative (a first finite exploration and a
reduction to a top-cell pivot: Section~\ref{log:two-dim-transport}).  Second, a \emph{coefficient-inflated
Kummer dual}: the contraction shows that any near-feasible vector must carry
exponentially inflated positive tails, which changes the comparison scale for the
structural-prime route --- a carry-free Kummer valuation of size $O(n)$
(\eqref{fc:eq-carry-free}, kernel-verified) multiplied by inflated coefficients is no
longer negligible against a terminal window, so a hybrid dual combining terminal-window
rows with one structural row deserves a fresh Farkas search \emph{without} a span bound.
Third, the report independently adopts the control principle of
Section~\ref{log:control} as a design rule and confirms that the contraction itself is
satisfied by the controls $(2^m,3^m)$: it closes a method, and a proof of the conjecture
must consume the external prime, the least-generator decomposition, or spectrum
saturation.

\emph{Assessment.}  This merge upgrades the corpus in the strongest sense available for a
negative result: a named open target (Target~\ref{fc:target-linear}) becomes a theorem
with a kernel-checked finite core, and two session-log partial closures
(Corollary~\ref{log:cor-target-dead}, the LP experiment) are subsumed and explained ---
the critical constant $\log_23-1$ was never the true obstacle; the $M$-weighted mass
balance was.  The conceptual residue is permanently useful: any auxiliary-integer
construction whose archimedean cancellation shares a base with its coefficient weighting
is subject to the same contraction, so future designs must either decouple the bases
(two-dimensional transport) or exploit coefficient inflation at a structural prime.  The
conjecture itself is untouched --- the closure holds for controls too --- but the search
region left to the factorial idea is now exactly two well-posed interfaces, both
primitive-sensitive only through the standard three channels.

\section{Compact charts, the exponent-two ceiling, and the relation-counting lock}
\label{sec:compactcharts}

A further external report recasts the conjecture as a rational-point counting problem on a
\emph{fixed compact curve}, and audits the strongest counting technology available against
it.  Its foundational layer --- the canonical least generator $\beta$, the conditional
monoid $\Sol=\N_0+\N_0\beta$, and the shell counts
$\#(\Sol\cap[N,N+1))=1+\lfloor(N+1)/\beta\rfloor$ --- is the kernel-verified corpus monoid
(Section~\ref{cd:generator}) and is inherited, not re-proved.  What is new is the geometry
built on top of it and two sharp negative ledgers.

\subsection{Two rational charts and the counting dichotomy}
\label{cc:charts}

The \emph{reciprocal chart} sends $t\mapsto(2^{-t},3^{-t})$, compactifying the power curve
$y=x^{\thetaq}$ into the unit square with a cusp at the origin; solutions land exactly on
the points with unit numerators.  The \emph{logistic (Farey) chart} sends
$t\mapsto\bigl(\tfrac m{m+1},\tfrac n{n+1}\bigr)$ with $(m,n)=(2^t,3^t)$; solutions land
exactly on the unit-gap points, and the two charts are rationally conjugate.  Both closures
are $C^1$ but not $C^2$ at the cusp, with curvature blowing up like $s^{\thetaq-2}$ ---
the entire difficulty of the counting problem concentrates at one non-smooth boundary
point.  On either chart the conjecture becomes a \emph{dichotomy on a single fixed compact
curve}: marked-point counts of height $\le T$ grow like $T/\log3$ under the conjecture and
like $T^2/(2\beta(\log3)^2)$ under failure, so
\[
 \text{Conjecture~\ref{conj:AE}}
 \iff N_{\mathrm{marked}}(T)=o(T^2)
 \iff Z_{\mathrm{unit}}(s)=o(s^{-2})\ (s\downarrow0)
 \iff\#\mathcal S_N=o(N),
\]
where $Z_{\mathrm{unit}}$ is the height zeta function of the marked points and
$\mathcal S_N$ the shell occupancy.  The report assembles an eight-item certificate
package of such equivalences (marked counts on either chart, zeta pole order, shell
occupancy, a one-sided $S$-integral identity, absence of a second diagonal contraction,
two-sided foreign valuations in a rank-two group), together with strictly stronger
sufficient statements: any $o(T^2)$ bound for \emph{all} rational points on the compact
cusp, or $o(N)$ points per shell, proves the conjecture, while six exponentials gives the
unconditional ceiling $O(T^2)$ --- the rank of the full rational-point group
$\Gamma_{\thetaq}$ of $y=x^{\thetaq}$ is at most two, and the count is $O(T^r)$ for rank
$r$.  Subquadratic all-rational counting is therefore \emph{exactly} the four-exponentials
rank drop in counting clothes: it is equivalent to
$\Gamma_{\thetaq}=\langle(2,3)\rangle$, the specialized four-exponentials statement of
Section~\ref{sec:barrier}.  The cleanest member of the package is the \emph{one-point
$S$-integral target}: the conjecture is equivalent to
\[
 \Gamma_{\thetaq}\cap\bigl(\Z[1/2]_{>0}\times\Z[1/3]_{>0}\bigr)
 =\langle(2,3)\rangle,
\]
so it suffices to exclude a \emph{single} noncyclic rational point whose denominators are
concentrated on the structural primes.  All of this consumes the canonical monoid (channel
(ii) of the control principle, Section~\ref{log:control}); the equivalences cannot even be
stated for the integer controls.

\subsection{The integer-area certificate and the marked three-point ledger}
\label{cc:area}

On the Farey chart the marked points have unit-gap coordinates, and the oriented area of
any three of them is a rational number with an \emph{integer numerator} over the six unit
denominators: $\Delta=D/\prod_i(m_i+1)(n_i+1)$ with $D\in\Z$, so three genuinely
non-collinear marked points obey
$|\Delta|\ge\prod_i(m_i+1)^{-1}(n_i+1)^{-1}$, against the exact geometric value
$\Delta=\tfrac12F''(\xi)\prod_{i<j}(X_j-X_i)$ and the spacing identity
$X_j-X_i=(m_j-m_i)/((m_i+1)(m_j+1))$.  The arithmetic ledger is kernel-checked in the new
module \lean{CompactChartArea} (\lean{area_eq_div}, \lean{abs_area_ge},
\lean{coord_diff}); the curvature side is classical.  The certificate is a local exclusion
tool adapted to the compactification --- near the cusp the curvature blow-up compensates
part of the small spacing, so it does not close anything by itself, but it iterates in
higher-order determinants without undoing the chart, and a two-logarithm bound gives
polynomial shell separation ($e^{-N^\rho}$-balls contain at most one marked point).

\subsection{The alternant deficit and the relation-counting lock}
\label{cc:lock}

Two negative ledgers quantify why the two most plausible counting technologies fall short.
First, for plain two-variable exponential alternants
$\det(m_i^{p_j}n_i^{q_j})$ on $D$ marked points of one shell, the report proves a strict
sign-regularity theorem (no such determinant vanishes at distinct curve points), an exact
unit-numerator lower bound, and a Harish-Chandra--Itzykson--Zuber upper bound, whose
combination forces the \emph{shell ledger}: a monomial determinant can exclude $D$ shell
points only if some extra arithmetic divisibility compensates a loss of size
$N\mathfrak d(\Lambda)$, and the minimal monomial deficit obeys
\[
 \delta_D=\tfrac{2^{3/2}}3\sqrt{ab}\,D^{3/2}+O(D).
\]
Every plain monomial-determinant route therefore pays an unavoidable $ND^{3/2}$; the
required compensation is exactly the output-sensitive divisibility that the corpus
identifies as the frontier everywhere else (Sections~\ref{sec:masks},
\ref{bh:localized}).  Second, the report audits the 2026 relation-counting theorem
(small-ball covering for algebraic points near trajectories of polynomial vector fields,
admissible codimension $k<\sqrt n-1$): a planar coefficient obstruction shows no nonzero
polynomial vector field over a number field is tangent to either chart (so the plane is
unusable), while the natural parameter and jet lifts to $n=3$ represent the arithmetic
event by codimension-two varieties, and
\[
 n-2<\sqrt n-1
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 n=2
\]
--- the \emph{coefficient--codimension lock}, kernel-checked in squared form as
\lean{codimension_lock}.  An invariant-prime trichotomy closes the redundant-coordinate
escapes, and even a repaired covering theorem would need its polynomial exponent pushed
below one before the shell-separation lemma could convert coverings into cardinality
bounds.  The route through relation counting is thus locked for structural reasons, not
technical ones; the lock identifies precisely which two improvements (admissible
codimension, covering exponent) would change the situation.

\emph{Assessment.}  The compact-chart frame adds no new unconditional theorem about the
conjecture --- its dichotomies consume the kernel-verified monoid and reprove the
$O(T^2)$ ceiling from six exponentials --- but it is the corpus's cleanest common
coordinate system for the counting family of approaches, and its two ledgers are
permanent: the $D^{3/2}$ alternant deficit quantifies the determinant wall on shells, and
the codimension lock retires the hope that the 2026 relation-counting theorem applies
off the shelf.  The surviving interfaces it leaves are the one-point $S$-integral target
(the sharpest known restatement of the four-exponentials special case) and
determinant-with-divisibility hybrids, which reconnect to the shared-face mask target.
\statusnew{} for the charts, dichotomies, ledgers, and lock analysis; monoid, counting,
and rank inputs \statuslean{}/\statusknown{} as cited.

\section{Synchronized gaps: global gcd rigidity against local congruence cost}
\label{sec:syncgap}

A further external report studies the synchronized gaps
$D_2(r,s)=M^s-2^r$, $D_3(r,s)=A^s-3^r$ of a hypothetical counterexample, with
$\delta_{r,s}=s\beta-r$ and the exact identities $D_2=2^r(2^{\delta}-1)$,
$D_3=3^r(3^{\delta}-1)$: along $r/s\to\beta$ both gaps are simultaneously small relative
to their ambient powers, so their common divisors are the natural place to look for a
contradiction.  The report proves matching global and local theorems whose \emph{gap} is
the finding.

\subsection{Global rigidity and the closed approximation route}
\label{sg:global}

The global theorem is the \emph{full synchronized-gap rigidity}: under a counterexample,
\[
 \log\gcd\bigl(M^s-2^r,\;A^s-3^r\bigr)=o(r+s),
\]
by a Bugeaud--Corvaja--Zannier-type subexponential bound away from the structural primes
\cite{BCZ2003} plus an $O((\log(r+s))^2)$ bound at $2$ and $3$; the two-logarithm input
$|\delta_{r,s}|\ge c\max(r,s)^{-C}$ \cite{BakerWustholz1993} is exactly where
irrationality of $\beta$ enters, so the statement is control-sensitive (for an integer
control the gcd explodes on the diagonal $r=ms$).  Two consequences are permanent.
First, with $M_0=M/2^{v_2(M)}$, $A_0=A/3^{v_3(A)}$ (both $>1$ precisely because
$\beta\notin\Z$), the synchronized quotient
$R_{r,s}=(3^{\delta}-1)/(2^{\delta}-1)\in\Q$ converges to $\log_23$ but has exact height
$\log\operatorname{height}(R_{r,s})=s\log(M_0A_0)+o(s)$: the gcd is too small to cancel
the primitive exponential mass, so
\[
 \frac{-\log|R_{r,s}-\log_23|}{\log\operatorname{height}(R_{r,s})}\longrightarrow0 .
\]
The \emph{rational-approximation route is quantitatively closed}: these approximants have
logarithmic quality relative to height, and no improvement of the irrationality measure
of $\log_23$ can rescue them --- a closed door, recorded in the ledger next to the
factorial closure of Section~\ref{sec:criticalwindow}.

\subsection{The local congruence lattices and the square-root tax}
\label{sg:local}

The local theorem is an exact Smith-index law for the principal-unit congruence lattices
$\Lambda_p(k)=\{(r,s):M^s\equiv2^r,\ A^s\equiv3^r\pmod{p^{k+1}}\text{ on units}\}$: with
Smith invariants $p^{\alpha_p}\mid p^{\gamma_p}$ of the local logarithm matrix $B_p$,
\[
 [\Z^2:\Lambda_p(k)]=p^{(k-\alpha_p)_++(k-\gamma_p)_+},
\]
stably $p^{2k-\tau_p}$; the mod-$p$ shadow is the Fermat-quotient determinant
$\det B_p\equiv q_p(M)q_p(3)-q_p(A)q_p(2)\pmod p$, whose kernel-verified form the corpus
already holds (\lean{FermatQuotientDeterminant}, Section~\ref{fp:fermat}); the
finite-place product law multiplies the indices, giving $I=G^2/E$ where $G$ is the
enforced principal-unit precision and $E=\prod p^{\tau_p}$ the aggregate determinant
credit.  Against this, a \emph{constrained Dirichlet theorem} (Minkowski applied to the
sheared lattice, Lean-ready) finds $(r,s)\in\Lambda$ with $0<s\le H$ and
$|s\beta-r|\le(1+\eta)I/H$: any symmetric convex-body use of finite-index information
conserves the product $H\cdot|s\beta-r|\asymp I$.  Generic local precision therefore
costs a \emph{square} ($I=G^2$): the corpus's one-prime covolume conservation law
(\lean{RestrictedDenominatorDirichlet}) is exactly the $|S|=1$ case of this tax.

\subsection{The mismatch, the phase diagram, and the wedge}
\label{sg:mismatch}

The synthesis is a precise mismatch: the global theorem forbids forced moduli
$N=\exp(cH)$ at exponent height $H$, while generic local lifting produces only $N$
polynomial in $H$ because the congruence lattice has index $\approx N^2$.  Between
polynomial and exponential lies the entire gap; a proof must change the local cost
\emph{exponent}, not constants.  The report's phase diagram makes the necessary
structural shift explicit --- essentially rank-one behavior at many places
simultaneously ($I\approx G$), plus cross-prime coherence of the short directions ---
and organizes the missing principle adelically: the counterexample is the vanishing of
the archimedean wedge $(\log2,\log3)\wedge(\log M,\log A)$, the local data are the
finite-place wedges $-p^2\det B_p$, and there is no product formula tying them together
because each is bilinear in logarithms rather than a valuation of one algebraic number.
Its five targets (adelic defect transfer; projective coherence of rank-one places; a
second-order Fermat law; an auxiliary wedge with a product formula; the gcd
contrapositive) are all forms of one question --- transfer the archimedean rank loss to
aggregate finite-place rank loss --- which is the corpus's coupling problem
(Sections~\ref{ai:series}, \ref{nw:wall}) in adelic form.  \emph{Assessment}: nothing
moves the four-exponentials barrier; the durable additions are the closed approximation
route, the exact square-cost benchmark that any lattice-based strategy must beat, and
the cleanest adelic statement so far of what a decisive principle must do.  \statusnew{}
throughout; BCZ/Baker inputs \statusknown; mod-$p$ shadow and one-prime covolume law
already \statuslean{} in the corpus.

\section{Near-curve certificates: orbit pressure against fewnomial budgets}
\label{sec:nearcurve}

A further external report builds a computational front end for the conjecture from three
elementary components, then audits the 2026 near-curve algorithm against it.

\subsection{Pressure, locking, and budgets}
\label{nc:budgets}

\emph{Orbit pressure}: a counterexample $x$ places at least $\lceil(L+1)/x\rceil$ integer
points of $Y=X^{\theta}$ ($\theta=\log_23$) in every dyadic block $2^L\le X<2^{L+1}$ ---
linearly many per block, by the conditional monoid.  \emph{Subunit locking}: if
$P\in\Z[X,Y]$ satisfies $\sup_{z\in[1,2]}|P(2^Lz,3^Lz^{\theta})|<1$, every integer curve
point of the block is a zero of $P$ (an integer of modulus $<1$ vanishes).
\emph{Fewnomial budget}: for irrational $\theta$ the monomials $X^iY^j$ restrict to the
curve as $X^{i+j\theta}$ with pairwise distinct exponents, a Chebyshev system, so a
nonzero $P$ with support size $T(P)$ has at most $T(P)-1$ zeros on the curve.  Combining
the three: every global subunit certificate for block $L$ has
$T(P_L)\ge\lceil(L+1)/x\rceil+1$, hence degree $d_L\gg\sqrt{L/x}$, and every certified
cover of capacity $\mathrm{Cap}_L$ has $\mathrm{Cap}_L\ge\lceil(L+1)/x\rceil$.
Contrapositively --- and this is the report's central sufficient criterion --- exhibiting
certified covers with $\mathrm{Cap}_L=o(L)$ along an unbounded block sequence
\emph{proves} the conjecture.  Two conditioning barriers calibrate the search: no fixed
support is subunit for arbitrarily large $L$ (finite support libraries become extinct
effectively), and an unconditional near-critical degree barrier $L\le Cd^2\log(d+1)$
shows certificates cannot be cheap --- the hunt lives in the narrow corridor
$d\asymp\sqrt L$ up to logarithms.  The report specializes the Brisebarre--Hanrot
near-curve algorithm \cite{BrisebarreHanrot2026} into a proof-oriented certificate: a
single verified short-vector inequality for the rounded Chebyshev--Bernstein matrix
implies the uniform subunit bound, for dense or arbitrary sparse supports, giving a
machine-checkable route (Priority~A of its program) whose success criterion is a proven
sufficient condition.  The dense asymptotics do not yet meet the capacity criterion; the
open question is whether near-resonant sparse supports do.

\subsection{The toric no-go and the Carlitz model}
\label{nc:toric}

Why is a certificate search needed at all, rather than an operator argument?  The report
isolates the obstruction: the diagonal scaling $(X,Y)\mapsto(2X,3Y)$ admits only
\emph{monomial} polynomial semi-invariants --- $P(2X,3Y)=cP(X,Y)$ forces a single
monomial, since the eigenvalues $2^i3^j$ are pairwise distinct.  The coefficientwise
kernel core is verified in the new module \lean{ToricMonomialRigidity}
(\lean{toric_eigen_support_unique}, on top of the kernel-verified injectivity of
$(i,j)\mapsto2^i3^j$): geometric scaling never creates a coupled finite-rank system, so
any relation-lifting theorem must introduce a semilinear or inhomogeneous action --- the
same conclusion as the finite-rank cocycle target of Section~\ref{nw:qdiff}, reached
operator-theoretically.  As a model for what the missing rigidity would look like, the
report assembles the Carlitz-module picture: in positive characteristic the full relation
ideal of Carlitz logarithms is generated by $k$-linear relations
\cite{Papanikolas2008}, the two-direction multiplier rigidity ($c\lambda_1,c\lambda_2$
both Carlitz logarithms forces $c\in k$) is a theorem, and Estienne's 2026 Mahler-method
proof \cite{Estienne2026} shows the rigidity can be reached through functional equations
alone; the exact characteristic-zero analogue (its ``quadratic target'') would settle
the conjecture.  The differential lift of fixed-endpoint logarithm germs has the right
relation ideal but specializes incorrectly --- a defect the report exhibits already at
integral controls, and its route triage includes an exact mod-$7$ counterexample to
same-prime congruence transfer at the control $x=2$, applying the control principle of
Section~\ref{log:control} as a falsification tool.  Harrison's bounds on additive
relations in irrational powers \cite{Harrison2026} bound the additive energy of the
smooth grid and the exponential boundary fiber, quantifying additive isolation
(Section~\ref{ai:isolation}) at grid scale.  \emph{Assessment}: the durable additions
are the certified-search interface with its proven sufficiency threshold
$\mathrm{Cap}_L=o(L)$ --- the corpus's first falsifiable-by-computation route --- and
the toric no-go that explains, in operator language, why every naive lift has failed.
\statusnew{} throughout; near-curve algorithm, Carlitz rigidity, and additive-energy
inputs \statusknown; toric core \statuslean.

\section{Chebyshev trap lattices and the unconditional block bound}
\label{sec:blockbound}

A further external report develops the near-curve certificate frame of
Section~\ref{sec:nearcurve} into a quantitative theory and extracts from it the corpus's
first \emph{unconditional} counting theorem about the solution set itself.

\subsection{Rank--codimension traps and the Chebyshev lattice}
\label{bb:traps}

Strict total positivity of exponential systems ($\det(e^{\lambda_jt_i})>0$ for increasing
nodes and frequencies) upgrades the fewnomial budget of Section~\ref{nc:budgets} from one
polynomial to a family: $r$ linearly independent integer polynomials supported on a
common $q$-element support, all of absolute value $<1$ on a curve segment, leave at most
$q-r$ integer points on that segment (\emph{rank--codimension trap}); certified covers of
$[0,1]$ with total defect $o(H)$ for infinitely many $H$ would prove the conjecture,
matching the capacity criterion of Section~\ref{nc:budgets}.  Short trap polynomials are
produced from a \emph{Chebyshev lattice}: coefficient rows from Bernstein-ellipse
expansions of $z\mapsto P(2^{H+z},3^{H+z})$ on the block, diagonal tail rows to control
truncation, covolume bounded through Cauchy--Binet by
\[
 \log\Delta\le(H+R(\rho))\sum_{e\in E}\lambda_e-\frac{q(q-1)}2\log\rho+O(q\log q)
\]
uniformly in the support (diagonal tail rows never weaken the Chebyshev decay), and
Minkowski producing $r$ independent short vectors at fixed $r$.  The optimal supports are
weighted simplices (smallest frequency sums), and optimizing the ellipse against the
simplex yields the report's headline.

\subsection{The unconditional block bound}
\label{bb:theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Unconditional integer-point bound in a logarithmic unit block]
\label{bb:thm-block}
With $I(H):=\#\{x\in[H,H+1):2^x\in\Z,\ 3^x\in\Z\}$,
\[
 \limsup_{H\to\infty}I(H)\,\frac{(\log H)^2}{H^2}
 \le\frac{32\log2\log3}{9}=2.70755559\ldots,
\]
via supports of size $(32\log2\log3/9+\varepsilon)H^2/(\log H)^2$ (outer frequency scale
$L=(8ab/3)H/\log H$, ellipse $\rho=3L/(2ab)$, $a=\log2$, $b=\log3$); the same argument
gives $32\log u\log v/9$ for any multiplicatively independent bases $u,v>1$.
\end{theorem}

The inputs are only multiplicative independence, Bernstein--Chebyshev decay,
Cauchy--Binet, Minkowski, and total positivity --- no conditional monoid.  This is a
\emph{pointwise} per-block bound, complementing the cumulative $O(T^2)$ ceiling of six
exponentials (Section~\ref{cc:charts}), which controls only block averages; under a
counterexample the true count is $I(H)=H/\beta+O(1)$, so the theorem is a
$H/(\log H)^2$-factor short of a contradiction --- the first unconditional statement in
the corpus to come within a quantified polynomial factor of the conjecture.
\statusnew{}; the constant checks numerically and the mechanism is elementary throughout.

\subsection{The two ceilings: rank tax and the conservation law}
\label{bb:ceilings}

The report then audits, with unusual honesty, why its own mechanism stops there.  The
macroscopic-window optimization has exact constant
$\kappa_*=\tfrac{64\log2\log3}9\cosh(t_0)/t_0^2=5.08726658\ldots$ with $t_0\tanh t_0=2$,
and a \emph{closing} trap must certify a short-vector rank fraction
$R_H/q>0.98596$ --- a threshold computed directly from the corpus's kernel-verified
zero-free region $\beta\ge14$ (Section~\ref{co:finite}; the software exclusion
$\beta>27$ raises it to $0.99272$).  Against this stand two proved ceilings.  The
\emph{rank-tax inequality} shows the covolume-plus-Minkowski mechanism carries a
$(r-1)q\log\rho$ penalty, so it cannot certify any rank fraction beyond $1/2$ --- volume
is not spectrum, and near-full short rank is a shape statement requiring genuine
successive-minima or transference input.  And a \emph{conservation law}: trading support
size against rank fraction leaves the leading block constant invariant at $32ab/9$ ---
within the volume method, fixed-rank and fractional-rank optimization are exactly
equally strong.  The surviving routes are therefore structural: parametric geometry of
numbers for the trap lattices (switch-density as a finite combinatorial target), the
compound-matrix spectrum of the $H$-independent Bessel core ($A=D_{\mathrm{row}}
K_N(E)D_H$ with $K_{n,e}=I_n(\lambda_e/2)$, all $H$-dependence diagonal), and arithmetic
rows tied to a primitive pair --- the only channel that could be control-sensitive.

\subsection{Dilation rigidity and the certificate program}
\label{bb:dilation}

Two supporting layers round out the framework.  First, \emph{consecutive-dilation
rigidity}: a $q$-monomial polynomial vanishing at $q$ consecutive diagonal dilations
$(2^nX,3^nY)$ of one positive point is identically zero, so no fixed sparse trap retires
a persistent normalized orbit point --- traps must move with the block.  The finite core
is kernel-checked in the new module \lean{ConsecutiveDilationRigidity}
